en: Now begins the *Bodhāyana-Gṛhya-Śeṣa-Sūtra*.
Now, therefore, we shall explain that which remains to be said regarding the seven *pākayajñas*, as has been stated.

(1) The preparation of the purifiers (*pavitra*), the consecration of the sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇī*), the bringing forward of the *praṇītā* water, and the wiping of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are performed silently, as in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. (2)

Then, having strewn grass around the fire, having spread *darbha* grass in the seat of the *brahmán* to the south of the fire, and having spread *darbha* grass with tips pointing eastward to the north of the fire, he places the vessels upon them. Having made the vessels face upward with water purified silently, and having loosened the fuel-bundle, he sprinkles it three times with all [the waters]. He seats a *brāhmaṇa* on the *darbha* grass to the south, silently, as in the New and Full Moon sacrifices. (3) The enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are one cubit (*aratni*) long, or they may be fresh and possessed of bark. (4) There are twenty-one pieces of wood for the fuel-bundle (*idhma*), each a span (*prādeśa*) long; thus it is explained in the *Brāhmaṇa*. (5)
Now, if he lays down the *śamyās*, they are made of *śamī* wood or fashioned like *śamyās*, measuring one cubit (*aratni*) in length.
(6) Then, having anointed the fuel-wood (*idhma*), he sets aside a *parisamit* stick.

(7) Having placed it on the fire with the utterance of "svāhā" and having poured the two libations (*āghāra*), he offers the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) facing each other and extending outwards. (8)

Having performed the well-known rite beginning with the mouth of the fire, he spreads an underlayer of ghee in the *darvī* spoon with the *sruva* ladle, cuts a portion from the eastern half [of the sacrificial cake], then cuts a portion from the western half, pours ghee over it, and anoints the place from which the portion was cut.

(9) If he is one who offers five portions (*pañcāvattin*), having spread an underlayer of ghee in the *darvī* spoon, he cuts a portion from the middle, then from the eastern half, and then from the western half; he pours ghee over it and anoints the place from which the portion was cut.
(10) Having wiped the *sruva* ladle, and having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*) for the respective deity, he makes the offering with the offering verse (*yājyā*). (11)
Then, having spread an under-layer of ghee once, he cuts a portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt* from the northern half; he pours ghee over it twice and does not re-anoint the offering.
(12) Having placed it within the enclosing sticks, he offers the oblations of clarified butter according to the traditional injunctions.
(13) In cases where no specific mantras are prescribed, [he uses] the *vyāhṛtis*. (14)

Then, taking the portion for the Sviṣṭakṛt, he offers it in the eastern part of the northern half, or rather in the eastern part [of the entire fire]; he then throws the stirring-stick (mekṣaṇa) after it into the fire.
15. Then he pours the remnants of the offering over it. 16. Having poured water into the ladle, he pours the wash-water inside the enclosing sticks. 17.

Having washed the *sruk* ladle, heated it, and filled it with water, he pours it out outside the enclosing sticks. 18. Then, having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, he offers the *jaya* oblations with the formula: "Consciousness, svāhā! and so forth. 19.

Having offered thirteen spoonfuls (*sruva-āhuti*), he offers the *abhyātāna* oblations with the formula: "Agni is the overlord of beings; may he protect me in this sacred knowledge (*brahman*), in this domain (*kṣatra*), in this blessing, in this office, in this rite, in this invocation of the gods, svāhā! 20.

Having offered seventeen oblations with the *sruva* ladle, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite: "O fathers, grandfathers, those further back and those nearer, our ancestors and their ancestors—protect us here! (21) Then he offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations: "The Gandharva Agni, victorious through truth, whose abode is truth—may he protect this spiritual power (*brahman*) and this ruling power (*kṣatra*). To him, svāhā! His Apsarases, the plants named Ūrj—may they protect this spiritual power and this ruling power. To them, svāhā!
(22) In this very same manner, he proceeds until the end of the section, except for the two verses beginning with "O Lord of the world" and "O Lord of the world, do thou... (23).
Then he offers the *amātya* oblations, verse by verse, from the end of the section beginning with "Whatever offense we have committed against the gods" (*yad devā devaheḍanam*) up to its conclusion.

(24) Then he offers the oblation to Prajāpati with the verse: "O Prajāpati, none other than you [has encompassed these creatures]" (*prajāpate na tvadetāny anyaḥ*). (25) Then he offers the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with the verse: "Whatever in this rite... (*yad asya karmaṇo*). (26)
27. He anoints the enclosing sticks with the *sruva* ladle.

28. Then, having smeared the ground around the altar, having cut a blade of sacrificial grass from the *barhis* and placed it in the *ājya* pot like the *prastara*, having thrown a blade of grass into the fire silently, and having removed the *śamyā* pegs, he throws the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) into the fire.
29. Having thrown the middle enclosing stick into the fire, he then places the other two together.
Then he makes an oblation over them with the residue of the offerings (saṃsrāva). 30.

Then, having placed the remains of the oblations in front of the fire according to the traditional injunctions, he should dispose of the remainder, except for the portion remaining from the marriage rite. 31. In the same manner, he sprinkles water around the fire; he joins the ends of the mantras together with the words: "Thou hast assented," and "Thou hast granted permission. 32.
Then he pours out [the water] from the *praṇītā* vessels toward the quarters silently, as in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice.
(33) Having dismissed the Brahman priest, he eats the remainder with the formulas: "Thou art life; thou art all-life.
(34) Having eaten and sipped water, he touches his belly with the two verses: "That from which, O Indra, we fear... and "The giver of well-being, the lord of the people... (35)
One should give the remainder, having been sprinkled with clarified butter, to a Brāhmaṇa.

(36) The wife does not partake of the sacrificial oblations, except for the remnants of those poured together as *abhisampāta* offerings and the remainder of the *piṇḍa* offerings; nor indeed does she eat the remains of what was offered to the deities, except for the *brahmaudana*.
(37) Thus ends the first chapter of the first book in the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣa Sūtra.
Now begins the second chapter of the first book.
The fire [consecrated] by the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and others is called the *aupāsana*.
(1) It must be maintained perpetually at the time of marriage or at the time of inheritance. (2)
When [the fire] has gone out, the penance is well known.

(3) In that [fire], the divine rites belonging to the Pākayajña categories are performed. (4) The procedure beginning with the *upasthāna* (reverential salutation) is the same, except for the consecration of offspring (*prajāsamskāra*). (5)

For the sake of consecrating the offspring, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in another clean place and scratch it: first toward the east in the middle, then likewise to the south, then likewise to the north; from the middle, then toward the north, then likewise to the west, and then likewise to the east. (6) Having brought a portion from the *aupāsana* fire with the syllable *praṇava* and established it with the *vyāhṛtis*, or else having brought it from the house of a learned *śrotriya*. (7) Having thus kindled the *aupāsana* fire, and having taken the fire into oneself with the two verses, "I take Agni within me first" and "The Agni who is ours, O fathers," the procedure from the worship (*upasthāna*) onwards is the same up to the placing of the vessels (*pātrasādana*). (8)

Now, what indeed is the sequence for setting down the sacrificial vessels? He places them in pairs, turned downwards, neither deficient nor redundant: the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the *sruva* ladle, the *juhū* ladle, the *darvī* spoon, the vessel for the *praṇītā* water, the vessel for the *prokṣaṇī* water, the vessel for the *caru* oblation, the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), the fuel and sacrificial grass (*idhmabarhis*), and the wood-chips for trimming the fuel; and likewise other items in pairs. (9) The ritual procedure is the same up to the wiping of the *sruk* ladles. (10) Having wiped the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and having taken four portions of clarified butter into the *sruk*, he offers the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the verse: "Seven are thy kindling-sticks, O Agni, seven thy tongues... (11)
The bringing forward of the fire from the *aupāsana* hearth is prescribed. 12. Now, from the wrapping of the sacrificial grass onwards, the procedure is the same.

13. Furthermore, they cite this: "One must not perform the sacrifice with unprepared sprinkling-water, nor with unpurified vessels, nor with *sruk* and *sruva* ladles that have not been cleansed, nor with clarified butter that has not been heated over the fire or is already cooked; for if one were to proceed in such a manner, the Yātudhānas, Asuras, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas would seize the sacrifice. 14.
Thus ends the second chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhya-śeṣa-sūtra.
Now begins the third chapter in the first book.
Now, therefore, we shall explain that which has not been previously mentioned. 1.

Having swept around [the fire], sprinkled water around it, strewn grass around it, poured water around it, added fuel, and adorned it, he offers the oblations as prescribed. At the beginning and the end, there are oblations of clarified butter with the *vyāhṛtis*. The laying down of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the bringing forward of the *praṇītā* water, and the seating of the *brahmán* priest do not exist; or rather, they do exist. Having recited the preceding mantras in a whisper, he says "Release! loudly; thus it is understood that he prepares everything in this very manner.

(2) Regarding the forms of the *pākayajña* sacrifices, the standing oblation (*tiṣṭhaddhoma*) does not exist; and it is understood from another [text] that all those forms of the *pākayajña* are performed except for the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*). (3)

Then, at the conclusion [of the sacrifice], there is sprinkling around at the beginning and the end, as previously described. It is known: "One should not offer into a fire that lacks fuel; for if one were to offer into a fire that lacks fuel, it would be as if one were to give food to one who has no tongue. Therefore, one must offer only into a fire that possesses fuel.
When no specific instruction is given, one should offer after adding fuel; when no specific instruction is given, one should offer only after having taken [the portion].

With the stirring-ladle (*mekṣaṇa*), he offers to the deity, saying: "Svāhā to such-and-such; Svāhā to such-and-such. (7) Now they also quote: "Herbs, groats, flowers, wood, roots, fruits, and grass—these may be offered with the hand; nothing else, unless there is a specific injunction. (8) As in the case of herbs and so forth, the offering of the *bali* oblation, the giving of the remnants of the sacrifice, and the consumption [of the remains] are likewise performed until the sprinkling around [the fire]. The offering of the residue in the head and the circumambulation are likewise performed until the initiation (*upanayana*). (9)
For each purpose, he leads forward the fire while reciting the Sāvitrī verse.
(11) When the ritual action has been completed, it becomes ordinary.
(12) Now, if [the fire] is on the utkara mound, the rites beginning with the worship of the fire are the same; the full-offering (pūrṇāhuti) is the same from this point onward. (13)
Thus ends the third chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the fourth chapter in the first book:
"Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). 1.

Having removed sand four *aṅgulas* deep from the east, he prepares a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) measuring five *aṅgulas* in height at the west, with a specific increase of one *aṅgula* in height toward the south and a decrease of one *aṅgula* in height toward the north; it is five *prasthas* of pure, white, dry sand, square, measuring one *aratni*, and sloping toward the east.

(2) Not with a clod of earth, not with wood, not with pebbles, and not with his fingernails. By using wood there would be disease; by a clod of earth, the destruction of the family; by pebbles, the loss of sons; and by fingernails, the destruction of kinsmen. (3)

Therefore, having grasped [the earth] with a fragment of gold, silver, or copper, or with rice or barley, or with *darbha* grass, using both the thumb and the ring finger (*mahānāmni*), one should draw a continuous, straight line toward the east through its middle. "To which deity does it belong? What is its mantra? "It belongs to Brahman; 'Brahma jajñānam' (The Brahman was born). 4. To the south of that, one should draw a continuous, straight line toward the east. "To which deity does it belong? What is its mantra? "It belongs to Yama; 'Nāke suparṇam' (The fair-winged bird in the vault of heaven). 5.

To the north of that, he should draw a continuous, straight line toward the east. "What is its deity? What is its mantra? "Soma is its deity; 'May you swell, may [the waters] come together unto you' is its mantra.
(6) In the middle of that, he should draw a continuous, straight line toward the north. "What is its deity? What is its mantra? "Rudra is its deity; 'The Rudra who is in the fire' is its mantra.
(7) To the west of that, he should draw a continuous, straight line toward the north. "What is its deity? What is its mantra? "Viṣṇu is its deity; 'This Viṣṇu strode forth' is its mantra. (8)

To the east of that [fire], one should draw a continuous, straight line directed toward the north. "Of what deity? With what mantra? [He asks. "It has Indra as its deity; it is from the mantra *indraṃ viśvā avīvṛdhan* (All have magnified Indra) that the rule for the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) follows.

(9) "There is no [fault] if there is no potsherd, no smoke, no flame, no crackling, and no drooping mouth, provided one avoids a drop that has fallen or one that has ignited the mouth," says the venerable Bodhāyana, reciting: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan—*bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar om*. (10)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣa-sūtra. Now begins the fifth chapter in the first book. Now, therefore, we shall explain the defects regarding the sand. 1.
One should avoid ground containing ashes, hair, chaff, potsherds, gravel, grass, bones, or ants, as well as moist sand.

(2) The venerable Bodhāyana has declared that by means of ashes there is the ruin of the sacrificer; by hair, the death of a wife; by chaff, the loss of sons; by potsherds, the destruction of wealth; by gravel, separation from kinsmen; by grass, the failure of undertakings; by bones, the ruin of the village; by ants, the ruin of the kingdom; and by moist sand, there arises the fear of disease.
(3) Thus ends the fifth chapter of the first book in the Bodhāyana Gṛhya-śeṣa-sūtra.
Now begins the sixth chapter of the first book.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for strewing the sacrificial grass (paristaraṇa). 1.

One should cut the roots of *darbha* grass that have unbroken tips, are not cut by fingernails, are not discolored, are free from disease, and whose roots are not burnt; they should be more than four finger-breadths long and equal in length to the hand. Having anointed them with clarified butter, or having touched them with clarified butter, or having wiped them with water, one should strew them around: first to the east with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I strew thee"; then to the south with the *vyāhṛtis*; then to the west with [the verse] "Up from the darkness" (*ud vayaṃ tamasas pari*); and then to the north with "O Agni, come hither" (*agna āyāhi*).

Having seated the Brahman priest to the south of the fire on the seat of the Brahman with the words, "For the enjoyment," and having prepared his seat to the north of the fire for the *praṇītā* waters with the formula, "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ; O Brahman, you are the Brahman; homage to you, O Brahman; [homage] to the Brahman," and [having prepared the seat] for Varuṇa with the words, "You are Varuṇa, whose vow is firm; you belong to Varuṇa"—this procedure for the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*) has been explained. Thus ends the sixth chapter in the first book of the *Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra* of Bodhāyana.

Now begins the seventh chapter of the first book. For all *darvihoma* offerings, there are one hundred and eight *darbha* blades; two as hand-purifiers (*pavitra*), two for the seat, and sixteen for the surrounding strewing (*paristaraṇa*) with tips pointing east and north. To the south, seventeen with tips pointing east; behind, eighteen with tips pointing north; to the north, seventeen with tips pointing east. There are five vessels, seventeen [blades] for the Brahman’s seat, two for the *praṇītā* water-vessel, two each for the clarified butter and the purifiers, two for lighting the fire, two at the tips of the *darbha*, two for the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*), and four for the sweeping (*saṃmārjana*). Thus it is said. 1.

Having made three enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) measuring one *aratni* (elbow-length) and six *aṅgulas*, [one should prepare the following]: the middle finger, the ring finger, and the little finger [are used for measurement]; the thickest is the middle [stick], the medium is the thinnest, and the longest is on the south side, while the shortest is on the north side. There are eighteen sacrificial wood pieces (*kāṣṭha*) each the size of a thumb-joint. The *pavitra* strainer is one span (*prādeśa*) long, made from two young blades of *darbha* grass. The *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling-vessel and the *ājyasthālī* ghee-pot are each the size of a thumb-joint. The vessel for carrying forward the *praṇītā* water is filled with a quarter of a *prastha*, while the *praṇītāpraṇayana* itself is filled with half a *prastha*.

The *carusthālī* (grain-pot) should be one *prastha* in capacity; the measure of the *avadāna* (portion for offering) is four finger-breadths, or the size of a thumb-joint. The measure of the *darvī* (ladle) is twenty-one thumb-breadths, with a height of two thumb-breadths and a cavity of five thumb-breadths. Likewise, the *sruk* (spoon) is one span (*prādeśa*) high, or four finger-breadths; it is slightly raised on the right side. The *mekṣaṇa* (stirring-stick) is the same measure as the *homadarvī*. Thus spoke Baudhāyana. Thus ends the seventh chapter of the first book in the *Baudhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣa*. Now begins the eighth chapter of the first book.

Now, having prepared on a pure and level spot a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide, smeared with cow-dung, raised one span or four finger-breadths high, it should be slightly elevated toward the south. (1) [Question: For what purpose is it sloping toward the east? For what purpose is it sloping toward the north? [Answer: One who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) [should have it] sloping toward the east; one who desires food (*annādya*) [should have it] sloping toward the north; one who desires offspring (*prajā*) [should have it] sloping toward the northeast; one who desires stability (*pratiṣṭhā*) [should have it] level. (2)

The smearing belongs to the Viśvedevas; the lifting up belongs to the Nākasads; the sprinkling belongs to the Pitṛs; the sand belongs to the Sindhu; the scraping belongs to Yama; the throwing away belongs to Rudra; the touching belongs to Varuṇa; the preparation of the fire-places belongs to Agni; the spreading [of the fires] belongs to Viṣṇu; the ritual action belongs to Vāyu; the strewing of darbha grass belongs to Gāyatrī; the butter-pot, the *sruva*-ladle, and the *juhū*-ladle belong to the Earth; the *sruk*-ladle belongs to Soma; the clarified butter belongs to the Vasus; the strainer belongs to Viṣṇu; and the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) belongs to Viṣṇu.

The stirring-stick has Prajāpati as its deity; the cleansing-brush has Agni as its deity; the ritual grass-bundle has Rudra as its deity; the water-pot has Prajāpati as its deity; the water has the Waters as its deity; the *praṇītā* water has Varuṇa as its deity; the stone has Mahendra as its deity; the garment has Soma as its deity; the performer has Bṛhaspati as his deity; the smoke has the Guest as its deity; the fuel has Agni as its deity; the middle enclosing-stick has the Sacrificer as its deity; the southern enclosing-stick has Indra as its deity; the northern enclosing-stick has Varuṇa as its deity; and the two upright fuel-sticks have the Upper Regions as their deity.

The sun is the deity of the [first] offering; Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, and Īśāna are the eight deities of the directions; the fan has Vāyu as its deity; the scent has the Aśvins as its deity; the flower has the Gandharvas as its deity; the incense has Indra as its deity; the lamp has Bhanu (the Sun) as its deity; the *prayāja* and *anūyāja* offerings have the Seasons (*ṛtu*) as their deities; the cooked food has the Principal Deity (*pradhānadevatā*) as its deity; the subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*) have as their deities those indicated by their respective characteristics (*yathāliṅga*); wherever there is a prescription of a mantra for an oblation, there the deity is that indicated by its characteristic; the assembly (*pariṣad*) has Brahmā as its deity; and the members of the assembly (*sadasyas*) [have the same].

For others not mentioned, [the offering] belongs to all the deities; for those whose deity is not specified, it belongs to Prajāpati. He who, having ascertained the deity of a sacrifice through the mantra or the ritual action, offers the oblation, attains prosperity, longevity, health, and heaven. (3) A fire-sacrifice lacking the sacred fire brings drought; one lacking the mantra brings ruin to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); one lacking clarified butter (*ājya*) destroys the family; and one lacking the correct tone (*svara*) ruins the wives. (4) One lacking the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) ruins the sacrificer; one lacking food ruins the kingdom; and one lacking everything ruins the members of the assembly (*sadasya*). There is no enemy equal to a sacrifice [when performed incorrectly]. (5)
Therefore, one who desires prosperity should perform some ritual with every effort; one should perform everything in its entirety, accompanied by abundance and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
(6) Thus has been declared by the sages who know the truth, according to the injunctions of the seers, this daily Vedic rite (vedāhnika) and fire-oblation (homa), which is honored in all the worlds.
(7) "It is honored in all the worlds"—thus said the venerable Bodhāyana. (8)
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhya-śeṣa-sūtra.
Now begins the ninth chapter in the first book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the deities of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*). May Agni be pleased at the wedding; may Agni, Sūrya, and Prajāpati be pleased at the *aupāsana* (domestic fire) rite; on the fifth day, Udumbara; on the tenth day, the *citrya* offerings; for the *sthālīpāka*, Agni; for the *garbhādhāna*, Brahmā; for the *puṃsavana*, Prajāpati; for the *sīmanta*, Dhātṛ; for the *bali*, Savitṛ; for the *jātakarman*, Mṛtyu; for the *nāmakaraṇa*, Savitṛ; at its conclusion, Prajāpati; for the *upaniṣkrāmaṇa*, Savitṛ; at its conclusion, the *citrya* offerings.

Savitṛ is the deity for the *annaprāśana* (first feeding of solid food) and for the *caula* (tonsure) of the long-haired child; Prajāpati at its conclusion; Indra for the *upanayana* (initiation); Śraddhā and Medhā at its conclusion; Suśravas for the *visarga* (concluding rite); Agni for the re-initiation (*punarupanayana*). Now, if the religious student (*brahmacārī*) should act as if violating his vow, Savitṛ is the deity for the *adhyāya-homa* (study-vow offering). For the *samāvartana* (return home), Śrī or Indra is the deity. For the *śūlagava* (sacrifice of the spit-ox), Īśāna is the deity. For the *pratyavarohaṇa* (descent from the high bed), Savitṛ is the deity. For the *upākarma* (commencement of study) and the vows, Savitṛ is the deity. For the *vāstuhoma* (offering for the house-site), Vāstoṣpati is the deity; Prajāpati at its conclusion.

At the conclusion of the *adbhutahoma*, Prajāpati; at the end of the *āyuṣyahoma*, Agni Āyuṣmān; at the *nakṣatrahoma*, that which has been stated regarding the *nakṣatreṣṭis*; at the eighth [offering] of the evening, Īśāna; at the *āgrayaṇahoma*, the deities of the *āgrayaṇa*; at the *sarpabali*, the serpents; "May the planets, with Āditya at their head, be pleased"; and at the conclusion of the *ekoddiṣṭa*, Prajāpati. For tanks and similar works, Varuṇa is the deity; for the *yakṣibali*, the Yakṣīs; for the *gṛhaśāntihoma*, the nine planets beginning with Āditya; and for the *tantrahoma* pertaining to the *garbhādhāna* and other rites, Brahmā and the others.

"For the other *homa*s, the deity of the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* [is invoked] with the formula: 'May such-and-such a deity be pleased (*prīyatām*). At the end of a period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), at the end of a period of death-impurity (*pretaka*), and at the first appearance of a woman's menses (*udakyā*), Prajāpati is the deity. For the *kūśmāṇḍa-homa*, Agni and the others are the deities; for the *cāndrāyaṇa-homa*, Agni and the others are the deities; at the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), Agni, Soma, and Indra are the deities. Thus, in rites for which no specific deity is prescribed, Prajāpati is the deity. (1) Thus ends the ninth chapter of the first book in the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣa*. Now begins the tenth chapter of the first book.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the rite for the auspicious day (puṇyāha). 1.
On a clean and level spot, four Brāhmaṇas, holding darbha and dūrvā grass, with their hands not empty, stand facing the east in pairs. 2.
To their south, facing north, stands the one who causes the recitation (vācayitṛ), holding a water-pot with its mouth covered; leaning against his right arm, the wives stand. 3.

Having worshipped the full water-pot (*pūrṇakumbha*), sitting upon *darbha* grass and holding *darbha* blades, he should seek permission, saying: "Permitted by you, I shall cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited. They should reply, preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, "Let it be recited. (4) Having stood, he pours water into their hands, which hold the purifiers (*pavitra*), saying: *oṃ āpaḥ*. They respond: "May the waters be auspicious; may they protect the thread [of life]. (5) Then, saying "Fragrances," he offers fragrance. They accept it, saying: "May fragrant things protect us. (6)
To them he gives flowers with the words, "May there be *sumanas* (good-mindedness). They accept them with the words, "May there be *saumanasya* (good-mindedness). 7.

Into their hands he gives unbroken grains (*akṣata*) with the words, "May there be *akṣata*. By the word *akṣata*, rice-grains mixed with *vrīhi* are meant. They accept them with the words, "May there be *akṣata* and may there be *ariṣṭa* (freedom from harm). 8. If the Brahmins have not yet eaten, he gives cooked rice with the words, "May there be *āmanvāhārya*. They accept it with the words, "May there be *svanvāhārya*. 9.
"To them [he gives] sacrificial fees," thus he gives the fee. "May the sacrificial fees protect us; may there be much to give! they replied.
(10) Then the officiant, having placed his right knee on the ground and raised his left, facing north, mutters: "Iḍā, the invoker of the gods. "Taking the water-pot, stand near! they replied.
(11) Then the officiant says, "Let your minds be concentrated. "Our minds are concentrated," the others reply. (12)
Having caused [the officiant] to say, "May the performer be gracious; may you be pleased," or having caused him to recite all the mantras without pausing, [he says]: "13.

May there be peace, may there be nourishment, may there be contentment, may there be growth, may there be freedom from obstacles, may there be health, may the rite be auspicious. The others respond in exactly the same way. 14.
He utters the name of whichever deity it belongs to, saying, "May that one be pleased. The others do likewise. 15.
The reciter says, "Sirs, declare it a meritorious day! and the others reply, "Oṃ, it is a meritorious day! This is repeated three times.

(16) Then [the reciter says], "Sirs, declare it auspicious! and the others reply, "Oṃ, it is auspicious! (18) Then the reciter says, "Oṃ, sirs, declare it a success! and the others reply, "Oṃ, may it succeed! (18)

In this very manner, having caused [the officiant] to recite three times, [the others respond]: "Oṃ! May there be the prosperity of an auspicious day; so be it! and "Oṃ! May the rite be auspicious; so be it! (19).
He takes the name of whichever deity it may be, saying, "May such-and-such be pleased" (20).
They should reply, "May such-and-such be pleased" (21).

Then, having poured water on the ground with the *vyāhṛtis* and sat down, he purifies himself with the *surabhimatī*, the *bṛhaṅgā*, the *vāruṇī*, the *hiraṇyavarṇā*, the *pāvamānī*, and the *vyāhṛti* verses; and he sprinkles his wife as well—so says the venerable Bodhāyana. (22) Thus ends the tenth chapter in the first book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣa*. Now begins the eleventh chapter in the first book.

Then, after the feeding has been performed and the well-known birth-rite (*jātakarman*) has been completed, on the tenth or twelfth day, the mother and father, having bathed and prepared a pure chamber, should establish the name of the son. (1) Having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce "An auspicious day!", "Prosperity!", and "Success!", and having performed the rites from the drawing of lines for the sacrifice to the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), he offers oblations with the *prājāpatya* hymn, using the six verses beginning with "O Prajāpati, none other than you... according to their respective meters. (2) The ritual proceeds from the *jaya* offerings until the successful completion ending with the gift of a cow as a boon. (3)
Having served food to the Brahmins and having caused them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Well-being! Prosperity!", he gives him a name according to the name of a lunar mansion (nakṣatra).
(4) His second name is secret; another, used for formal salutation, his parents keep known until the time of the initiation ceremony (upanayana).
(5) And it is declared: "Therefore, a Brahmin who has two names prospers. (6)

It is known from tradition that one who has performed the Soma sacrifice should give a third name. (7) For a girl, it should consist of an odd number of syllables and end in a long vowel, such as Svasti-Śrī-Somā. (8) Furthermore, they cite this: the name of a Brāhmaṇa should end in Śarman, that of a Kṣatriya in Varman, that of a Vaiśya in Gupta, and that of a Śūdra in Bhṛtya or Dāsa—or indeed, simply in Dāsa. (9)

Now, if he should not find a Brāhmaṇa, he takes the name of his son with the *jyotiṣmatī* verse in the *aupāsana* fire, or he worships [the fire] with it. (10) Now, regarding the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*): among Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Ārdrā, Citrā, Jyeṣṭhā, Śravaṇa, Śatabhiṣaj, Revatī, and Aśvinī, there should be an increment of the first syllable; for example, in the case of Rohiṇī, one says "Rauhiṇāya. The others are treated similarly. (11) In the case of Tiṣya, Āśleṣā, Hasta, Viśākhā, Anūrādhā, Āṣāḍhā, and Śraviṣṭhā, it is according to the original form, as "Tiṣyāya. The others are treated similarly. (12)
On the day of Phalgunī, [he should offer] to Phālguna; 13. on the days of Svātī and Punarvasu, to Svāti and Punarvasu; 14. on the days of Mūla and Ārdrā, to Mūlaka and Ārdraka. 15.
In the case of the Proṣṭhapadās [nakṣatra], [the offering is made] to Proṣṭhapada or to Prauṣṭhapada (16). In the case of the Apabharaṇīs, [it is made] to Apabharaṇa or to Apabharaṇa (17).
For Agni Kṛttikā or Kārtika, the rules have been explained as those for the Agnihotra (18).
"For a woman, [the offerings are made] to Kumārī, Rohiṇī, Suśrī, Gaurī, and Svasti. 19.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣa-sūtra.
Now begins the twelfth chapter in the first book.

The piercing of the ears takes place in the seventh or eighth month. (1) Having served food to the Brāhmaṇas and caused them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity!", he then performs the rites beginning with the drawing of lines for the sacrifice to the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (the invocation of Agni), and offers oblations of cooked food. Having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*), "With the ear, [he hears] what is auspicious," he offers the oblation with the offering verse (*yājyā*), "By which [he hears] from the east... (2). Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter, verse by verse, with this section: "Prāṇa protects all that moves... (3).
The rite from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established up to the giving of the cow as a gift.
4. Then, in front of the fire, he places the remains of the oblation upon bamboo leaves with the formula: "Homage to the ocean, to Vāyu, to the lord of the rivers! 5.

Then, having caused [the sacrificer] to pronounce the blessings, he pierces the right ear with a red needle or a thorn, reciting: "The cow, the *triṣṭubh*"; and for the left ear, "The two-footed [man]. 6.
Then he ties the two ears with either a red thread or a bamboo thread, saying: "Thou art the support of Varuṇa.
(7) On the following day, he unties them, saying: "Thou art the release of Varuṇa's support.
(8) He causes them to grow by means of a thread or a bamboo stalk. (9)

Moreover, they cite this: "The Vedic rites for a son and a daughter are equal; however, from conception until birth, the ritual for a female is performed with mantras, while from birth onwards it is veiled.

(10) "In all rites not specifically prescribed, one should know the *vyāhṛtis* [are required]; they are to be offered into the fire for one who has become a *brahman*. A *brāhmaṇa* does not exist without ritual action. (11) "One without the sacred fires and without ritual action is a *śūdra*; therefore, one born [with them] is twice-born (*dvija*) by means of the fire. The naming ceremony and other rites should be performed, beginning with the preparation of the two kindling woods (*araṇī*). (12)
Alternatively, having churned the fire-sticks with mantras over a well-kindled fire, he should himself [maintain] the perpetual sacred fire by means of the fire-drill (araṇi).

There, evening and morning, according to the prescribed rule, oblations are offered with fuel-sticks while remaining devoted to service of the teacher. Having personally ascended the fire into his own self, and having offered it into the common fire with the mantra "O Agni, that which is thine... and the words "descend," he should perform the observances of the vow once he has returned home from the teacher's presence, according to the teacher's instruction.

Having performed the marriage according to the prescribed rule, one should enter the householder stage of life; for women, this rite of marriage is traditionally held to be equivalent to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). Both of them [husband and wife] must therefore maintain the sacred domestic fire (*aupāsana*); such is the Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the first book of the *Bodhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣa*.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter of the first book.

Now we shall explain the *nakṣatra-homa* (the oblation to the lunar mansions). It should be performed every year, or every six months, or every four seasons, or every month, on the birth-mansion (*janmanakṣatra*) of the boy. Having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity!", he then proceeds from the tracing of the lines for the sacrificial ground up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), and offers oblations of cooked food with the two verses beginning, "Agni is the head of the world" (*agnirmūrdhā bhuvaḥ*). 2.

Then he offers oblations to the deities of the lunar mansions (nakṣatra) according to the respective nakṣatra. 3. "May Anumati favor us today," and "O Anumati, may she favor [us]"—this is the third [offering]. 4.
Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter (ājya) to the deities of the lunar mansions according to the respective nakṣatra. 5.

"To the moon, svāhā! To the one appearing in the west, svāhā! To day and night, svāhā! To the half-months, svāhā! To the months, svāhā!"—thus month by month. (6) "To the seasons, svāhā!"—thus season by season. (7) "To the year, svāhā!"—thus at the end of the year. (8)
The ritual from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established up to the giving of the cow as a boon.
(9) The remaining food is eaten by [the sacrificer] together with his attendants.
(10) Then, when a year has elapsed, having performed the rites from the *agnimukha* offering in the well-known manner, he offers the cooked oblation to Agni, the principal deity. (11)

The second [verse] is *yathā nakṣatram*. (12) The third is *anu no adyānumatiḥ* and *anvid anumate tvam*. (13) From *navo navo bhavati jāyamānaḥ* up to the end of the section, including *yam ādityā aṃśum āpyāyayanti*. (14)
Then, as before, he offers additional oblations of clarified butter to the deities of the lunar mansions according to their respective asterisms:

"To the Moon, svāhā! To her who is seen facing [the observer], svāhā! with these utterances of *svāhā* until the end of the section. From the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the rite is established up to the granting of the boon from the cow.
The *nakṣatra-homa* has been explained. 18.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the first book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaparibhāṣāsūtra*.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter in the first book.

Now, it is indeed said in the Brāhmaṇa: "The waters are faith; he thus begins with faith itself. "The waters are the sacrifice; he thus begins with the sacrifice itself. "The waters are a thunderbolt; having hurled the thunderbolt at his enemies, [he proceeds]. "The waters are indeed slayers of the Rākṣasas; for the purpose of driving away the Rākṣasas. "The waters are the dear abode of the gods. "The waters are indeed immortality; therefore they sprinkle one who has fallen into distress with water. "The waters are all the deities; he thus begins with the deities themselves. "The waters are peaceful; with the peaceful ones he pacifies his impurity. 1.

Therefore, one performs the rite of auspicious water (*śāntyudaka*) with the *pavitra* [strainer] on one's birth-star, on an auspicious star, or for marriage, tonsure, initiation, the return home from study, the parting of the hair (*sīmanta*), the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), and other auspicious rites; or during an eclipse of a planet, or when there is a planetary portent, or if danger should befall bipeds or quadrupeds, then one should commence this rite of pacification. 2.

Having had an even number of Brāhmaṇas wash their hands and feet and having made them sip water (ācamana), he seats them on seats facing the various directions. Having smeared a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung, he sits upon it facing east, holding *darbha* grass and *dūrvā* grass, with *darbha* blades in his hand as a purifier (*pavitrapāṇi*). Having prepared the mound, sprinkled it with water, scratched the ritual mark (*lakṣaṇa*), sprinkled it again with water, scattered *dūrvā* and *darbha* grass over it, and sprinkled it with scented water, he scatters flowers over it.
He winds a thread around the *brahmapātra* vessel and places that *brahmapātra* upon those [seats] with the verse: "Brahma, being born... (RV 10.72.4). 3.
Then, they pour water through the strainer while he recites: "That most excellent [splendor] of Savitṛ... (RV 3.62.10).
(4) He scatters barley, unhusked rice, and grain while saying: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ om.

(5) Then, having strewn flowers, dūrvā grass, and fruits, and having covered it with dūrvā and darbha grass, he touches it while reciting: "May the goddesses be for our well-being and protection" (RV 10.9.4). (6)

While they have taken hold of him, he mutters the verse "That excellent splendor of Savitṛ," reciting it foot by foot, half-verse by half-verse, and without pausing; having spoken thus, he mutters the beginnings of the Vedas.

One should extract the *anuvāka* beginning with "rākṣoghnaṃ kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ prasitim" and the half-verse "made cid asya," and [instead recite] the *anuvāka* beginning with "induṃ vo viśvatas pari havāmahe janebhyaḥ," the two verses beginning with "yata indra bhayāmahe" and "svastidā viśaspatiḥ," the two verses beginning with "mahāṃ indraḥ sajoṣā" and "indraḥ," the five rounds (*paryāya*) beginning with "ye devāḥ puraspadaḥ," the five [verses] beginning with "agnaye rakṣoghne," the five [verses] beginning with "aṅgirāyuṣmān," and [the verse] beginning with "yā vām indrāvaruṇau."

The four [verses] beginning with "O Indra and Varuṇa," the eight beginning with "O Agni, glorious one," the four *Rāṣṭrabhṛt* verses beginning with "The upholder of truth, the abode of truth," this Anuvāka beginning with "Homage be to the serpents" recited with three [repetitions], the five *Coḍā* verses, the five sections beginning with "This golden-haired one in front," the *Apratiratha* hymn, this Anuvāka beginning with "Shining brightly," this Anuvāka beginning with "May there be peace for me and prosperity for me," the *Vihavya* hymn, this Anuvāka beginning with "O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations," and the *Sṛgāra*.

One should recite the section beginning with "I meditate on Agni" (*agnermanve*); the *sarpāhuti*s with six rounds beginning with "Thou art Samīcī, the eastern quarter" (*samīcī nāmāsi prācī dik*); the *gandharvāhuti*s with six [rounds] beginning with "Ye are the weapons, O ye whose houses are foremost" (*hetayo nāma stha teṣāṃ vaḥ purogṛhāḥ*); the *ajyānī*s with five [verses] beginning with "For him who has a hundred weapons" (*śatāyudhāya*); the section beginning with "The past, the present, the future" (*bhūtaṃ bhavyaṃ bhaviṣyat*); the *Atharvaśiras*; the section beginning with "Indra [conquered] by means of the bones of Dadhyañc" (*indro dadhīco asthabhiḥ*); and the *Pratyāṅgirasa*, starting with "These are from the eye, these are from the mind," ending with "We cause our rival to fall" (*cakṣuṣo haite manaso haite... bhrātṛvyaṃ pādayāmasi*).

"Thus far the vital breath protects all that moves"—with this section; "In the lion, in the tiger, and also in the adder"—with this section; "I am he"—with this section; "Those two, Sūrya and Candramas"—with this section; with these three final sections beginning with "May Agni protect us," "May we prosper," and "New, ever-new," and with the secondary oblations (*upahoma*), with the *surabhimatī* verses, the *abhliṅga* verses, the *vāruṇī* verses, the *hiraṇyavarṇā* verses, the *pāvamānī* verses, the *vyāhṛti*s, and the section beginning with "That blessing of Śamyoḥ we choose," he recites three times the concluding verse, "Homage to Brahman"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. 8.

Having established [the vessel] with the *praṇava*, he sprinkles it with the *vyāhṛtis*. 9. Then he gives the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*): he gives gold to one seated in front, silver to the south, bell-metal to the west, and a garment to the north. 10.

Then he sprinkles those seized by planets, those seized by fever, those possessed by spirits, as well as friends, kinsmen, well-wishers, relatives, companions, connections, and blood-relations; kings and royal priests; children, the elderly, pregnant women, those afflicted by evil diseases, those with chronic illnesses, and the emaciated and suffering. 11.
He sprinkles elephants, horses, camels, cows, buffaloes, goats, sheep, servants, as well as wealth and grain.
12. Thus, by [sprinkling] for one night, three nights, five nights, seven nights, or nine nights, one conquers death again; so said the venerable Bodhāyana.
13. Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣa Sūtra.
Now, the fifteenth chapter in the first book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the binding of the *pratisara* (protective amulet). On the night of the day on which one performs the *nāndīmukha* rite, one should begin the *pratisara* at the end of the evening watch (*pradoṣa*).

On a clean, level spot, having smeared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung, and having caused an even number of Brahmins to wash their hands and feet and to sip water, and having seated them on seats according to the directions, the teacher sits behind them facing east.
Another sits to his right, facing north.

Then, having prepared a sand altar (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit, having scraped it, sprinkled it with water, and spread darbha grass upon the center of the altar with its tips pointing eastward; having placed a water-pot (kumbha) upon them, filled it with pure water while reciting the Vyāhṛtis, scattered it with dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, and fruits, worshipped the water-pot with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, covered it with dūrvā and darbha grass, and finally placed a protective thread (pratisara-sūtra) smeared with perfume upon a layer of śāli rice to the north.

Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) from the mouth of the teacher and having touched the water-pot, he mutters the Sāvitrī verse, "tatsaviturvareṇyam," reciting it foot by foot, then half-verse by half-verse, and finally without pausing; thereafter, he mutters the beginnings of the Vedas. 5.

The Anuvāka beginning with *rakṣoghnam kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ*, the four verses beginning with *agne yaśasvin*, the Anuvāka beginning with *āpyam hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*, the Anuvāka beginning with *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*, the Varuṇa-sūkta consisting of six verses beginning with *ud uttamaṃ varuṇa pāśam*, the Rudra-sūkta consisting of six verses beginning with *pari no rudrasya hetiḥ*, the Brahma-sūkta consisting of six verses beginning with *brahma jajñānam*, the Viṣṇu-sūkta consisting of six verses beginning with *viṣṇornukam*, the five Durgā hymns, and [the hymn] beginning with *jātavedase*.
"The Śrīsūkta consisting of fifteen verses beginning with 'hiraṇyavarṇām hariṇīm' and the verse 'namo brahmaṇe' as the concluding verse—he recites these three times; so says the Brāhmaṇa. (6)

Having raised [the child] with the *praṇava*, having sprinkled [him] with the *vyāhṛtis*, with the *surabhimatī* verses, and with the *abliṅga* verses, and having taken the protective thread (*pratisara-sūtra*), meditating upon Vāsuki, he should wipe it three times upwards with ashes using the thumb and the ring finger while reciting the *tryambaka* mantra; then, having grasped the boy’s right hand with the five verses beginning "Agni is long-lived," and having tied it with the verse "The Bṛhat Sāman," and for girls the left hand, he should perform the protection with ashes using the *ghṛtasūkta* and the eight-verse hymn beginning "He who is the Brahman of Brahman"—thus says the venerable Bodhāyana. 7.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter in the first book:
We shall now explain the offerings for the planets, the guest-offering, the Bali-oblations, and the ritual gifts.
The planets clearly lead a person who lacks faith, is impure, does not recite prayers, and has abandoned auspicious rites to the abode of Yama.
[1] [This applies even to those] planets of fierce activity that move along the path of the constellations.
I shall now declare the ritual services for the purpose of pacification according to the prescribed rule:

||2|| By performing hospitality toward those planets every month, every season, at the solstices, during lunar and solar eclipses, at the equinoxes, or on auspicious or inauspicious birth-asterisms—even throughout the year—one attains all desires. ||3||
The ritual procedure for the single fire has been stated. 4. Or, even if one [of the planets] is in an unfavorable position, all of them are indeed to be worshipped. 5.
The Sun and Mars are red; Venus and the Moon are white.
The son of Soma (Mercury) and Jupiter—both of these are traditionally considered yellow.
One should know Saturn to be black, as well as Rāhu and Ketu; a wise person should provide flowers there that correspond to the colors of the planets.
"One should present offerings, oblations, perfumes, and garlands to all [the planets] in due order and succession.

(8) "For the Sun, sacrificial fuel of *arka*; for Mars, of *khadira*; for Venus, of *udumbara*; for the Moon, of *pālāśa*; for Mercury, of *apāmārga*; for Jupiter, of *aśvattha*; for Saturn, of *śamī*; for Rāhu, *dūrvā* grass; and for Ketu, *kuśa* grass. (9)

If none of these are available, [the ladle] shall be made of *pālāśa* wood. Having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce "An auspicious day!", "Well-being!", and "Success!", he then performs the rites beginning with the drawing of lines for the sacrifice to the gods up to the point of the *praṇītā* waters, and offers the oblations.
10. Then, having risen and prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with rice grains in front of the fire, he invokes the deities of the planets.
11. He should know that the Sun is in the center, while the Red One (Mars) is to the south.
One should know Venus to be in the east, and the Moon in the southeast;
one should know Mercury in the northeast, and likewise Jupiter in the north;
one should know Saturn in the west, and Rāhu in the southwest. (12–13)
In the north-west, the position for Ketu is prescribed;
on the southern and northern sides, however, are the presiding deities and their sub-deities.
A circle is for Āditya, a triangle for Aṅgāraka, a pentagon for Śukra, a square for Soma, and an arrow-shaped figure for Rāhu.
For Mercury, a long quadrangle; for Jupiter, a bow; for Saturn, a winnowing basket; for Rāhu, a banner; and for Ketu, a flagstaff.
(15) The Sun, Venus, and Mercury face east; Jupiter faces north; Saturn and the Moon face west; and the remaining planets face south. (16)
One should add barley, *āḍhakī*, rice, *śyāmāka*, mung beans,
chickpeas, sesame, black gram, and horse gram in successive order. Indeed,
Agni and Īśvara are the lords of the Sun, while Earth and Kṣetreśa belong to Mars.
Indrāṇī and Indra are for Venus; then the Waters and Gaurī for the Lord of Night (the Moon); Viṣṇu and Viṣṇu for Mercury; Indramarutvat and Brahmā for Jupiter;
Prajāpati and Yama for Saturn; and Sarpa and Nirṛti for Rāhu. 18–19.
Ketu, Brahmā, and Citra, with their respective mantras and names,
[should worship] the world-protectors (lokapālas), Durgā, Vighna, Kṣetrapāla, Vāstudeva, Tryambaka, Abhayaṅkara, Mṛtyu, and Vaiśvānara Agni in due order.
One should invoke [the planets] with the *Āvāhana* mantras and worship them with the eightfold offerings (*aṣṭopacāra*).

Having performed the rites from the *paridhāna* up to the *agnimukha*, one should offer to Āditya with the mantra "ā satyena," to Aṅgāraka (Mars) with "agnirmūrdhā," to Śukra (Venus) with "pra vaḥ śukrāya," to Soma (Moon) with "āpyāyasva," to Budha (Mercury) with "udbudhyasva," to Bṛhaspati (Jupiter) with "bṛhaspate atiyadaryo arhāt," to Śanaiścara (Saturn) with "śaṃ no devīrabhiṣṭaye," to Rāhu with "kayā naścitra ā bhuvat," and to Ketu with "ketuṃ kṛṇvan. (21–22)
"Having recited the *puronuvākyā*, he offers with the *yājyā* for the sake of having the deities present," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(23) Where [the verse] is prescribed as one, he should repeat it twice; or, having recited "That desirable [splendor] of Savitṛ," he offers with the prescribed [verse].

(24) Having brought the cooked [portion] of the nine cups, he should offer eight thousand, or eight hundred, or twenty-eight fuel-sticks anointed with ghee, verse by verse. He should offer the oblation verse by verse; he should offer the clarified butter verse by verse. (25)

One should offer rice with molasses to Āditya; sacrificial food (haviṣya) to Aṅgāraka; rice with ghee to Śukra; milk-porridge with ghee to Soma; rice with curds to Budha; rice with beans mixed with sesame paste to Bṛhaspati; meat-rice to Śanaiścara; and variegated rice to Rāhu and Ketau. [26] In the absence of all these, one may offer sacrificial food (haviṣya) for all.

[27] When the number is eight thousand, one should offer twenty-eight oblations for the presiding deities (adhidevatā) and the secondary deities (pratyadhidevatā); when it is one hundred and eight, then eight each; when it is twenty, then three each. In this very same manner, one should offer oblations for the world-protectors (lokapāla) and the others. [28]

"agnim dūtam yeṣām īśe" for Āditya; "syonā pṛthivi kṣetrasya pate" for Aṅgāraka (Mars); "indrāṇīm indraṃ vo viśvataḥ" for Śukra (Venus); "apsu me somo abravīt gaurī mimāya" for Soma (Mercury); "viṣṇornukam viṣṇo ragaṭam" for Budha (Mercury); "indra marutvaḥ brahma jajñānam" for Bṛhaspati (Jupiter); "prajāpate imam yama prastaram" for Śanaiścara (Saturn); "āyaṅgauḥ yatte devi" for Rāhu; and "brahmā devānām savitre citram" for Ketu. 29.

"Indra, the deliverer; Agni, the giver; Yama, who maintains wealth; Pṛthivī, who supports the non-pressing [sacrificer]; the exhilarating ones, resplendent; O Soma, with thy teams bring us thousands of cows in a thousand ways"—these are for the World-Guardians (Lokapālas).

"To Jātavedas"; "Thee among the hosts"; "Of the lord of the field we [worship]"; "O Vāstoṣpati"; "Tryambaka we worship"; "From whatever fear we fear, O Indra"; "Bestower of well-being, Lord of the people"; "Thy thousands and tens of thousands of nooses"; "The head of heaven, the steward of earth"—these are for Durgā and the others.

In this very manner, having prepared the oblation and offered it with sesame and rice mixed with clarified butter while reciting the *vyāhṛtis*, he takes a single portion from each [of the substances], pours clarified butter over it twice, and offers it to Sviṣṭakṛt. Having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*) beginning with "To Aryaman," he offers the oblation with the offering verse (*yājyā*) beginning with "To King Soma. (32) Having placed the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) back into the fire, the ritual is completed with the *jaya* formulas and the subsequent rites. (33)

Having offered the full oblation with the verse, "The head of heaven, the messenger... (RV 8.44.16), he worships the Grahas in front of the fire with the three verses beginning, "O Waters, you are most beneficent... (RV 10.9.1–3), with the four verses beginning, "Golden-hued, pure, purifying... (RV 9.1.6–9), and with this entire Anuvāka beginning, "Pavamāna, born in the light... (RV 9.57.1–3). Having performed the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*), having gratified them by their respective names, having worshipped them with their own respective mantras using perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, having presented the sacrificial offering (*bali*), and having given gifts of parched grain, cakes, flattened rice, and so forth, he prepares them and dismisses them.
Sitting behind the fire, he sprinkles himself with water using the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*, the three verses beginning with *devasya tvā*, and the *śaṃyuvāka* formula.

(34) Then he gives the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*): a tawny cow to Āditya, a red ox to Aṅgāraka, silver to Śukra, a conch-shell to Soma, gold to Budha, a garment to Bṛhaspati, a black cow to Śanaiścara, a goat to Rāhu, and an elephant to Ketu.
(35) In the absence of all these, gold may be given instead. (36)
Or by whatever means the teacher might be satisfied. Furthermore, they also cite this:
"Just as a terrible [disease] that has arisen is countered by a mechanical device,"

One should always quickly bring to peace such terrible [calamity] as has thus arisen. (38) Just as armor serves as a protection against the striking of weapons, so does pacification serve as a warding off against the afflictions caused by fate. (39)
For one who is non-violent, self-controlled, who has acquired wealth through righteous means, and who is constantly established in his observances, the planets are always benevolent.
The planets, the cows, the lords of men, and especially the Brahmins [are likewise so]. 40.
When honored, these [planets] bestow honor; when insulted, they consume [the offender]. One should know Īśvara as the Sun (Bhāskara), and likewise Aṅgāraka as Skanda;
one should know Śukra as the Lord of Śacī (Indra), and Niśākara as Umā. 41–42.
One should know Budha as Nārāyaṇa and Bṛhaspati as Brahmā;
one should know Yama as Śanaiścara, and likewise Rāhu as Kāla. One should know Ketu as consisting of fire; such are the gods, O gods, who are the planets. 43.
"The deities manifest in the form of planetary spirits (grahas) and show what is auspicious and inauspicious;
they show what is auspicious and inauspicious," so said the Blessed Bodhāyana. 44.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the first book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣa*.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter of the first book:
the procedure for the worship of the nine planets.
[One should worship] the God who is the lamp of the three worlds, whose nature consists of qualities, and who is composed of the three Vedas.
With great devotion, I install Bhāskara, the leader of the planets:

situated in the center of a circular maṇḍala, facing west, born in the Kaliṅga country, of the Kāśyapa lineage, with Viśvāmitra as his seer, born under the Viśākhā nakṣatra, having the Triṣṭubh metre, possessing the Kapila fire, seated upon a lotus-throne, lotus-colored, two-armed, wearing red garments, anointed with fragrant perfumes, adorned with ornaments of ruby gems, wearing a crown, possessing a red parasol, banner, and flag, and mounted upon a divine, red, single-wheeled chariot drawn by seven green horses representing the Vedic meters and yoked to seven reins, [I install him] on Mount Meru.
I bow to the Sun, the jewel of the sky, who circumambulates the circle of planets, who has entered the presiding deity Agni and the secondary deity Rudra, and who, seated upon a lotus,
holds two reddish lotuses in his hands as the lord of the planets.
Adorned with rubies, red garments, perfumes, and garlands,
he shines like the sun of immeasurable splendor, the friend of the lotus; O Kapilā,
Rohiṇī is worthy of worship by all the gods.
Since you consist of all the gods, therefore grant me peace.
4 I bow down to the Sun, who resembles the hibiscus flower, the son of Kaśyapa, possessed of great splendor, the dispeller of darkness, and the destroyer of impurity. 5

I always take refuge in Dīvākara, who possesses a thousand blazing rays, who is composed of splendor, the witness of the world’s deeds, the friend, the radiant Sun, the first of the planets, and Ravi. 6.
[I seek refuge in him] who wears red garlands, garments, and ointments, and who wields the mace, the spear, the sword, and the trident.
I install the four-armed son of Bharadvāja, the offspring of the Earth, who rides upon a ram;
he resembles red gold and is like the red filaments of a lotus—this most fierce form of Rudra, possessed of great power. 7–8.
In a triangular mandala in the southern direction from the sun, facing south, [is the deity] born in the land of Avanti.

Born of the Bhāradvāja lineage, having Jamadagni as his sage, the Gāyatrī as his meter, and Agni Dhūmaketu as his fire; four-armed, wielding a sword, a spear, a trident, and a mace; wearing red garments and adorned with ornaments of red coral and gems; wearing a crown and possessing a red parasol, banner, and flag; mounted upon a red ram as his vehicle and a golden chariot drawn by eight fiery horses; circumambulating the divine Mount Meru and having entered the circle of planets—he is the presiding deity of the Earth and the local guardian (Kṣetrapāla) of the secondary deity. 9.
Bearing red garlands, perfumes, and garments, with mace, spear, sword, and trident held in his hands;
the son of Bhāradvāja, three-eyed, the son of the Earth, red-limbed yet of auspicious body;
having a ram and a tiger as his banners, with ears adorned by great earrings resembling the brilliance of the sun.
May he protect us, adorned with a glittering crown, bracelets, and coral ornaments. 10.
O Dharma, you who take the form of a bull, the cause of joy for the world, and the foundation of the eightfold form [of Śiva], grant me peace. 11.
I bow to the youth who is born from the womb of the *dhāraṇī*, who resembles lightning and gold, who holds a spear in his hand, and whose limbs are red;
he who was born upon the earth from a drop of sweat from the mouth of Maheśvara, and is adorned with red garlands and garments. 12.
I always take refuge in the son of Aṅgiras, the red-limbed youth Aṅgāraka, who possesses excellent luster.

(13) [I seek refuge in] Śukra, whose body is white, who is richly adorned with white garments, the minister of the Daityas, the descendant of Bhṛgu, who holds a staff, the gesture of granting boons, a water-pot, and a rosary of beads. (14)
I install the great peaceful one, Bhṛgu, the lord and preceptor of the Daityas, who possesses a luster like the kunda flower and a radiance like a pearl. 15.

In the eastern quarter of the sun, within a five-cornered mandala, [one should visualize] him who was born in the region of Bhojakataka, belonging to the Bhārgava gotra, a descendant of Śaunaka, born under the constellation Tiṣya, having the Triṣṭubh meter, possessing the fire of gold (Hāṭakāgni), white in color, four-armed with a rosary, staff, water-pot, and the gesture of granting boons, adorned with white garments, perfumes, garlands, and vajra-jewel ornaments, wearing a crown, accompanied by a white umbrella, banner, and flag, mounted upon a white horse as his vehicle, and riding a white chariot yoked to ten horses born of the earth, while proceeding toward the divine [realm].
I pay homage to him who circumambulates Mount Meru, who has entered the circle of planets, whose presiding deity is Indrāṇī and whose counter-presiding deity is Indra;
who is adorned with radiant white garments, perfumes, and garlands, who is mounted upon a pure white horse, and whose body is resplendent with the jewel of the vajra.
I praise the venerable son of Bhṛgu, the preceptor of the Asuras, who bears in his hands a staff, a fine water-pot, and a rosary;
for you, O Viṣṇu, are born from the nectar in the form of a horse.
May he be the vehicle of Viṣṇu and of the Sun; therefore, O Lord, grant me peace. 18.
I bow down to Bhārgava, who resembles snow, the kunda flower, and frost, the supreme preceptor of the Daityas, and the bestower of all weapons. 19.

I always take refuge in Śukra, the descendant of Bhṛgu, whose boat is the rainy season, who accords with his intended purposes, who is preeminent in policy, endowed with discipline, and whose being is purified by yoga. (20) He wears white garments and has a chariot drawn by ten white horses as his vehicle.

I install the Moon-god, who has two arms, who holds the gesture of fearlessness and a mace, who is accompanied by Mātṛkā and Amṛta, who possesses the crescent moon, who is peaceful, the lord of the stars, the beloved of Rohiṇī,
and whose form is as radiant as a jasmine flower. 21-22.

In the south-eastern quarter of the Sun, within a square-shaped maṇḍala, one should meditate upon the planet [Sūrya], born in the land of Yamunā, of the Ātreya gotra, having Ātreya as his ṛṣi, born under the constellation Kṛttikā, possessing the Gāyatrī metre, having Piṅgala and Agni as his presiding deities (adhidevatā and pratyadhidevatā), holding the gesture of fearlessness and a mace, two-armed, adorned with white garments, perfumes, garlands, and pearl ornaments, wearing a crown, and possessing a white umbrella, banner, and pennant; mounted upon a white chariot produced from the waters, having ten horses and three wheels, circumambulating the divine Mount Meru, entered into the circle of planets, with Prajāpati as his adhidevatā and Gaurī as his pratyadhidevatā. 23.

I bow to the Moon, the lord of the night, who is adorned with white garments, garlands, and unguents; who was born from the eye of Atri; whose vehicle is a chariot drawn by ten horses; who is the lord of medicinal herbs; who holds the gestures of fearlessness and the medicine-bowl in his two hands; who wears beautiful pearls; and who is the embodiment of nectar.
(24) O Conch, you are the most meritorious among merits and the most auspicious among auspicious things;
since you are eternally held by Viṣṇu, grant me peace. (25)
With devotion, I bow to the Moon, who resembles curd, a conch shell, or frost, who was born from the ocean of milk, and who serves as the ornament upon the crown of Śambhu;
he who undergoes waning and waxing for the sake of Time, and whom the gods and ancestors drink. 26.
I always take refuge in that most excellent Soma, who is worshipped by Brahmā and Indra;

[27] who is richly adorned with garlands, perfumes, and garments, who has a golden luster, possesses four arms, and holds a spear, shield, sword, and mace; the wise son of Atri, who rides upon a lion. [28]
I place here the great and gentle Lord Budha, son of Soma, who resembles the Campaka flower and possesses the luster of pure gold. 29.

In the north-eastern direction of the Sun, within a bow-shaped maṇḍala, he is seated facing east upon a divine yellow chariot drawn by eight yellow horses of wind and fire; he is born in the Magadha country, of the Ātreya gotra, with Bhāradvāja as his ṛṣi, Śraviṣṭhā as his lunar mansion, and Triṣṭubh as his metre; he has the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni) as his deity, holds a spear, sword, shield, and mace in his four arms, is adorned with yellow garments, perfumes, garlands, and emerald jewel-ornaments, wears a crown, possesses a yellow umbrella, banner, and flag, rides a yellow lion, and ascends Mount Meru.

I bow to Mercury, the son of the Moon, born of the lineage of Atri, who circumambulates [the sun] and has entered the planetary mandala; I salute him whose presiding deity (adhidevatā) is Viṣṇu and whose counter-presiding deity (pratyadhidevatā) is Viṣṇu; he possesses the radiant luster of a body like emerald, his limbs adorned with yellow garments, garlands, and unguents;
he holds a spear, a sword, a shield, and a mace in his arms, bears a lion-banner, and belongs to the lunar dynasty. 31.
Residing within the womb of Hiraṇyagarbha, the golden seed of the sun, which bestows the fruit of infinite merit—therefore, grant me peace.
O wise one, who is incomparable in form and possesses the luster of a *priyaṅgu* berry! 32.
I bow to the son of the Moon, who is gentle and endowed with gentle qualities.

I always take refuge in Budha—the one of pure intellect, whose awakening comes through sacred learning and time, who speaks what is true, the lamp of the Lunar dynasty, the one of brilliant luster, the knower of the Vedas, the universal-formed. 34.
[One should meditate on] the descendant of Aṅgiras, the preceptor of the gods, wearing yellow garlands, perfumes, and garments;
holding a staff, granting boons, yellow in color, and carrying a rosary and a water-pot;
possessing a luster like the kunda flower and resembling molten gold. 35.
With great devotion, I establish the Guru of serene countenance.

[I place him] in a long square mandala to the north of the Sun, facing north, born in the land of Sindhu, of the Āṅgirasa gotra, with Vasiṣṭha as his ṛṣi, born under the constellation Uttarā-phalgunī, having the Triṣṭubh meter, with Śikhin-Agni as his deity; four-armed, holding a yellow rosary, a staff, a water-pot, and displaying the gesture of granting boons; adorned with yellow garments, perfumes, garlands, Puṣyarāga gems, and jewel ornaments; wearing a crown; possessing a yellow umbrella, banner, and flag; and mounted upon a golden divine chariot drawn by eight white horses named Viśvarūpa, [toward] Mount Meru.
He circumambulates the circle of planets; he has entered [the mandala] with Indra as his presiding deity (adhidevatā) and Brahmā as his counter-presiding deity (pratyadhidevatā).
He wears yellow garments, possesses a slender and radiant body marked by a topaz gem, and his limbs are adorned with armlets, necklaces, jewels, and earrings.
I bow to the preceptor of the gods, the descendant of Aṅgiras, who rides upon a horse and bears a staff, a rosary of beads, and a water-pot;
for he wears a pair of yellow garments that are dear to Vāsudeva. 38.
Through the offering of this, may Viṣṇu be pleased with me at all times.
(39) I bow down to Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods and the sages, who resembles gold and is worthy of high honor in the three worlds. (40)
There is no other equal to him in intelligence; the gods themselves depend upon his wisdom. I always seek refuge in Bṛhaspati, the son of Prajāpati, who is eternally devoted to dharma.

(41) I salute the son of Kaśyapa, who resembles a sapphire, who is gentle, adorned with variegated ornaments, bearing a bow and arrows, carrying a shield and a trident, and having a vulture as his vehicle. (42)
I install the most fierce Śanaiścara, the son of the Sun, who possesses a luster like sapphire and a radiance equal to the blue lotus. 43.

In the western quarter of the sun, within a bow-shaped maṇḍala, he is facing north; born of the Kāśyapa lineage, with Bhṛgu as his ancestral seer, born under the Revatī asterism, native to the Saurāṣṭra country, having the Gāyatrī metre, possessing great splendor like fire, blue in color, four-armed and holding a shield, arrow, bow, and trident; adorned with blue garments, perfumes, garlands, and blue gemstone ornaments; wearing a crown, possessing a blue umbrella, banner, and flag; mounted upon a blue chariot drawn by eight horses of the sky-born Jambāla breed and yoked to a blue vulture as its vehicle, [he traverses] the divine Meru.
He circumambulated Prajāpati, the presiding deity who had entered the circle of planets, and Yama, the counter-deity;
[he saw him] holding a bow, arrows, and a shield in his arms, bearing a trident,
and with a radiant crown and diadem blazing with sapphires.
I bow down with humility to the son of the Sun, who is adorned with blue parasols, flowers, garments, perfumes, and ornaments, and who is seated upon a vulture.
Within the limbs of his cows reside the fourteen worlds.
Therefore, may there be auspiciousness for me; for that reason, grant me peace.
46 I worship with devotion Śanaiścara, who has the appearance of a mass of blue collyrium, the son of the Sun, the neuter one, born from the womb of Chāyā. 47

I always take refuge in Śanaiścara, the Lord of Creatures, whose enjoyment, movement, and activity are slow; who is born from the Sun, who is wrathful yet easily propitiated. (48) [He is] the son of Siṃhikā, with a formidable face, the descendant of Kuṇḍina, composed of darkness, bearing a sword and a shield, terrifying, and seated upon a dark-blue lion-throne. (49)
I establish Rāhu, the enemy of the moon and sun, who has the appearance of blue collyrium and the splendor of a dark cloud, and who possesses a great face. 50.

In the south-western direction of the Sun, within a winnow-shaped maṇḍala, [one should visualize] him who was born in the Barbarian country, belonging to the Paiṭhīnasi gotra, equal to Aṅgiras, born under the asterism Aśvinī, having the Gāyatrī metre, with Hutāśana as his fire; he is black, holding a sword and a shield, two-armed, adorned with black garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments of the gomeda gem, wearing a crown, possessing a black umbrella, banner, and flag, with a fierce face, decorated with serpents, and mounted upon a chariot drawn by eight horses, seated on a black throne.

He beheld Rāhu, the enemy of the moon, who does not circumambulate the divine Mount Meru, who has entered the circle of planets, whose presiding deity is the serpent and whose counter-deity is Nirṛti;
he was terrifying, his body composed of darkness, and adorned with a shield and sword in the tips of his hands. 51.

I bow to the son of Kauṇḍinya, who is adorned with dark garments and perfumes, whose body is embellished with *gomedaka* gems, and who rides upon a green horse. (52) Since you, O goat, are established as a constituent part of sacrifices, [I bow to you].
O you who constantly contemplate the vehicle [of liberation], therefore grant me peace!
53 I bow down to that Rāhu, whose body is half-formed, who possesses great heroism, who crushes the sun and moon, and who is born from the womb of a lioness. 54
He who, having severed the head of Viṣṇu while he was drinking the nectar, was appointed to the state of a planet,
and who swallows both the sun and the moon at the time of the lunar nodes.

I always go for refuge to Rāhu. [55] I salute the comets (Ketus), the sons of Brahmā, who are smoke-colored, two-armed, wielding maces, with distorted faces, possessing hundreds of forms, seated upon vultures, and bestowers of boons. [56]
I establish this great and fierce banner, which possesses the luster of a dark blue cloud, is multicolored, endowed with great strength, and bestows all fruits. 57.

In the northwestern direction of the Sun, upon a banner-shaped maṇḍala, one should visualize Raudrāgni, born from the Antarvedī region and originating from the Jaimini-sūtras. He is smoke-colored, facing south, two-armed, holding a boon-granting gesture and a mace. He is adorned with variegated garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments of vaidūrya gems; he wears a crown and is accompanied by a smoke-colored parasol, banner, and flag. Seated upon a chariot drawn by eight smoke-colored, ruddy horses and a variegated vulture as his vehicle, he ascends and circumambulates Mount Meru in a counter-clockwise direction, having entered the circle of the planets.
Brahmā is his presiding deity (adhidevatā), and Citragupta is his secondary deity (pratyadhidevatā). 58.

One should visualize the Kumāras, who have faces like those born from the womb of water-fowl and sit upon vultures; they are smoke-colored, possess beautiful arms, grant boons and fearlessness with their hands, have bodies adorned with lapis lazuli, and belong to the excellent Jaiminīya school.
I bow to the Ketu-nāgas with terrifying faces and two arms.
(59) O Great Being, O Great Body, born from the Ocean of Milk, O Victorious One in all battles, O Elephant, grant me victory! (60)

I bow down to the Rudras, who resemble terrifying smoky clouds, whose heads are like the peaks of mountains, who are of a fierce nature, and who are the terrible comets. (61) Those who are the sons of Brahmā, whose faces are equal to that of Brahmā—
Born of Brahmā, equal to Brahmā, youthful, supreme Brahmins, and givers of boons— those followers of Jaimini,
I always go for refuge to their banners. 62.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the first book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhya-śeṣa-sūtra.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter of the first book.

Now, therefore, one who desires the prosperity of his house should commence the *gṛhaśānti* (propitiation of the house) on the waxing moon, under an auspicious lunar mansion, either month by month, season by season, or year by year. 1.
Having tied together *apāmārga*, *palāśa*, mustard seeds, *udumbara*, *sadābhadra*, *amṛtatṛṇa*, and *indravallī* [plants], he sweeps the house with the two verses, "Mā no mahāntam" and "Mā naḥ toke.
(2) He sprinkles [the house] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and a handful of *darbha* grass with the two verses, "Yata indra bhayāmahe" and "Svastidā.

(3) Having scattered white mustard seeds with this entire section beginning with "Kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ," and having performed the rites from the marking of the sacrificial ground for the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), he offers oblations of cooked food with the two verses, "Vāstoṣpate" and "Vāstoṣpate. (4)
Then he offers oblations of clarified butter with the six verses beginning "O Lord of the Dwelling, firm is the pillar," according to their respective meters.
He should offer a thousand oblations with the Sāvitrī verse.
The rite is completed from the Sviṣṭakṛt offering up to the giving of the cow as a boon.

Having served food to the Brāhmaṇas and having caused them to recite, "An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity!", one who employs [this rite] in this manner thrives with great nourishment; many sons are born, and no children die young; no malignant diseases seize them; fanged beasts do not kill them; and thieves, serpents, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas do not harass them.
(8) If cows should suffer from heat, one should offer a thousand oblations in the midst of the cows; this is called "the pacification of cows. (9)
"This same [rule] has been explained for bipeds and quadrupeds: 'The garment [should be placed] on the right,' so said the venerable Bodhāyana.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the first book of the *Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra* of Bodhāyana.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter in the first book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the propitiatory rite for the horse (*aśvaśānti*). Having performed the rites from the marking of the sacrificial ground up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), he offers oblations of cooked food, reciting as the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*): "May the Aśvins, the yokers of horses, come hither," and as the offering verse (*yājyā*): "The two physicians of the gods. (1) Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*), saying: "Svāhā to the Aśvins! Svāhā to the yokers of horses! Svāhā to hearing! Svāhā to the act of hearing! (2) The remainder of the ritual, beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, is established as complete up to the gift of the cow as a boon (*dhenuvara*). (3)

Then, in front of the fire, he places the remnants of the oblation upon *aśvattha* leaves with the verse: "The *aśvattha* tree that has grown from the womb of the *śamī*, which has ascended together with thee—that I bring for thee, O Brahman, along with the sacrificial signs.

(4) Having poured the rinsings of the cooking pot, the remainder of the clarified butter, and the remainder of the water into a vessel, he goes three times around the horses clockwise, sprinkling them with an *aśvattha* branch while reciting the section beginning: "He who knows the hairs of the sacrificial horse... Thus spoke the venerable Bodhāyana.
(5) Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the first book of the *Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra* of Bodhāyana.

Now begins the twentieth chapter of the first book. Now, therefore, we shall explain the *gajaśānti* (the propitiatory rite for elephants).
