On the eighth, eleventh, or fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, or under the asterism Śroṇā, having served food to the Brāhmaṇas and caused them to pronounce "Auspicious Day!", "Well-being!", and "Success!", one should pour out sesame seeds and rice in front; having brought water with the *Sāvitrī* verse, and having wrapped two full jars with a new cloth and filled them with fruit, one places them behind; then, having set down the cooked sacrificial porridge (*caru*) as prescribed, one establishes it upon a cluster of five *dūrvā* grass blades. 1.

Then, having adorned the elephant stable with garlands of *darbha* grass, the elephant smells the fragrance of the oblation. (2) He makes a stirring-spoon from *aśvattha* wood and prepares the sacrificial fuel and the sacred grass.

(3) Then, having performed the rites beginning with the smearing of the altar for the sacrifice to the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), he should offer the cooked food with clarified butter while reciting the *Gajasūkta*, beginning with the verse: "O Indra, [give us] that which is rich in food. (4)
Then he offers oblations of clarified butter with these five verses beginning with "Homage to you, O Rudra, to your wrath," and he should sacrifice eight thousand times.
(5) From the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the rite is established up to the granting of the boon by the cow.
(6) In front of the fire, he places the remains of the oblation upon clumps of *dūrvā* grass with the formula: "To the beings, svāhā! (7)

Then, having caused [the child] to eat the remainder of the *sthālīpāka* and a bunch of five *dūrvā* grasses with the *Āyuṣya-sūkta*, he sprinkles [him] with water from the *praṇītā* vessel with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," with the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ," and with this entire section beginning with "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ. Having purified [him], he leads the one of the *nāga* class to his own place; "The elephant becomes long-lived," so says the venerable Bodhāyana.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the first book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣa*.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter in the first book.
The sacrifice to Yama has been proclaimed by myself; I shall now explain the supreme procedure.
Indeed, this offering to Antaka (the Ender) should be performed month after month.
A twice-born man who desires intelligence, wealth, or even sons [should perform it].
On a day when the moon is in conjunction with the asterism Yāmya (Bharaṇī), one attains all desires.
One should diligently offer the bali-oblation on the Kārttikī full-moon day of the year;
for by failing to do so on that Kārttikī day, one sinks into hell.
Therefore, on the full moon day of Kārttika, a twice-born man desiring all his wishes should indeed prepare an oblation of a prastha of sesame seeds mixed with molasses;
it should not be performed by one alone, but rather together with many others. 4.

Having set out the oblation, touched it, and taken the oblation, he goes out from the village toward the east or the north. In a place that is not marshy, on a riverbank, or on some other clean level spot, he prepares a sacrificial altar (vedi) with its ridges facing the cardinal directions, making it either of clay or of sand. (5) There are three ridges on the northern altar (uttaravedi) facing the cardinal directions. (6)

Having dug a pit for the water-jar (karaka) to the south and established the fire to the north, he covers the northern altar (uttaravedi) with *darbha* grass. Having laid down a seat-grass mat (*viṣṭara*) pointing eastward in the same manner, and having placed the sacrificial grass bundle (*prastara*), he invokes Yama over the *prastara* with the mantra: "May the god Yama come here with his gracious aids, being well-disposed toward us; may he sit upon this well-prepared sacred grass (*barhis*) for strength, for progeny, and for the slaying of my enemies. Then, [he recites] "Like two Yamas striving together, when they brought them forth... and "This one, O Yama... (RV 10.14.1).

Having consecrated the *prastara* grass-bundle with the three verses beginning "Sit down upon the *prastara*," and having, with *pavitra* blades in hand, offered the water for honor (*arghya*), the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and the water for bathing (*snānīya*), he purifies [the guest] with the *vāruṇī*, *hiraṇyavarṇā*, and *pāvamānī* verses; then, having offered all kinds of fragrant perfumes and garlands, he presents whatever else has been obtained.
(7) Black protective cords (*pratisarāḥ*) or black thread [are also given]. (8)

With a medium-sized leaf of the *palāśa* tree, while the [disciple] has taken hold of the fire, he should offer oblations of clarified butter, saying: "Svāhā to Yama! Svāhā to Antaka! Svāhā to Dharma! Svāhā to Ananta! Svāhā to Vaivasvata! Svāhā to Mṛtyu! Svāhā to Viṣṇu! (9).

Having offered with the *vyāhṛtis*, and having laid down leaves of the *arka* or *udumbara* trees with their tips pointing eastward, he presents the sacrificial food upon the middle one, which serves as the northern altar (*uttaravedi*), with the three verses beginning, "Press the Soma for Yama. (10).

On the southern *uttaravedi*, he offers the oblation to the two dogs with the verse: "O Yama, those two dogs of yours, the four-eyed guardians who watch over men and protect the paths—to them entrust this man, O King; bestow upon him well-being and freedom from disease. Om! (11) On the northern *uttaravedi*, he offers the oblation to the two messengers of Yama with the verse: "The broad-nosed, insatiable, long-tongued messengers of Yama wander among the people. May they give us back our life here today, so that we may behold the sun, for our welfare. Om! (12)
With the three verses beginning "That which is his breath in the belly" (*yo 'sya kauṣṭhyaḥ*), he sings around [the mound] clockwise with the *Yamagādhā* verses.

(13) Having gone to the south of the water-pit, having arranged the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), and having bent the left knee, he pours out three handfuls of water with the formula, "Food, food, *svadhā* to the fathers! (14) Having restrained their breaths, they walk seven steps forward with the seven *Vyāhṛtis*. It is known from tradition: "The three worlds are heaven; thus the seven worlds become descended. (15)

Having replenished his vital breaths again with the mantra, "I have performed the praise of Dadhikrāvan," he returns to him and pays homage to the water-jars with the formula, "Homage to the water-jars that receive homage; homage to the water-jars that receive homage. Then, for whatever purpose they offer salutations, he recites the three verses beginning with, "Yama has established... and "All those are placed in Yama," as well as, "The eagle upon the vault of heaven. They carry the vessel away. 16.
To the north, he himself goes to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) with the five *vyāhṛtis* and with this section of the text beginning, "For wide indeed is King [Varuṇa]. 17.
It is known that those who recite [this] become free from all impurities at the ritual bath (avabhṛtha) and possess healthy bodies. 18.
With the four verses beginning "Trita, he whom Yama gave," one worships the Āditya. 19.
With the verse "Upwards from the darkness," they tie on the protective amulet (pratisara). 20.

Having taken all fragrant perfumes and garlands, and having offered the oblation for the expiation of all faults (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) with clarified butter, they immerse themselves in the water while consuming the remnants of the oblation, saying: "Thou art food; thou art the food of immortality. Of thee, who hast been drunk by Death, who hast died, who hast been made *svagā*, who art honeyed, and who hast been invited—I, being invited, partake.
(21) He pours out the remainder for his dear son who speaks kindly, or for the wife of the son; it belongs to the son. (22)

"Yama, having taken the sacrificer who has departed from here onto his lap like a father taking his son, shall go as a friend; he shall not go by a path different from his own, but shall go together with him.
Thus indeed said Baudhāyana.
This is the twenty-first chapter in the first book of the *Gṛhyaśeṣa* of Baudhāyana.
Now, in the first book, the twenty-second chapter:
I shall proclaim the Tṛṇagarbha rite, which removes all sins, destroys all diseases, and is righteous and eternal; know this! 1.

During all planetary transits, during the eclipses of the moon and the sun, on both types of festival days (parvan), at birth, and likewise during the Śravaṇa asterism; ||2|| as well as when one is overcome by disease, and likewise during the Vyatīpāta yoga.
One should begin in a pure place smeared with cow dung;
(3) the purification for all four castes shall likewise take place there, having invited four pure Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas. (4)
Having first established the preceptor— the best of the twice-born and an expert in all scriptures—
in the eastern direction, and having positioned those other brahmins in the cardinal directions and the center,
one should fashion a square altar out of pure rice grains.
In the center of that, one should have a lotus drawn, and then place a golden lotus within it.
Seated upon that, covered with cloth after cloth,
and accompanied by the preceptor and Brahmins, one should cause the benedictions to be recited.
Having covered it with pure grass, especially with dūrvā grass,
the preceptor should then mutter either the Thousand Names of Viṣṇu or those of Śiva; or else,
he should mutter the Gāyatrī, or a mantra dedicated to Śiva or Viṣṇu.
The Brahmins should recite Vaiṣṇava mantras all around;
then, having lifted up a blade of grass, one should sprinkle the madhuparka in due order and gaze upon the vessel of ghee while reciting the Pāvamānī verses.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and to the Brāhmaṇas according to one's ability;
one should give garments to the preceptor and especially gold.
One should also offer a vessel of ghee to him and pay obeisance to that preceptor.
Having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to them according to the prescribed rule, especially one of distinction, he attains the world of Viṣṇu or even the world of Śiva;
freed from all diseases, he shall obtain all his desires. 12–13.
One should offer grass, especially to cows, with the Gosūkta;
whoever hears or even recites it attains the supreme goal.
The wise man who is dear to the God shall attain the station of the God.
"One shall attain the station of the god," so said the venerable Bodhāyana. 15.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the first book of the *Gṛhyaśeṣa* of Bodhāyana.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter in the first book.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the consecration of a king.

(1) On the fifth or the thirteenth day of the waxing moon, under the asterism Tiṣya or Śroṇā, or under whichever other auspicious asterisms there may be, on the preceding day itself, he should feed an even number of Brāhmaṇas.

(2) Having caused them to pronounce benedictions, he should choose as his domestic priest (*purohita*) a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with noble birth, lineage, sacred learning, and good conduct, [saying]: "For intention thee; for desire thee. (3)
The domestic priest mutters: "For his protection, [I invoke] his intention; for the fulfillment of his desire, [I invoke] Indra's thoughts. (4) He himself mutters:
"I place before my mind the divine Intention, the mother of sacrifice, who is easy to invoke for me. Whatever I desire with my mind, may I obtain that wish, established within my heart. (5)

Then, when the sun has set, having fashioned a lotus-shaped mandala, he prepares [the materials]: rice, barley, sesame, and beans; the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*); sea water and river water; and a throne made of *udumbara* wood covered with a tiger skin. Having gathered these together with golden jars and the horns of cows, he sets them down, according to the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning, "Because all human things are together.

(6) In the north-eastern part of the house, according to the procedure for the *pākayajña*, he offers eight thousand oblations of rice, barley, sesame, and beans, using the *Vyāhṛtis*, the *Mahāvyāhṛtis*, the *Sāvitrī*, and the *Tryambaka* mantra. (7)
Then, having worshipped the Goddess Śrī in the southern half according to the ritual procedure of the Śrīsūkta, he washes the crown.

(8) Having taken cow-urine with the Gāyatrī, cow-dung with "Gandhadvārā," milk with "Āpyāyasva," curd with "Dadhikrāvṇo," clarified butter with "Śukram asi," and Kuśa-water with "Devasya tvā," [he performs the cleansing].
(9) Having washed the crown, he ties the protective thread with the mantra: "pratatte adya śipiviṣṭa. (10)
He should consecrate King Rājavāhana first. 11.
Then, on that night, he should either remain seated or lie down. 12.

Then, when the sun has risen, having placed a throne and spread a tiger skin upon it, he sits upon it facing the east; taking golden jars, he draws water with the three verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ" and with the four verses beginning "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ. 13.

Having sprinkled [the candidate] with the two verses beginning "Ava te heḍaḥ" and "Uduttamam," as well as with the verse "Āpo bhadrāḥ," and then with those mantras containing the word *ap* (water), those addressed to Varuṇa, those of golden color (*hiraṇyavarṇābhiḥ*), the *pāvamānī* hymns, and other purificatory (*pavitra*) mantras, he then sprinkles him with water from the horns of a bull. 14.

"The essence which is in the flow of the waters—that I sprinkle upon this [candidate], the son of such-and-such, for the sake of splendor, prosperity, fame, Vedic luster, and the enjoyment of food. When he has been thus cleansed, they shout together; this is the same procedure up to the wiping of the face. 15. At this time, one should also sprinkle Rājavāhana. 16.
Having bathed [the image], he gives a thousand *niṣkas* and a hundred female slaves to the Brahmins.
(17) Having caused the recitation of benedictions (*svastyayana*), he places upon [the image] either a crown or a turban, saying: "O Agni, O glorious one, bestow glory upon this [person].
(18) Then he causes the sound of drums to be made; "they beat the drums," so says the *Brāhmaṇa*. (19)
"Having performed the circumambulation, he protects his own kingdom," so said the venerable Bodhāyana.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the first book of the *Bodhāyana-gṛhya-śeṣa-sūtra*.
[The twenty-fourth chapter in the first book follows.]
Now, therefore, we shall explain the hundredfold consecration (śatābhiṣeka).

For one who has lived for a hundred years, or who has seen a thousand moons, during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion—having performed the rites from the tracing of the sacrificial ground up to the pouring of the praṇītā water—one prepares a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of the fire, mixed with rice or barley, made of gold according to his means, and of appropriate size.

There, having washed vessels made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, and having wrapped them with thread, one should place the principal vessel in the center; then, having scattered perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, fruits, and jewels, one should set out the other vessels in the order starting from Indra (the east), namely to the south, west, and north. Having placed a strainer across [the mouth], filled them with pure water, scattered the nine gems into the central principal vessel, covered it with a new cloth, and adorned it with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps—

In the center, he invokes Brahmā into the principal pitcher; then, in the order beginning with Indra, he invokes Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, Caturmukha, and Hiraṇyagarbha, saying, "I invoke [Hiraṇyagarbha]. Having performed the rites from the laying on of the enclosing sticks (*paridhāna*) up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), he worships the deity. Having purified them with the three verses beginning "The waters are indeed our source of bliss," with the four verses beginning "Golden-hued, pure, and purifying," and with this entire section beginning "Pavamāna, the dweller in heaven," he then honors them with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, saying, "Salutation to [the deity] named so-and-so."
"Salutation to such-and-such," [he says]. "With food, svāhā to such-and-such; svāhā to such-and-such. 3.

Then he offers from the cooked [food], reciting the invitatory verse (puronuvākyā): "Bestowing life upon you from every side," and he makes the offering with the offering verse (yājyā): "O Agni, giver of life. 4.

Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter (ājya) with the six verses of the Brahma-sūkta beginning with "The Brahman was born first," and with the five sections of the "Agni is long-lived" hymn. From the Sviṣṭakṛt offering onwards, the rite is established as usual until the gift of the cow and the granting of the boon. 5.
Then, in front of the fire, he places the remnants of the oblation upon clumps of *dūrvā* grass with two verses beginning, "May life be yours, O Agni, the giver of life" (Āyuṣṭe).

6. Then he performs the consecration over him with water. With four verses beginning, "In which there are fragrances, tastes, and colors," he sprinkles him verse by verse using the principal pitcher, proceeding in the order starting from Indra. With four verses beginning, "Those that flow eastward," he performs the consecration according to the meter. With the verse beginning, "Those that flow upward," he sprinkles him with the remainder of the contents of the principal pitcher. 7.

Having put on unwashed garments, sipped water, and adorned himself, he then causes him to gaze at the sun with the verses: "Up from the darkness," "Up that bright one," "That eye, established by the gods," and "It has risen. (8) Then, returning by the same way he came, having spread out an Erakā-grass mat with its fringes directed eastward, he sits down upon it facing the east. Having placed the sacrificial oblation, clarified butter, and gold into a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or bronze, he looks at them while closing and opening his eyes, and then presents them to a Brāhmaṇa. (9)

Then, having mounted his chariot, having circumambulated the village, and having entered his home to the sound of drums and with the recitation of the *Svastisūkta*, he gives a gift to his teacher, honors the Brāhmaṇas, and causes them to pronounce blessings; he purifies twenty-one generations—ten preceding, ten following, and himself—and through his sons and grandsons, he attains after sixty thousand years the world of heaven and union (*sāyujya*) and residence in the same world (*salokatā*) with Brahman. Thus said the venerable Bodhāyana. 10.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the first book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣa*.

Now, therefore, the hundredfold consecration; now, therefore, the royal consecration, which indeed removes all sins and is itself proclaimed as the sacrifice to Yama. Now, therefore, the pacification of elephants; now, therefore, the pacification of horses. Now, therefore, the rites for the house; now, the procedure for the worship of the nine planets. Now, therefore, the offering to the planets and guests; now, therefore, the binding of the *pratisarā* amulet. Now, it is indeed said: "Every year," or "in the seventh or eighth month. Now, when the oblation has been offered, it is well known. Now, therefore, the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*); now, therefore...

The deities of the *puṇyāha* [rite]. Now, on a pure and level spot—in all cases of *darvīhoma* offerings. Now, therefore, the rule for strewing [the grass]. Now, therefore, the defect regarding the sand. Now, therefore, the rule for the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*). Now, therefore, that which is unprecedented. The fire beginning with the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). Now, therefore, the seven *pākayajña* sacrifices. 24.

Now, therefore, [concerning] the seven *pākayajñas*. The fire [is established] at the initiation (*upanayana*) and subsequent rites. Now, therefore, [concerning] that which is unprecedented (*apūrva*). Now, therefore, [concerning] the rule for the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*). Now, therefore, [concerning] the defect regarding the sand. Now, therefore, [concerning] the rule for the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*). [This applies] in all cases of *darvī-homas*. Now, on a pure and level spot. Now, therefore, [concerning] the deities of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*). Now, therefore, [concerning] the auspicious day itself. Now, when the offering has been made, it is well known. In the seventh or eighth month. Now, year after year. Now, indeed, it is said. Now, therefore, [concerning] the binding of the *pratisara* amulet. Now, therefore...

The offering for the planets and guests; now, the procedure for the worship of the nine planets; now, concerning household duties; now, the pacification of horses; now, the pacification of elephants; the sacrifice to Yama has been proclaimed by himself, which indeed removes all sins; now, the consecration of a king; now, the hundred-fold consecration. 24.

Thus ends the first book of the *Bodhāyanagṛhyaśeṣa*. Now begins the second book. Now, therefore, we shall explain the *pañcamī-śrāddha*. Beginning in the month of Śiśira, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight or the seventh day of the dark fortnight, one desiring a son should undergo initiation (*dīkṣā*) for one year. On the evening preceding that [first anniversary], after the *aupāsana* oblation has been offered, he should, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "I shall perform [the rite] during the first year.
(1) When the mental resolve has been made, he fasts in the evening and invites at least three Brahmins. (2)
Having washed their feet and adorned them with perfumes and other offerings, he says: "O sons, you must desire [this]; tomorrow the fifth *śrāddha* will take place, and you should show me your favor.
(3) On the following day, having invited them and washed their feet, he says: "Today the *śrāddha* takes place.
(4) At midday, there is the third invitation. (5)
The digging of the pit and so forth are as in the monthly *śrāddha*.
(6) One should perform the *śrāddha* for the paternal ancestors and the *śrāddha* for the maternal great-grandfathers.

(7) Then, having performed the "mouth-of-fire" rite (*agnimukha*) and having performed the oblation (*homa*) as in the monthly *śrāddha*, one should also perform the oblations separately for each. (8)
Having adorned [the Brahmins] with garments, ornaments, earrings, and so forth, and having caused them to recite, "May there be prosperity," he should feed them. 9.
At the time of the meal, there shall be the recitation of the *Divākīrtya*, the narration of meritorious stories, and the recitation of the *Smṛtis*. 10.

Having bowed to those who have sipped water for purification (*ācānta*), and having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his means after they have eaten, and having again caused them to recite, "It is accomplished" (*siddham*), he should dismiss them, follow them as far as the door, perform the offerings of rice-balls (*piṇḍadāna*) as in the monthly *Śrāddha* ceremony, and thereafter the husband and wife should eat the remainder. 11.
He causes the wife to eat the middle portion of the rice-ball. 12.
On the day before and on the night after [the funeral], those who have eaten at the *śrāddha* should not engage in eating, sexual intercourse, or similar activities. 13.
By acting thus, the son becomes endowed with a [prosperous] retinue; the son does not perish. Therefore, one should perform the *pañcamī-śrāddha*. 14.

The etymological derivation of "putra" is as follows: *pud* refers to hell; because he protects (*trāyate*) from that, he is called a *putra*. "He who has no son has no refuge," so said the venerable Bodhāyana. (15) Thus ends the first chapter in the second book of the *Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra* of Bodhāyana. Now begins the second chapter in the second book.

Now we shall explain the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite). During the bright fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce "An auspicious day!", "Prosperity!", and "Success!", he then performs the rites from the drawing of the lines for the sacrificial ground up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*). He offers an oblation of cooked food with the verse: "To the wise seer, the pure one, the bull, the vigorous one, let there be a word of praise; may that from which fear arises be free from fear for us. I sacrifice away the wrathful gods, Svāhā! (1)

Having taken a portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and placed it within the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he then offers additional oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*), saying: "Svāhā to the eldest! Svāhā to the best! Svāhā to the youngest! Svāhā to the state of being the youngest! Svāhā to the firm foundation! Svāhā to the state of being firmly established! Svāhā to the household! Svāhā to the path! Svāhā to the lord of the path! Svāhā to Prajāpati! Svāhā to Brahman! (2) From the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the ritual is established until the gift of the cow and the granting of the boon. (3)
He consecrates the sacrificial food with the mantra: "We choose that food of the god Savitṛ; we meditate upon it as the most excellent, the most sustaining, and the swiftest gift of Bhaga.
(4) To the west of the fire, both the wife and the husband should eat it with the mantra: "The desirable [gift] of Savitṛ.
(5) Having eaten and then sipped water, he touches his belly with two verses: "O Indra, from whatever we fear... and "The giver of well-being, the lord of the people... (6)

"One should meditate in the mind upon whatever desire one desires"—thus is the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) explained. 7. Thus ends the second chapter of the second book in the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣa*.
Now begins the third chapter of the second book.

Then, having been adorned with auspicious items, they should receive [the bride] from the women with the *invakās* [constellation]; she is welcomed by the suitors when she has stepped forward. Whichever daughter one might desire, thinking, "May she be dear," he should give her away under the *niṣṭyā* [constellation]. She indeed becomes dear, and she does not return [to her father's house] again; such is the rule according to the Brāhmaṇas.

(1) The word *invakā* refers to Mṛgaśīrṣa, and the word *niṣṭyā* refers to Svāti. (2) One should avoid [giving away] a girl who is asleep, weeping, or has gone out at the time of the formal request for her hand. (3)

One should avoid a girl who has been given away, one who is hidden, one who is radiant, one who is a bull-like, one who is bent, one who is a *śarabha*, one who is misshapen, one who is bald, one who is frog-like, one who is from a place of conflict, one who is red, one who is a boundary-guard, one who is a friend, one who is her own younger sister, and one who brings rain.

(4) Those named after constellations, rivers, trees, mountains, servants, birds, and ghosts are censured; furthermore, all those whose names end in or have the letters *ra* or *la* as penultimate sounds should be avoided in marriage. (5)

Having placed various substances concealed within the range of her power—namely, various seeds mixed together, dust from the sacrificial altar (*vedi*), a clod of earth from a field, dung, and a clod of earth from a cemetery—one should say, "Touch them. Upon touching these, as indicated by the respective signs, there is success; however, they declare the last one to be the most significant.
(6) One should marry a woman who is endowed with noble lineage, good character, and auspicious marks, and who is free from disease.
(7) "A man of noble lineage, good character, and auspicious marks, who is eloquent and free from disease"—this is the excellence of the groom. (8)
Some say that one should apply effort toward that object upon which the binding of the mind and eyes is fixed, and not attend to anything else.

(9) Now, if one should desire to bring about non-existence, one should have the coarse *āḍhārikā* seeds made into powder by others, and while she is asleep, one should scatter it into her private parts, saying: "As the string from a bow, so do I stretch away your heart's anger; O Indra, having removed his malice, [place it] among other men, not elsewhere than me.
(10) For the sake of success, one washes [the powder] with the urine of a brown cow. (11)

Then, at the time of birth, having quickly placed a water-pot at the head [of the bed] for an easy delivery, he touches her belly while she is groaning, saying: "Just as the wind blows, just as the ocean surges, so let your fetus stir; let it come forth together with the afterbirth. (12) Now, if the afterbirth does not fall away, he wipes the belly with *darbha* grass, saying: "O sesame seed, fall away! You are not flesh, nor are you a covering. O solid one, fall away; I shall sleep. (13) The birth-rite (*jātakarma*) is performed according to the established rule. (14)
Thus ends the third chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the fourth chapter in the second book: Next is the oblation for one desiring offspring. 1.

On an auspicious lunar day in the bright fortnight, on the new moon, at the equinox, or at the solstice, having prepared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung either on a riverbank or in the shade of an *aśvattha* tree, and having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce "An auspicious day!", "Prosperity!", and "Success!", he should establish Brahmā in the eastern direction, Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ on the two sides—Dhātṛ to the south and Vidhātṛ to the north.

Then one should first worship them. Having invoked Brahmā Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin with the mantra, "I invoke Hiraṇyagarbha," one offers water for the feet (*pādya*) with the Sāvitrī verse and should present the offering with the Sāvitrī verse. With these very names, one should offer white rice to Brahmā, mung-bean rice to Dhātṛ, and yellow rice to Vidhātṛ. Then, having sipped water with the Sāvitrī verse and offered oblations one hundred and eight times with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), one worships Brahmā with the words: "Salutation to Speech, salutation to the Lord of Speech, salutation to the Great Brahman, I pay homage"; likewise, "Salutation to Dhātṛ, salutation to Vidhātṛ."

He should worship the fire with the mantra: "Obeisance to Agni! Seven-rayed, seven-tongued, Agni is established sevenfold. Seven indeed are all beings; for who is it that establishes Agni? You are the Reality (Tattvamasi), you are the All (Viśvamasi), you are the Source (Yonirasi). (5) Then, having summoned a woman and bathed her with one thousand and eight Palāśa leaves while reciting the Sāvitrī, he should offer oblations with the Puruṣasūkta. With the remnants of those oblations, he should offer them upon her head, and he should pay obeisance with the syllable Om (Praṇava). (6) He adorns the Adhvaryu priest with a garment and earrings. (7)
"Then she becomes pregnant," so said the Blessed Bodhāyana. 8.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣa-sūtra.
Now begins the fifth chapter in the second book.

Then, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity!", and having performed the rites from the drawing of the lines for the sacrifice to the gods up to the preparation of the *praṇītā* water, one should draw a circle of the sun in front of the fire, strew grass around it, spread a mandala clockwise with sixteen *arka* leaves whose tips point inward, sprinkle it with scented water, scatter flowers over it, and fumigate it with incense; then, having filled a *praṇītā* vessel with water and purified it, one should invoke the Sun into that [mandala]. 1.
"I shall board the boat of the Sun—full, with its seat above, leakless, capable of carrying one across, and possessing a hundred oars—for my well-being. Om, obeisance to the Sun. (2)

Having performed the rites from the putting on of the garments up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), he offers an oblation from the cooked food with the verse: "May the divine Savitṛ come; may he approach on his golden, well-rolling chariot, bringing the blessed one, skilled in action through wisdom, bestowing abundance and holy wealth. Having offered this single oblation, he cuts a portion for the Sviṣṭakṛt from the northern half, places it within the enclosing sticks, and gratifies Āditya with various kinds of food, saying: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Āditya; obeisance! Klaṃ! O you who roar like a river against the banks!"
"May the debtors, the non-debtors, the gods, and the seers, having loosened the knots of the thighs, loosen the joints of my limbs with a mantra—svāhā!

(3) Then he offers oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with these four hymns: *sthavire svāhā*, *tejase svāhā*, *yam indram āhuḥ svāhā*, *id vatsam ud u tyam citram tat cakṣuḥ*, *ya udagāt maśśuciṣat*, *tvayā sumṛḷīkāḥ*, *aviśvadevam sūryo devīm*—these amount to twelve. There are twelve months in a year; by means of the year, one obtains all desires. (4) The ritual from the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established [as usual], up to the granting of the boon and the cow. (5)

Having gratified them mentally and meditated upon them, he causes [the water] to flow: "Savitar, Mitra, and Aryaman have lifted it up; with his yoke, he has slain all enemies. Rest in the *Ṛk* verses, which are great and rich in heroes, in the *Rathantara*; Svāhā! Rest on the earth, in the *Vāmadevya*; Svāhā! Rest in the intermediate space, in the *Bṛhat*; Svāhā! With the *Bṛhat*, I support thee in heaven!
(6) Then, taking these [verses], he rises together with the *Sāhara* leaves, reciting: "Up with life... (7)

Having gone to where there is water, he pours out water with the formula: "I send you to the ocean, your own source; enter it. May I be without flaw among my offspring; may this milk of mine not be spilled. (8) With his hand holding a strainer, he sprinkles himself with water using the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*, the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*, and this entire section beginning with *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*; then he sprinkles himself with the verses beginning with *yāḥ sugandhā rasā varṇāḥ*. (9)

"This [rite] bestows both kinds of merit—pertaining to sons and grandsons, conferring long life, leading to heaven, and attaining union with and residence in the same world as the sun and moon. Thus he should illuminate it with this [mantra]. (10) Thus ends the fifth chapter in the second book of the *Bodhāyanīya-gṛhyaśeṣa-sūtra*.
The sixth chapter in the second book begins.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual for the adoption of a son. (1) A son is produced from the union of blood and semen, having the mother and father as its cause; in the acts of giving, abandoning, or selling him, the mother and father are the agents. However, one should not give away or adopt an only son, for he is for the sake of the lineage of the ancestors.
(2) A woman, moreover, may neither give nor adopt a son without the permission of her husband. (3)

Intending to adopt a son, he prepares two garments, two earrings, a finger-ring, a teacher who has mastered the Vedas, sacrificial grass made of *kuśa*, and fuel-sticks made of *parṇa* leaves. (4) Then, having announced his intention among his kinsmen and to the king, and having served food to the Brahmins either on a common seat or within the house, and having caused them to pronounce "An auspicious day!", "Prosperity!", and "Success!", he then performs the rites beginning with the digging of the sacrificial site up to the pouring of the *praṇītā* water; then, going to the presence of the giver, he should beg, saying, "Give me a son," and the other replies, "I give. (5)

He receives that son with the words: "I receive you for the sake of dharma; I receive you for the sake of continuity. (6) Then, having adorned him with a garment, earrings, and a ring, and having performed the rites from the putting on of the garment up to the offering to Agni, he offers an oblation of cooked food. Having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*): "He who, honoring you with a yearning heart... (RV 10.38.1), he offers with the offering verse (*yājyā*): "To which virtuous man, O Jātavedas, you [grant wealth]... (RV 10.38.2). (7) Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with the *vyāhṛtis*. Having offered these, the ritual is established from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards until the giving of the cow as a boon. (8)
Then he gives the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*): these two garments, these two earrings, and this ring. 9.
If, after this has been done, a legitimate son (*aurasa*) is born, he becomes entitled to a fourth share; so said the venerable Bodhāyana. 10.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the second book of the *Bodhāyanīya-gṛhya-śeṣa*.
In the second book, the seventh chapter:
Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). 1.

When it has become worn out, torn, or destroyed, one should wash one's hands and feet, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and take a thread spun by a pure, bathed Brāhmaṇa girl or a Brāhmaṇa widow who has performed *ācamana*. Having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, one should wash with water three threads—each measuring four finger-breadths and ninety-six [threads] in total, whether circular or otherwise—reciting the three verses beginning with "The waters are indeed our source of bliss" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*) and the verse beginning with "Golden-colored, pure, and purifying" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*).

Having performed the purification with the section beginning "The purifying one, the winner of heaven" (RV 9.1.6–9), he hangs [the image] upon the branch of a sacrificial tree—such as the *bilva*, *khadira*, *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, or bamboo—or wherever there may be a pure place, such as a temple, a cow-pen, a riverbank, or any other clean spot; having suspended it, he binds it while it is still alive, first with his right hand turned away (apasavya), saying: "Homage to the ancestors. (2)

When it is completed, having taken [the image] in his hand, he establishes it, saying: "Oṃ bhūḥ, I establish; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I establish; Oṃ suvaḥ, I establish; Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ, I establish. Having thus established it, he recites with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apassavya) the *anuvāka* beginning with "bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ" and "Ojas, bala. 3.

Then, having tripled [the thread] with the Sāvitrī mantra, he should consecrate the rightward winding with "Bhūr agniṃ ca," the middle winding with "Bhuvo vāyuṃ ca," the upward winding with "Suvar ādityaṃ ca," and the threefold winding with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaś candramasaṃ.
(4) Then he ties it at the end of the thread with the four [verses] beginning with "yathā naḥ śreyasaḥ karat," so that there are two folds in the middle.
(5) Having established it again with "tāṃ bhūḥ pratiṣṭhāpayāmi" and having murmured the Ṛgvedic verse "uśantas tvā havāmahe," he makes it firm by circling it to the right. (6)

Taking the measure of the three—Brahmā, Īśvara, and Viṣṇu—one should [prepare the thread]. 7. The thread should be doubled by the [measure of] the threads; it is tripled by Viṣṇu. For one who knows the four Vedas, there should be four [loops]; for one who knows three, three; for one who knows two, there should be two; and for one who knows only one Veda, there should be just one. 8. Thus the rule for the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) has been explained. 9.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣa.
Now begins the eighth chapter in the second book:
Next, the initiation (upanayana) of the Rājanya and the Vaiśya is well known. 1.

The difference is only this much: ||2|| the teacher himself offers from the cooked [oblation]. Having untied the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), he offers for a Kṣatriya with *triṣṭubh* verses: "I sprinkle Agni for thee," "I sprinkle thee," "O Agni, giver of life, enjoying the oblation. For a Vaiśya, he offers with *jagatī* verses: "The guardian of the people, the watchful one, has been born," "Thee, O Agni, the human clans praise," "Seven are thy kindling-sticks, O Agni, seven thy tongues. ||4||
For a Vaiśya who is a chariot-maker, there is only this much difference: he offers cooked food with the verse, "That excellent glory of Savitṛ... (RV 3.62.10).

Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with the six verses beginning, "For Kṣetrī, for thee; for Nirṛti, for thee," in accordance with their respective meters. For a Vaiśya, he does not offer with verses in the Jagatī meter.
Then, having placed the remains of the offering in front of the fire, he should cease.

One born of a Brāhmaṇa from a Kṣatriya woman is exactly like a Brāhmaṇa; this much is the difference: for him there is an additional secondary offering (*upahoma*) with the *vyāhṛtis* and the formula "For the sake of the field, thee" (*kṣetriyai tvā*).
(8) For an Ambaṣṭha, it is like a Kṣatriya; the secondary offering is exactly "For the sake of the field, thee.
(9) One born of a Kṣatriya from a Vaiśya woman is exactly like a Kṣatriya; the secondary offering is "For the sake of the field, thee" and with the Sāvitrī verse. (10)
But one born from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother should perform [the rite] silently, like a Vaiśya. 11.
The Sāvitrī mantras for the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya, respectively, are: *gāyatrī*, *triṣṭubh*, and *jagatī*; and *tatsaviturvareṇyam* and *āsatyena yuñjate manaḥ*. 12.

The ritual of returning home (*samāvartana*) has been described. From the time of his return, the *snātaka* should exit and enter the village by the eastern or the northern gate. Outside [the village], he may release his speech after having first placed his hand [on a support]. Having bathed as prescribed, having offered libations (*tarpaṇa*) to the gods, the seers, and the ancestors, and having sat down on *darbha* grass facing the east while holding *darbha* and *dūrvā* grass, he should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). He should then recite the *Sāvitrī* one thousand times, or one hundred times, or an unlimited number of times—at least ten times—after having studied the Vedas.
"He should study either a *praśna* or an *anuvāka*, as far as he is able," so it is known; "then he goes to his home; whatever he gives, that is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)," says the Brāhmaṇa.

13. Then he worships the deities and performs the *vaiśvadeva* offering; the presentation of the *bali* oblations is well-known. 14. Now, indeed, it is said: "These five great sacrifices proceed continuously and conclude continuously—the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to the beings, the sacrifice to men, and the sacrifice to Brahman. This is the sequence. 15.

Now follows the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*): "To the gods, svāhā! and with the *vyāhṛtis*. Even if it consists merely of a fuel-stick, that sacrifice to the gods is thus completed. 16. Now follows the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*): one should feed Brāhmaṇas representing the ancestors, or else, having strewn Darbha grass with its tips pointing south to the south of the fire, and having honored and adorned them with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, one offers a rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) upon them, saying: "To the ancestors, svadhā! Adoration! Even if it consists merely of water, that sacrifice to the ancestors is thus completed. 17.

Now follows the sacrifice to the beings (*bhūtayajña*). Having strewn darbha grass with tips pointing eastward to the north of the fire and having adorned it with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, he offers an oblation upon them, saying, "Obeisance to the beings," extending as far as the flowers; thus the sacrifice to the beings is completed. (18) Now follows the sacrifice to men (*manuṣyayajña*). He should give food to Brāhmaṇas from his vessel of cooked rice; thus the sacrifice to men is completed. (19) Now the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*) has been explained. (20)

What indeed is the sequence of the obligatory rites? They are: the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*), the attendance upon the fires (*agnyupasthāna*), the obligatory private recitation (*nityasvādhyāya*), the domestic duties, the bath, the attendance upon the sun, the libation (*tarpaṇa*), the silent sacrifice (*japayajña*), the worship of the household deities (*gṛhadevatārcana*), the *vaiśvadeva* offering, the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), the sacrifice of the self (*ātmayajña*), the twilight worship, the *agnihotra*, the sacrifice of the self, and retiring to bed. This is the sequence for one who performs the oblation after sunrise, for one who maintains the perpetual fire (*ajasrāgnihotrī*), and for one who performs the oblation before sunrise; for the latter, the sequence is the *agnihotra* followed by the twilight worship. These obligatory rites are well known to extend from just before dawn until retiring to bed. Morning and evening, accompanied by his wife, he should increase their mutual affection.

During the first watch of the night, his wife lies down; from midnight until the *brāhma-muhūrta*, she remains on a lower bed. Then, having risen, he begins his daily obligatory rites. (24) Thus the initiation (*upanayana*) has been explained.
(25) Thus ends the eighth chapter in the second book of the *Bodhāyanīya-gṛhyaśeṣa*.
Now begins the ninth chapter of the second book.
Now we shall explain the sacramental rites for those who are mentally deficient, deaf, and mute.
(1) The season [for conception] may be according to one's desire. (2)

Having fed the Brahmins under an auspicious constellation and having caused them to pronounce blessings, he shaves his hair; then, having caused him—who has bathed, is dressed in clean clothes, has tied his topknot, and wears the sacred thread—to sip water, he leads him to the place of sacrifice. 3.

Then, having performed the rites from the marking of the sacrificial ground for the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), he silently causes [the student] to place a sacrificial fuel-stick (samidh) smeared with clarified butter onto the fire. He silently places a stone [in his hand]. He silently causes him to put on a garment according to what is available. He silently ties the girdle (mekhalā) around him; he makes the knot with the appropriate mantra. He silently fastens the deerskin (ajina). He silently hands over the staff (daṇḍa). He gives him the name of a tree suitable for sacrifice. 4.
Then he takes hold of him by the right hand with the verse: "In whom the past and the future... 5.
Then he entrusts him to the deities with the words, "To the gods thee! (6).
Then he leads him forward with the words, "Of the god thee," performing everything except the utterance of the [student's] name. (7).
The teacher himself offers the cooked oblation with the verse, "That excellent glory of Savitṛ... (8).
Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with the six verses beginning "For Kṣetrī" and with the vyāhṛtis.
(9) Then, from the sviṣṭakṛt offering onwards, the rite is established as usual up to the gift of the cow and the granting of the boon.
(10) Then, in front of the fire, he places the remains of the oblation on leaves of a sacrificial tree; this has been explained previously. (11)
Then, taking from the cooked portion, he eats. 12.
According to some, the teacher alone should mutter all the mantras silently. 13.

According to some, those who are born impotent, the dull-witted, the eunuchs, the blind, those addicted to vices, the diseased, the insane, those with missing limbs, the deaf, those with extra limbs, those suffering from chronic illness, epileptics, those with vitiligo, those with leprosy, and those with long-term illnesses are explained by this same rule. 14.
15. He immediately offers the honey-mixture (madhuparka).

16. When three nights have passed, he performs [the rites] with the honey-mixture until the end of the vow. 17. Then he dismisses the fire with the verse: "O Agni, giver of life, enjoying the oblation..."
"Either the father or the brother should perform the self-entrustment," say some.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the second book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the tenth chapter in the second book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the consecration of the *aśvattha* tree. 1. The season may be according to one's desire. 2. Having fed the Brahmins under an auspicious lunar mansion and having had them pronounce blessings, he sweeps around the *aśvattha* tree from left to right with the verse: "In the *aśvattha* is your seat. 3.
Having honored him, he fastens on the sacrificial cord (yajñopavīta). 4.

Then, having performed the rites from the smearing of the altar for the sacrifice to the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), he silently causes a sacrificial fuel-stick (samidh) smeared with clarified butter to be placed [into the fire]. He silently causes a garment to be put on, according to what is available; he silently girds him with a belt (mekhalā); he ties the knot with a mantra; he silently fastens on a deerskin (ajina); he silently hands over a staff (daṇḍa); he gives him the name of a sacrificial tree. 5.
Then he should bring forward a *aśvattha* tree, omitting the mention of the deity with the formula "devasya tvā... 6.
The teacher himself offers the cooked oblation with the verse, "That excellent glory of Savitṛ...
(RV 3.62.10). Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with the six [verses] beginning with "For Kṣetriyā thee... and with the *vyāhṛtis*.
From the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the rite is established as usual until the giving of the cow and the granting of the boon.
Then, in front of the fire, he places the remains of the oblation upon *palāśa* leaves; that has been explained previously.
Then, taking [a portion] from what has been cooked, he presents it to him.
"The teacher alone should mutter all the mantras silently," says the venerable Bodhāyana.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣa.
Now begins the eleventh chapter in the second book:
Now follows the well-known initiation (upanayana) for one for whom the [sacrificial] oblation has not been offered. 1.
The difference is only this much:

[2] Having fed the boy, having smeared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung, and having spread auspicious items upon it, the teacher sits down facing east. To his front, the boy sits on *darbha* grass facing west. He sprinkles both kinds of water; he pours cold water into hot water. Having silently shaved the hair as in the tonsure ceremony (*caula*), having bathed him, clothed him, and adorned him, standing facing the sun, he puts on a skin or a garment as a sacred thread (*upavīta*) over the right shoulder, and raises his right arm.

"He takes up the left [arm]"—this refers to the *yajñopavīta* (sacrificial thread), according to the Brāhmaṇa. Having caused him, who wears the *yajñopavīta*, to sip water, he leads him to the place of sacrifice. "A black antelope skin for a Brāhmaṇa," and so forth; he fastens it like the *yajñopavīta*: four finger-breadths wide for a Brāhmaṇa, three finger-breadths for a Rājanya, and two finger-breadths for a Vaiśya.

Then, having said, "O sir, recite the Sāvitrī," some say that he should instruct it into the right ear of the boy. Having said, "From both ears, much has been heard," and having looked upward, he causes him to recite the Sāvitrī. (6) Then, in the evening and morning, he completes the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*) as is done by a householder.

(7) Then, having established the fire for him, having prepared the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*), having swept around [the fire] and poured water around it, he causes him to place fuel sticks upon the fire with the *vyāhṛtis*, and he causes him to stand in attendance [before the fire] according to the sixfold rule. (8)

Then, having taken that sacred ash (*bhasma*) pertaining to Agni and placed it in the left hand, one should mix it with water while reciting the mantras "mā nas toke" and "śaṃ no devīr abhiṣṭaye," and apply it as either a horizontal triple-mark (*tripuṇḍra*) or a single mark (*ekapuṇḍra*). For a Brāhmaṇa, it should be circular in shape; for a Kṣatriya, it should be semi-circular; and for a Vaiśya, [it should be square]. 9.

One applies the vertical marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) as follows: with the mantra "Sarasvatī" on the limbs; "Medhāvī" on the head; "Tejasvī" on the forehead; "Varcasvī" on the chest; "Brahmavarcasī" on the right arm; "Āyuṣmān" on the left arm; "Bhūyāsam" on the neck; and "Svasti" on the head. For other women, the same applies. Having washed his hands in the *prokṣaṇī* water and having paid homage, he should pour out the remainder of the *prokṣaṇī* water over the top of the house; so says the venerable Bodhāyana. Thus ends the eleventh chapter of the second book in the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣa*.
Now, the twelfth chapter of the second inquiry:

Regarding this matter—that people perform a marriage during the dark fortnight, on an inauspicious day, or while being impure, or if one should think that the marriage has not been successful through the rite—then one should perform the marriage again from the beginning of the household life (*āvasatha*).
Furthermore, if the fire should go out before the commencement of the *aupāsana* rite, one should perform the marriage again.
Now we shall explain remarriage.
During the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious constellation, having performed the *nāndīmukha* rite on the preceding day, he observes a fast.

Then, when the next day has dawned, having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Well-being! Prosperity!", both of them, being pure and having bathed, dressed in white garments and adorned with ornaments, he gazes at his wife. Beginning with the verse, "One who does not kill her brother," and having performed the rite up to the end of the seven steps, he then performs the rites from the tracing of the lines for the sacrifice to the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (the *agnimukha*). Then, having stood up near her, he touches the region of her heart; this procedure is established as complete up to the gift of the cow and the granting of the boon. From this point onward, he need not pay further attention [to the specific ritual details]. 5.

Furthermore, regarding remarriages, the venerable Bodhāyana states that one should omit these remnants of the marriage ceremony: the *pratisara* cord, the bath, the garment, the goad, the arrow, the prior meal, the *arghya* offering, and the three-night vow, and so forth.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter of the second book in the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhya-śeṣa-sūtra.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter of the second book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the installation of Viṣṇu. On the twelfth day, the eleventh day, or under the asterism Śroṇā, or under whichever other auspicious asterisms there may be, on the preceding day one should serve food to an even number of Brāhmaṇas and have them pronounce the blessings: "Auspicious day!", "Well-being!", and "Success!". When night has arrived, having fashioned an image with a golden base using the five products of a tawny cow (kapilā-pañcagavya), along with gold, barley, dūrvā grass, and sprouts, as well as leaves of the Aśvattha and Palāśa trees, one sprinkles it while reciting: "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss... (*āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*).

With the three verses beginning "The golden-colored, pure, purifying," with the four verses beginning "Pavamāna, who dwells in heaven," with this entire Anuvāka, and with the *vyāhṛtis*, [he performs the rite].
(1) He places barley-grains mixed with *dūrvā* sprouts, flowers, fruits, and unbroken rice upon the footstool with the verse, "Viṣṇu strode across this.
(2) He ties on the protective amulet (*pratisara*) with the verse, "I anoint the demon-slaying steed. (3)

Then, having covered the image with a band of *kuśa* grass and a garland beneath a garment made of unbleached cloth at one of the riverbanks, ponds, pools, waterfalls, lakes, or sacred fords (*tīrtha*), he places it there while reciting the verses, "May your wrath depart" (*ava te heḍaḥ*) and "Up from the highest" (*ud uttamam*).
4. Then, when the next day has dawned, four Brāhmaṇas, having bathed and put on new garments, should raise up the image while reciting, "Arise, O Lord of Prayer" (*uttiṣṭha brahmaṇaspate*). 5.

Then, having established [the vessel] in a pure place, one takes cow urine with the *gāyatrī* mantra, cow dung with "gandhadvārā," milk with "āpyāyasva," curd with "dadhikrāvṇo," clarified butter with "śukram asi jyotir asi," and water from *kuśa* grass with "devasya tvā. This is called the *pañcagavya*. Regarding this, it is said: "The milk of a tawny (*kapilā*) cow is best, the curd of a white cow is best, the clarified butter of a red cow is most excellent; the remaining two [mantras apply] to the brindled and black cows. With this [mixture], one bathes [the image] with the verse beginning "ā vo rājānam."

He sprinkles [him] with a jar containing the bark-decoction of all sacrificial trees—namely, *śamī*, *palāśa*, *khadira*, *bilva*, *aśvattha*, *vikaṅkata*, *nyagrodha*, *panasa*, *āmra*, *śirīṣa*, and *udumbara*—with this anuvāka beginning, "Your seat is in the *aśvattha* tree" (*aśvatthe vo niṣadanam*).
(9) He sprinkles [him] with a full jar containing gems, pearls, coral, silver, and copper submerged in water, with the nine verses beginning, "Golden-hued" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*).
(10) With gold and brilliance, he should release his sight with the mantra, "Thou art brilliance" (*tejo 'si*). (11)

Then, having performed the rites from the marking of the sacrificial ground for the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (the oblation to Agni), he offers an oblation of cooked food. Having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*), "Viṣṇoḥ nukam," he offers with the offering verse (*yājyā*), "Paraḥ mātrayā.

12. Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *Puruṣasūkta*. With the verse, "Idam viṣṇur vicakrame," he should touch [the image] at the feet. 13. Again, he should offer oblations of clarified butter with that same hymn; with the verse, "Viṣṇoḥ nukam," he should touch it at the region of the navel. 14.
Again, one should offer oblations of clarified butter with that same [mantra] and then touch the head [of the image] while reciting "May the gods protect us" (devā avantu naḥ). 15.
Again, one should offer oblations of clarified butter with that same [mantra] and then touch all the limbs with the Puruṣa Sūkta. 16.

At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, having raised [the image] while reciting "Upwards that Jātavedas" (udu tyaṃ jātavedasam), and having entered the temple while reciting the Śākuna Sūkta, and having placed gems, pearls, coral, gold, and silver upon the footstool, one should install Viṣṇu while reciting "Hence may the gods protect us" (ato devā avantu naḥ). 17.

Then, having offered perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps directed toward the sky and having risen, he performs the invocation (*āvāhana*) with the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*, both separately and collectively: "Oṃ bhūḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa; Oṃ suvaḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa; Oṃ bhūrbhuvassuvaḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa. Having thus invoked, he sprinkles [the deity] with a jar of water containing jewels. It is known from scripture: "One should sustain [the deity] with the *praṇava* as Brahman. (18) He offers a seat (*kūrca*) with the *praṇava*. (19) He offers water for the feet (*pādya*) with a jar containing *dūrvā* grass, *viṣṇukrāntā*, *śyāmāka* grain, and lotus petals. (20)
He offers water for sipping (ācamanīya) from a vessel mixed with cardamom, cloves, takkola, and camphor.
(21) He offers the guest-offering (arghya) consisting of water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, unbroken grains (akṣata), barley, rice, sesame seeds, and white mustard seeds.

(22) "These waters are peaceful, auspicious, most auspicious, pure, most pure, holy, most holy, immortal, having the taste of nectar; they are for washing the feet, for sipping, and for the guest-offering; may they be enjoyed! May they be accepted! May the Blessed Mahāviṣṇu accept them! Salutation to Viṣṇu!"—with these words, he offers the water for the feet, the water for sipping, and the guest-offering. (23)
With the mantra, "Viṣṇu strode across this," he unties the protective thread (pratisara).

24. Having paid homage to the deity, he then offers perfume with the words: "These perfumes are auspicious and divine, adorned with all fragrances; they are purified by the Brahman-purifier and purified by the rays of the sun.
25. May they be accepted! May the Blessed Lord Mahāviṣṇu accept them! Salutations to Viṣṇu! 26.
He offers a garland: "These garlands are auspicious, divine, and adorned with all manner of flowers; they are purified by the Brahman-purifier and purified by the rays of the sun.

(27) May they be accepted; may the Blessed Lord Mahāviṣṇu accept them. Salutations to Viṣṇu. (28) He offers flowers: "These flowers are auspicious, divine, and adorned with all manner of blossoms; they are purified by the Brahman-purifier and purified by the rays of the sun. (29)

"May it be accepted; may the Blessed Mahāviṣṇu accept it. Salutation to Viṣṇu. (30) He offers incense: "Incense is the essence of the forest trees; among all incenses, this is the supreme. It is to be smelled by all the gods; may this incense be accepted. (31) "May it be accepted; may the Blessed Mahāviṣṇu accept it. Salutation to Viṣṇu. (32)
Then he offers a lamp: "Light, brilliance, and splendor—dear to the gods at all times, the illuminator of all beings—may this lamp be accepted.
(33) "May the Blessed Lord Mahāviṣṇu accept it; obeisance to Viṣṇu. (34)

Then one should offer flowers with the twelve names; having performed libations with those same [names], one should present the sacrificial oblations consisting of *kṛsara*, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), rice with jaggery (*guḍaudana*), and turmeric rice. One should offer the milk-rice with the mantra "Pavitraṃ te vitatam. One should offer a full bowl of rice with jaggery soaked in ghee. One should offer *kṛsara* mixed with sesame and clarified butter as an oblation, saying: "Svāhā to Vāsudeva! Svāhā to Saṅkarṣaṇa! Svāhā to Pradyumna! Svāhā to Aniruddha! Svāhā to Īśānī! Svāhā to Śrī! Svāhā to Sarasvatī!"

*Puṣṭyai svāhā*! *Viṣṇave svāhā*! With the *Puruṣasūkta*: "viṣṇornukam," "tadasya priyam," "pratadviṣṇuḥ," "paro mātrayā," and "trirdevaḥ"—and with the twelve names, [offering] "amuṣmai svāhā, amuṣmai svāhā. From the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards until the gift of the cow and the granting of the boon, it is established. (35) Then he presents the oblation of all the sacrificial offerings (*sarvahaviṣāṃ bali*) with the verse: "We worship you alone, the primordial, ancient Puruṣa, the Lord of the Nāgas, the creator of the universe. You alone are the sacrifice ordained and to be performed; as the Self, accept this oblation from the Self. (36)

Then, in front of the fire, he places the remnants of the oblation upon *aśvattha* leaves with the mantra: "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ om. (37) He circumambulates the fire twice or four times, keeping it to his right, saying: "Salutation to Viśvabhuj; salutation to Sarvabhuj; salutation to Ātman; salutation to Paramātman; salutation to Sarvātman.

(38) A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) or a householder should feed twelve self-controlled Brahmins with rice cooked in turmeric broth. Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the installation of Viṣṇu. (39)
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhya-śeṣa-sūtra.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter of the second book:
"We shall now explain the rule for the daily service of the Great Puruṣa. (1)

Having bathed and become pure, having smeared a clean, level spot with cow-dung, and having fashioned an image of the God, he should worship it with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and flowers as they are available. Then, together with water and flowers, he should invoke the Mahāpuruṣa, saying: "Oṃ bhūḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa; Oṃ suvaḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa; Oṃ bhūrbhuvassuvaḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa. Having thus invoked him, he should offer a seat with *kuśa* grass, saying: "May the Blessed Mahāpuruṣa come hither.
This is the Blessed One’s seat of *darbha* grass—triple-stranded, green, and golden; may you graciously accept it. (2)

Then, having washed the vessel with water by means of the Sāvitrī [verse], and having poured water across the strainer, he should again consecrate the water with that same [verse] and show it to the Sun along with the strainer, saying: "Om! From here until the end. He gives the water for the feet (*pādya*) with the verse: "Three steps he strode out. Then, having purified the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) with the *vyāhṛtis*, he should give the *arghya* with the verse: "Over this Viṣṇu strode."
6. "From heaven, O Viṣṇu," with these words, he offers water for sipping.

7. Then he bathes him with the three verses beginning "The waters indeed are most beneficent," with the four verses beginning "Golden-colored, pure, purifying," with this entire Anuvāka beginning "Pavamāna, dwelling in the light," with the Vāmadevya verse beginning "Brahma was born first," and with the Yajus formula beginning "By the purifier."

Then he satiates him with water, saying, "I satiate Keśava," using the twelve names; having sprinkled water clockwise with the *vyāhṛtis*, he gives a garment with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), a sacred thread with the *sāvitrī*, water for rinsing the mouth with "This Viṣṇu strode across," perfume with "The door of fragrance," unbroken rice grains with "Irāvatī," flowers with "That of Viṣṇu," incense with the *sāvitrī*, a lamp with "Be thou kindled," and the offering of food with "For thee, O God. 8.
Then one should offer flowers to him with his twelve names. One should offer them at each step with the verse "He strode out three steps," ending with the words "May they be very gracious unto us.

(9) Then they praise him with Vaiṣṇava hymns from the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas. (10) One should dismiss the Puruṣa with the Vyāhṛtis, beginning with "Om Bhūḥ, I dismiss the Puruṣa," and so forth, saying: "May the Blessed Mahāpuruṣa depart for our well-being, for victory, and for a future meeting. (11)

"In the places where images are located, they say that one should perform [the rites] every day, with the exception of the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the dismissal (*udvāsana*)," so said the venerable Bodhāyana.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the second book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣa*.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter in the second book.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme ritual bathing of Viṣṇu.
A wise man should construct a bathing pavilion in front of the temple.
And in the center of that pavilion, he should prepare an altar.
Where the deity is established as immovable, there is no altar (vedikā) there.
Near that [deity], in that place, is the supreme location for the pitchers; their number is nine, and their installation is performed with the syllable Om (praṇava). 3.
Whatever is performed here is declared to be done with the *praṇava* alone;
the installation of the jars, however, begins from the east and ends at the northeast (Īśāna).
By this very sequence, all ritual action is prescribed here.
The wise one should place the ninth pitcher in the center at the very end.
One should place them all upon grass mats (kūrca) situated within a prastha measure of rice;
indeed, rice and śāli paddy are prescribed by the learned for the placement of the pitchers. 5–6.
In their absence, whatever common grain is desired here should fill all the jars; one should fill them with waters resembling pure crystal,
and among those, the central one should be filled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having placed [the vessels] upon a grass mat and having covered them all with shallow bowls (śarāva),
they should always be covered with nine new bowls made of clay;
the act of covering those [vessels] should be done with rice grains grown from paddy.
The self-possessed practitioner should worship all the jars in sequence with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; then, when the auspicious moment has arrived, he should invoke the Supreme Self.
Having invoked the deity according to the previously mentioned procedure, he should bring it to the altar.
Then, having worshipped Viṣṇu with all possible honors,
[the image] was brought to the altar, which had been smeared with fresh cow dung and strewn with unbroken grains of rice and paddy.

One should then, in an instant, install the God seated facing east in that very place where the image was fixed; no formal invocation (āvāhana) is required there, because the Supreme Lord is eternally present in that very spot. 13.
One should offer [the offerings] beginning with the seat in sequence, relying upon the Puruṣasūkta.
Then, taking up the water-pot, one should first perform the ritual bathing;
these mantras indeed are to be recited during the bathing of the Supreme Self. 14–15.
The Vaiṣṇava hymn, the seven verses beginning with "āpo hi," and the Pavamāna section are all remembered as being common to all [rites].
A wise person should not employ any mantra whatsoever that has not been specifically prescribed.
Having performed this ritual bathing of the person according to the rules,
one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) as food and complete the remainder of the rite; indeed, this is the ritual bathing with the water-pot that occurs during the daily worship of the deity.
Three [mantras] for the ritual bathing are prescribed: beginning with the *brahmajajñāna* mantra, then the *vāmadevya*, and that which is the purifying *yajus*;
and the *pavamāna-anuvāka*—all these are remembered as being common [to all]. 19.
At the equinoxes, solstices, and transits; likewise during lunar or solar eclipses; or when there is an interruption in worship due to some lapse in time;
or even upon another injury, such as a terrifying bad dream. (20–21)
One should first perform the ritual bathing; all-pervading peace shall prevail.
Then, one should hold a festival for the deity, and one is liberated from all sins.
In this world and in the next, his happiness alone increases.
"Afterwards, he attains union with Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
"He who has performed the ritual bathing for Kṛṣṇa for the welfare of the world," so said the venerable Bodhāyana.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the second book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter in the second book:
"Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the installation of Rudra. (1)

On the fourth, the eighth, the Ārdrā, or the Apabharaṇī nakṣatra, or on the fourteenth, or under whichever other auspicious lunar mansions (nakṣatras) there may be, one should, on the day before, serve food to an even number of Brāhmaṇas and have them pronounce, "An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity! When night has arrived, having fashioned an image with a golden base using the five products of a tawny cow (kapilā-pañcagavya), along with gold, barley, *dūrvā* sprouts, and leaves of the *aśvattha* and *parṇa* trees, he sprinkles it while reciting the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ."
With the four verses beginning "The golden-colored, pure, purifying ones," with this Anuvāka beginning "Pavamāna, who dwells in heaven," and with the Vyāhṛtis;

2. He places upon the footstool barley mixed with flowers, fruits, unbroken rice, and sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, saying, "Salutation to you, O Rudra, to your wrath"; 3. He ties on a protective amulet (*pratisara*) with the verse, "The slayer of demons, the vigorous one. 4.

Then, having covered a bundle of *kuśa* grass with an unwashed garment at one of the riverbanks, ponds, lakes, waterfalls, pools, or sacred fords (*tīrtha*), he consecrates it with the verses "O Waters, remove [evil]" (*avate heḍaḥ*) and "Up from the highest" (*uduttamam*). 5.
Then, when the next day has dawned, four Brāhmaṇas, having bathed and wearing unwashed garments, shall raise up the image with the verse "Arise, O Lord of Prayer" (*uttiṣṭha brahmaṇaspate*). 6.

Then, having established [the materials] in a pure place, one takes cow urine with the *gāyatrī* mantra; cow dung with "gandhadvārām"; milk with "āpyāyasva"; curd with "dadhikrāvṇo"; clarified butter with "śukram asi jyotir asi"; and *kuśa* grass and so forth with "devasya tvā. This is called the *pañcagavya*. Regarding this, it is said: "The milk of a tawny cow is best, the curd of a white cow is best, the clarified butter of a red cow is best, and the remaining two [mantras] are for the brindled and black cows."
With these eight verses beginning with "Homage be to your bow" (*namaste astu dhanvane*), he bathes [the image].

(10) Then, he sprinkles [it] with a jar containing the tannin-extract of the barks of the *śamī*, *palāśa*, *khadira*, *bilva*, *aśvattha*, *vikaṅkata*, *nyagrodha*, *panasa*, *āmra*, *śirīṣa*, *udumbara*, and all other trees fit for sacrifice, using the verse "In the *aśvattha* is your seat" (*aśvatthe vo niṣadanam*).
(11) He sprinkles [it] with a full jar containing gems, pearls, and corals submerged in water, using the previously mentioned verse "Golden-hued ones" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*). (12)
One should release the eye with gold by means of its brilliance, reciting: "Thou art brilliance" (1.13).
If [the eye] does not return to the socket, it is because of the absence of the eye-socket (1.14).

Then, having performed the rites from the smearing of the sacrificial ground for the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), he offers oblations from the cooked food, reciting the section beginning with "That arrow of thine which is most auspicious" (1.16) until the end of the anuvāka.
Then he offers oblations of clarified butter with these two sections beginning with "drāpe sahasrāṇi," verse by verse; with the words "sarvo vai rudraḥ," he should touch the footstool.
(17) Again, he should offer oblations of clarified butter with those same [sections] and touch the region of the navel with the verse "kadrudrāya.
(18) Again, he should offer oblations of clarified butter with those same [sections] and touch the head with the verse "namo hiraṇyabāhave. (19)
Furthermore, one should offer oblations of clarified butter with those same [mantras] and touch all the limbs with the Rudra-mantra in its entirety.

Then, having raised [the image] with the mantra "udu tyaṃ jātavedasam" and having entered the temple with the five Anuvākas known as the Pañcabrahma, one should place gems, pearls, coral, gold, and silver upon the footstool and install the Rudra [image] with the mantra "namaste rudra manyave."

Then, having directed the perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps toward the sky and having stood up, he performs the invocation with the *vyāhṛtis* joined with the *praṇava*, both individually and collectively: "Oṃ bhūḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa; Oṃ suvaḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa; Oṃ bhūrbhuvassuvaḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa. Having invoked him with the words, "May the Blessed Mahādeva come," he sprinkles [the deity] with a jar of jewel-water and should maintain [the flow] with the *praṇava*. It is known from scripture: "This is Brahman. (22) He gives the *kūrca* grass seat with the *praṇava*. (23)
He offers water for the feet (*pādya*) with a vessel containing *viṣṇupada*, *āśyāmāka* grain, lotus petals, and a water-pot.
(24) He offers water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) with a vessel mixed with cardamom, cloves, nutmeg, and camphor.

(25) He offers the guest-water (*arghya*) with water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), barley, husked rice, barley, and white mustard seeds, saying: "May these waters—which are auspicious, most auspicious, most pure, most sacred, immortal, and of immortal flavor—be used as water for the feet, for sipping, and as guest-water; may they be enjoyed and accepted. May the Blessed Mahādeva accept them. Salutation to Rudra. Thus he offers the water for the feet, the water for sipping, and the guest-water. (26)
With the mantra, "Salutations to you, O Rudra, for your wrath," he unties the protective amulet (pratisara).

27. Having paid homage to the deity, he then offers the fragrance with the following words: "These fragrances are auspicious and divine, adorned with all perfumes; they are purified by the Brahman-purifier and purified by the rays of the sun. May they be accepted; may the Blessed One, Mahādeva, accept them. Salutations to Rudra. 28.

Then he offers the garland: "These auspicious, divine garlands, adorned with all manner of flowers, purified by the Brahman-purifier and purified by the rays of the sun—may they be accepted; may the Blessed Mahādeva accept them. Homage to Rudra! (29) Then he offers the flowers: "These auspicious, divine flowers, adorned with all manner of blossoms, purified by the Brahman-purifier and purified by the rays of the sun—may they be accepted; may the Blessed Mahādeva accept them. Homage to Rudra! (30)

Then he offers incense: "Incense is the essence of the forest trees; it is rich in fragrance, the most excellent incense, worthy of being smelled by all the gods. May this incense be accepted, may it be accepted! May the Blessed One Mahādeva accept it. Homage to Rudra! (31) Then he offers the lamp: "Light, brilliance, and splendor—this lamp is eternally dear to the gods and illuminating for all beings. May this lamp be accepted, may it be accepted! May the Blessed One Mahādeva accept it. Homage to Rudra! (32)

Then, with the eight verses beginning with "atha bhavāya," one should offer flowers; having performed the libations (tarpaṇas) with those same [verses], one should present the sacrificial oblations—kṛsara, milk-rice (pāyasa), rice with jaggery (guḍodana), and turmeric rice—with the verse "pavitraṃ te vitatam" while offering the milk-rice.
One should present a full bowl soaked in ghee along with the rice with jaggery.
One should offer kṛsara mixed with clarified butter with the eight [mantras] beginning with "to the god Bhava, svāhā! and "to the wife of the god Bhava, svāhā! and so forth.

Then one should offer oblations of rice cooked with turmeric (*haridrodana*) with these eight [verses]: "To Bhava, the son of the god, svāhā! and so forth. (36) Then [one should offer] with the twelve names: "We worship Tryambaka," "Do not harm us in our great ones," "Do not harm us in our offspring," "The weapon of Rudra is moist," "Far from us be the weapon of Rudra," "Agni," "O scatterer," "O red one," "Thousands in a thousand ways," "Thousands by the thousands," and with the names: "To Śiva, to Śaṅkara, to Sahamāna, to Śitikaṇṭha, to Kapardin, to Tāmra, to Aruṇa, to Apaguramāṇa, to Hiraṇyabāhu, to Sasthiñjara, to Babhluśa, to Hiraṇya, svāhā! (37)
