The ritual from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established as usual, up to the giving of the cow and the granting of boons (38).

He offers an oblation of the sacrificial remains with the mantra: "We worship you alone—the one, primordial, ancient Person, Rudra, Śiva, the creator of the universe. You alone are the sacrifice ordained; you are the one to be performed. By yourself, O Self, accept this oblation" (39). Then, in front of the fire, he places the remnants of the offering upon leaves of the *aśvattha* tree with the mantra: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ om" (40).

Twice or four times he circumambulates the fire, keeping it to his right, saying: "Homage to Viśvabhuj, homage to Sarvabhuj, homage to Ātman, homage to Paramātman. (41) A student or a householder should feed twelve self-controlled Brahmins with rice cooked in green gram broth. (42) Thus the ritual for consecration is completed. (43)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter in the second book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the daily service of Mahādeva. Having bathed and become pure, having smeared a level and clean place with cow-dung, having fashioned an image of the God, and having worshipped it with unbroken grains and flowers as they are available, one should invoke Mahādeva together with water and flowers, saying: "Om Bhūḥ! I invoke Puruṣa," and so forth, ending with: "May the Blessed Mahādeva come! (1)

Having consecrated the vessel with the Yajus formula, "Rudra who is in the fire," and having washed it, he pours water through the strainer; having consecrated it again with that same formula, he should show it to the sun together with the two strainers, saying, "Om, until death.
He gives the water for the feet, saying, "This is the water for the feet for them."

Then, having removed the remains of the offerings with the *vyāhṛtis* and having given the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), he sprinkles [the deity] with the three verses beginning "The waters are indeed our source of bliss" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*), with the four verses beginning "Golden-colored, pure, purifying" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*), with this entire section beginning "Pavamāna, born in heaven" (*pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*), with the hymn "Brahman was born first" (*brahma jajñānam*), with the "Kadrudrīya," with the "Tvaritarudra," with the "Vāmadevya," and with the verse "The waters indeed are this" (*āpo vā idam*).

(4) Then, having sprinkled water clockwise around [the deity] with the *vyāhṛtis* and having placed the purifier (*pavitra*) at the base of the foot, he satiates [the deity] with water using the eight [names] beginning "I satiate the god Bhava" (*bhavaṃ devaṃ tarpayāmi*). (5)
With the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Rudra, the three-eyed one," he should offer a cloth and a sacred thread (yajñopavīta).
(6) With the eight [mantras] beginning with "Obeisance to the god Bhava," he should offer flowers.
(7) With the Tvaritarudra [mantra], he offers perfume, flowers, incense, and a lamp. (8)
One should present the oblation with the mantra, "Devasya tvā" (TS 1.4.2.1).

(9) One should offer the sprinkling of water with the mantra, "Tryambakam" (RV 7.59.12). (10) Having performed the introductory rite with the mantra, "Amṛtopastaraṇam asi" (VS 2.28), one should offer all non-prohibited sacrificial food and every kind of savory substance, including bulbs, roots, and fruits. (11)

Having sat for a moment without looking around and announced, "I shall remove the oblation," he removes it; then, having performed the introductory formula, "Thou art the covering of immortality," he should offer water for sipping with the mantra, "To Tryambaka.

(12) Having worshipped with all the necessary implements, he offers the fragrant substances and so forth with the formulas, "Salutation to the god Bhava," and so on, as well as "Salutation to such-and-such, salutation to such-and-such.

(13) They praise him with hymns from the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, and with the praises of the seers; then, having paid obeisance, he dismisses him with the words, "May the blessed Mahādeva depart. (14)

"In the places of the *liṅga* [images], they say that one should perform the daily rite for well-being (*svastyayana*), with the exception of the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the dismissal (*udvāsana*)," so said the venerable Bodhāyana.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the second book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter in the second book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual for the bath and worship of Rudra. Having first bathed at a sacred ford (tīrtha) and emerged, having put on unwashed (fresh) garments, being pure, self-restrained, celibate, and dressed in white, one should fashion an image of Īśāna. Standing to the south-west of it, facing it, one should establish the deities within oneself: "May Brahmā abide in the organ of generation; may Viṣṇu abide in the feet; may Hara abide in the hands; may Rudra abide in the arms; may Agni abide in the belly; [may Varuṇa abide] in the stomach..."

May the Earth remain [in my feet]; may Śiva remain in my heart; may the Vasus remain in my throat; may Sarasvatī remain in my mouth; may Vāyu remain in my two nostrils; may the Moon and Sun remain in my two eyes; may the Aśvins remain in my two ears; may the Rudras remain on my forehead; may the Ādityas remain on my crown; may Mahādeva remain on my head; may Vāsudeva remain in my topknot; may Pinākin remain at my back; may the Trident-bearer remain in front; and may Śivā and Śaṅkara remain at my two sides.

"May [the deity] remain! May the wind remain on all sides! May the garlands of flames of fire remain encircling [me] on all sides! May all the deities remain in their respective places in all the limbs! May they protect me! Thus he should wipe the limbs according to their characteristics with the mantra "Agni is seated in my speech," and then he should worship him with perfumes, unbroken rice, leaves, flowers, incense, and lamps. 1. Then he propitiates him: "Worshipped by men, by the Siddhas, and by the gods, Asuras, and others, I worship you according to my ability; be gracious to me, O Maheśvara. 2. And also with the mantra: "We sacrifice to Tryambaka. 3.

Then he invokes him with the verse: "May the wise bay horses, together with white horses that possess banners, swift as the wind, powerful, and fleet as thought, carry you here quickly for my oblation, O Śarva! (4).
When [the deity] has been established, there is no invocation. (5)

Then he gives him a seat with the mantra "Sadyojāta"; water for the feet with "Bhave Bhave"; the arghya offering with "Bhavodbhavāya Namaḥ"; water for sipping with "Rudrāya Namaḥ"; and having removed the remains of previous offerings with the *vyāhṛtis*, he bathes him with these: the three verses beginning "Āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ," the four verses beginning "Hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ," this entire section beginning "Pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ," the verse "Brahma jajñānam," the verse "Kadrudrāya," the verse "Sarvo vai," the verse "Kayā naścitra ābhuvat," and the verse "Āpo vā idaṃ sarvam. (6)

Having sprinkled water clockwise with the *vyāhṛtis*, and having placed the purifiers at the base of his feet, he satiates him with water using eight [mantras]: "I satiate the god Bhava," and so on. With "Salutation to Vāmadeva" he offers a garment; with "Salutation to Jyeṣṭha" the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*); with "Salutation to Rudra" water for sipping (*ācamanīya*); with "Salutation to Kāla" perfume (*gandha*); with "Salutation to Kalavikaraṇa" unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*); with "Salutation to Balavikaraṇa" flowers (*puṣpa*); with "Salutation to Balapramathana" incense (*dhūpa*); and [with] "Salutation to Sarvabhūtadamana" [he offers the lamp].

Saying "Obeisance," he offers the lamp; saying "Obeisance to Manonmanā," he offers the food offering at the proper time; saying "Obeisance to Rudra," he gives the water for sipping. (7) Then he worships with the Aghora-form [of Śiva] using the mantra: "Not to the non-terrible ones, nor to the terrible ones... (8) Then he should mutter the Rudra-Gāyatrī, beginning with "We know that Tatpuruṣa..."; he should repeat this Raudrī verse a thousand times, or a hundred times, or an unlimited number of times, but not less than ten. (9)
Then he pronounces this blessing over him: "The Lord of all sciences...

(10). Then he sprinkles him continuously on the head with the stream from the water-pot while muttering the eleven sections beginning with "Homage to your wrath, O Rudra" (*namaste rudra manyave*). He should mutter as much as his strength permits the three sections beginning with "All is indeed Rudra" (*sarvo vai rudraḥ*), the five sections beginning with "He who was born at once" (*sadyo jātam*), the twelve verses beginning with "These [oblations] for Rudra" (*imā rudrāya*), and other Raudra mantras (11).
In this manner, he sprinkles him eleven times (12).
At the end of each recitation, one should recite one of the eleven sections beginning with "agnāviṣṇū sajoṣasā" (13).

At the conclusion of all [sections], one should again perform the worship, repeating everything previously mentioned from the seat (*āsana*) up to the lamp (*dīpa*), and then offer the great oblation (*mahāhavis*) such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) with the mantra "manonmanāya namaḥ," while praising [the deity] with hymns dedicated to Rudra (14).

This ritual of bathing and worship of Rudra should be performed by one who desires the destruction of sins, liberation from disease, prosperity, peace, nourishment, contentment, long life, health, or liberation (15).

Then, according to his ability, he gives a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*): ten cows adorned with gold and a bull as the eleventh; in the absence of these, he should give one cow—so says the venerable Bodhāyana.
(16) Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the second book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter in the second book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual for re-consecration (*punaḥ-pratiṣṭhā*). During the previously mentioned lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), or any other auspicious asterisms, in the bright fortnight, during the northern course of the sun, and in seasons such as spring; or even for that which has already been consecrated, when there is an intentional interruption of worship for one night, two nights, one month, or two months; or in the event of an affliction by *śūdras*, women in their menses, outcasts (*patita*), and so forth—on the day prior [to the ceremony], having served food to an even number of Brahmins and having caused them to pronounce "Auspicious Day," "Welfare," and "Prosperity," when they have assembled...

Having performed the ritual immersion in water during the night, one should rise on the following day and place two jars; having filled one with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should bathe the other with pure water together with jewels.

(1) Having bathed [the image] one thousand eight hundred or twenty-eight times with the root mantra and the Rudra-gāyatrī, one should offer flowers, worship according to one's means, and present an offering of rice cooked with molasses (*guḍaudana*).
(2) When this has been done, peace (*śānti*) comes to him. (3)
If the worship is interrupted intentionally, a ceremonial bathing (snāpana) must be performed. 4.
It is said that one who acts thus attains well-being and prosperity. 5.
Furthermore, the venerable Bodhāyana says that one should re-consecrate [the image] with the consecration mantra (pratiṣṭhāmantra). 6.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the twentieth chapter of the second book:
Hereafter, I shall explain the procedure for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in their proper order.
The best [dose] is one *droṇa*, while the middling is half of that;
the lowest is known to be half of that again—thus it is proclaimed to be of three kinds.
Clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is said to be one quarter-part, and cow’s urine should be double that amount.
Cow dung is said to be one *kuḍuba*, curd is provided in the measure of one *prastha*, and milk is said to be two *prasthas*.
Bathing [the deity] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) bestows enjoyment and liberation upon men. ||3||

The milk of a tawny cow is excellent, the curd of a white cow is excellent, the clarified butter of a red cow is indeed excellent, while the remaining two [products] belong to the brindled and black cows.

||4|| Having purified himself and gone to the temple of the God, he should smear with cow-dung a level area in front of the pavilion; then, having collected one *khārī* or half of that measure of rice or barley, he requests nine jars made of gold, silver, bell-metal, or clay. ||5||

Having wrapped it with thread and placed it in a clean location, sitting facing north to the south of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), he should invite ten Brahmins by their names, cause them to pronounce an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), and sprinkle [the ground]. Having prepared the sacrificial mound with rice grains, he should draw straight lines with a piece of gold—one on the right side and one on the left side from the center of it—with the verse "The Brahman was born" (*brahma jajñānam*) on the south; with "The father of the Virājs" (*pitā virājām*) on the north; with "The eagle on the vault of heaven" (*nāke suparṇam*) to the south of those two; and with "Swell up" (*āpyāyasva*) to the north of those two.

One should draw [the lines] continuously and straight with the mantra, "Rudra has drawn this in Agni" behind [the fire], and "Rudra is indeed all" in front [of the fire]. Behind those two [lines], one recites, "Viṣṇu strode across this," and in front of those two, "All have made Indra grow. 6.

Then, having sprinkled [the site], cast away the blade of grass, and touched water, he should worship in the central square with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ oṃ, obeisance to Brahman"; in the northeast square with "obeisance to Īśāna"; in the east with "obeisance to Tatpuruṣa"; in the south with "obeisance to Aghora"; in the north with "obeisance to Vāmadeva"; in the west with "obeisance to Sadyojāta"; in the southeast with "obeisance to the Heart"; in the northeast with "obeisance to the Head"; in the southwest with "obeisance to the Tuft (Śikhā)"; and in the northwest with "obeisance to the Armor (Kavaca)."

Having worshipped in the cardinal and intermediate directions with "To the Weapon (Astra), obeisance" in the north-west, and having placed the principal pitcher (pradhānakalaśa) in the center with "To Brahmā, obeisance," and having established the pitchers in the positions starting from Īśa with their respective mantras, one consecrates the sprinkling water (prokṣaṇī), sprinkles the vessels, and sprinkles the products of the cow (gavya). Then, taking kuśa-water in a quantity equal to that of the prokṣaṇī vessel, one pours it into the Brahmakumbha with the mantra "Devasya tvā. Having consecrated it with "Water indeed is all this," and having placed a grass-bundle (kūrca) within, one places milk in the pitcher of Īśa along with a purifier (pavitra), and curd in the pitcher of Puruṣa.

Clarified butter (*ghṛta*) in the Aghora [face], cow-dung (*gomaya*) in the Saumya, cow-urine (*gomūtra*) in the Vāruṇa, and ground paste of plantains and the like in the Heart; coconut in the Head, *āmalaka* fruit in the Tuft (*śikhā*), and turmeric (*hāridra*) in the Armor (*kavaca*). Having performed the rites from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the sipping of water (*ācamana*) with the respective mantras, and having strewn the sacrificial grass around, he then bathes it with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*, with the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*, with this entire section (*anuvāka*) beginning with *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*, and with the verses beginning with *brahma jajñānam*, *kad rudrāya*, and *sarvo*.

With the verse "vai kayā naś citraḥ" and the mantra "āpo vā idam," he sprinkles the water clockwise with the *vyāhṛtis*. Then he satiates [the ancestors] with water using their own respective mantras. Having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, and having offered the *bali* oblation, he takes the *sadyaḥ* vessel with the verse "tatsavitur vareṇyam" and joins it with the *brahmapātra* using the *anuvāka* beginning with "sadyojātam. Taking the *vāmadeva* vessel with the verse "gandhadvārām," he joins it with the *brahmapātra* using the *vāmadeva-anuvāka*. [He then uses the verse] "āpyāyasva..."

Taking a jar of milk, one should join it with the Īśāna-anuvāka. Taking curd with the mantra "Dadhikrāvṇo," one should join it with the Puruṣa-anuvāka. Reciting "Śukram asi" (Thou art light), one takes clarified butter and joins it with the Aghora-anuvāka. Having scattered fruits with the mantra "So 'ham" (I am that), having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, and having fully honored it with the Vyomavyāpin [mantra], it becomes the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). 7.

Then, having approached the deity and removed the *nirmālya*, he sprinkles [the disciple] with the *praṇava*: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I sprinkle you with the medicine of the Aśvins for splendor and for sacred luster (*brahmavarcasa*). At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I sprinkle you with the medicine of Sarasvatī for heroism and for the eating of food. At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan..."

With the three [mantras] beginning with, "By the two hands, by the power of Indra, for the sake of prosperity, fame, and strength, I consecrate you," he then bathes [the disciple] with ground *āmalaka*, turmeric, and other substances. He should perform the consecration with the *surabhimatī* verses, the *ābliṅga* verses, the *vāruṇī* verses, the *hiraṇyavarṇā* verses, the *pāvamānī* verses, the *vyāhṛtis*, and various other collections of purificatory texts such as the *camaka* and *namaka*.
(8) Once again, according to his capacity, he should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the teacher; he should give garments, earrings, ornaments, rings, cows, land, and so forth.
(9) He overcomes all evil, he overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin.
One attains union with Brahman or residence in the same world as Brahman. 10.
The three fruits of the coconut, the mango, and the jackfruit, when combined with sugar and honey, are known as the "five nectars" (pañcāmṛta). 11.
The water contained in the Brahma-vessel is said to be four prasthas, the size of a wood-apple fruit;
a wise person should prepare as much as has been prepared with devotion.
Thus spoke the Blessed Bodhāyana. 13.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter in the second book.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the procedure for the ritual bathing of the Lord.
A wise man should have an altar constructed at the site of the great *liṅga*,
and having first prepared the mandala as described in the Purāṇas, he should begin the bathing ceremony.
Where the Lord is established as immovable, there is no sacrificial altar (vedikā) there.
Near Him, in that very place, is the supreme location for the jars; their number is nine, and their installation is performed with the syllable Om (praṇava). 2–3.
Whatever is performed therein is declared to be done with the *praṇava* alone;
the installation of the jars, however, begins from the east and ends in the northeast.
By these very sequences, all ritual action is prescribed here.
At the end, the wise one should place the ninth pitcher in the center.
(5) One should place everything upon bundles of grass, with rice and grains;
rice is said to be of the *śāli* variety. The wise one should place the pitchers [therein]. (6)

In their absence, whatever common grain is desired here should fill all the jars; one should fill them with waters resembling pure crystal, and among those, the central one should be filled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). 7.
Having placed [the vessels] upon a bundle of grass and having covered them all with shallow bowls (śarāva),
the act of covering them should always be performed with nine new bowls made of clay alone; their lids should likewise be made from rice grains grown from paddy.
The self-possessed one should worship all the jars in sequence with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; then, when the auspicious moment arrives, he should invoke the Supreme Self—
the God Rudra, Śiva himself, who is the deity of all.
Therefore, the wise one should perform the invocation; this is the rule for invocation everywhere.
This is declared to be the general procedure for the satiation of deities:
for Viṣṇu, it begins with Nārāyaṇa and so forth, while for Rudra, it begins with Śiva and so forth.
One should take refuge in the mind, making all [acts] such as recitation and meditation free from conceptual construction;
one should perform the *raudra-sūkta* and the seven verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" using only optional [mantras], but the middle [verse] is not found there.

Now, some indeed say that for the bathing of the Great Lord, one should perform the bathing at all times with these [mantras]: the five beginning with Sadyojāta, as well as "Sarvo vai rudra" and others. 14–15.
"And one should act in this manner during a bath; likewise, such is the worship during the ritual bathing [of an image]," so said the Blessed Bodhāyana. 16.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the second book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now, the twenty-second chapter of the second book.

Now, regarding the performance of worship for the two deities, everywhere [the rites] are performed with the two verses, "He strode out three steps" (*trīṇi padā vicakrame*) and "We worship Tryambaka" (*tryambakaṃ yajāmahe*), according to their respective characteristics, for the seat, the water for the feet, and the water for sipping.

(1) Bodhāyana said that these are performed because they belong to the dharma of the three *varṇas*, because of the general injunction, and because there is no prohibition against what is already established by worldly custom. (2)
Having established it thus, one should perform [the rite]; thereby one attains union with or residence in the same world as those two deities.

(3) If it is performed after thirty years have passed, then he, together with his retinue, attains that very supreme station of the two deities known as Brahman. (4) If one is devoted to this, or if someone knows it thus—whether for whomsoever one explains it or for whomsoever one performs it—one should give a hundred māṣas; a Brāhmaṇa or a Rājanya should give a thousand, while a Vaiśya should give according to his faith. (5)

A woman and a Śūdra should not perform [the worship]; if they should perform it, the teacher must be relied upon for the independent instruction. (6) If those two were to perform it independently, even a Brāhmaṇa whose livelihood is exhausted would surely fall; so says Śālīki. (7) Now, regarding the two deities, one may act according to one's desire; in whatever state one may be—in water, on a sacrificial mound, or before images—having performed everything, one should worship them, but one must not be negligent. (8)

"In the absence of a place, in the absence of materials, or when [the materials] are common to others, one should perform [the rite] mentally or worship [mentally]. Regarding this, the Blessed One said: "Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water—that offering made with devotion by a person of self-restraint, I accept. (9) Bowing with devotion, one should study these mantras; however, one must never be a non-worshiper. Then, through either one or both of those [means], one attains union (*sāyujya*) or residence in the same world (*salokatā*) with them. (10)

11. To anyone other than his sons, disciples, or wife who performs the worship of these two [images], he should give a golden conch with a golden base, or a bull as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for Rudra; thus says the venerable Bodhāyana. 12. At the time of performing the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) or the ceremonial bathing (*snāpana*), having given all those implements to the teacher (*ācārya*), one should give eleven cows along with a bull; thus says the venerable Bodhāyana.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the second book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.

Now, regarding the performance of worship for the two deities: "Now, therefore, I shall fully explain"; "Henceforth, I shall explain"; "Now, therefore, again, the ritual for re-consecration"; "Now, therefore, the rule for the bathing and worship of Rudra"; "Now, therefore, the daily [rite] of Mahādeva"; "Now, therefore, the ritual for the consecration of Rudra"; "Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that of Viṣṇu"; "Now, therefore, the daily [rite] of the Great Puruṣa"; "Now, therefore, the ritual for the consecration of Viṣṇu"; likewise, "that which pertains to the planets"; "Now, it is well known that the initiation [takes place] after the oblation has been offered"; "Now, therefore..."

The consecration of the *aśvattha* tree; then the consecration of those who are dull-witted, deaf, or mute; then [the rites] for the *rājanya* and the *vaiśya*; then, therefore, the rule for the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*); then, therefore, the ritual procedure for the adoption of a son; then [the rites] in the month of Māgha; then the oblation for one desiring offspring; then the auspicious ceremonies; then the impregnation (*garbhādhāna*); then, therefore, the *śrāddha* on the fifth day. 22.

Now, therefore, the *pañcamī-śrāddha*; now, the *garbhādhāna*; now, the auspicious rites (*maṅgalāni*); now, the *prajārthi-homa*; now, in the month of Māgha; now, therefore, the ritual for the adoption of a son (*putrapratigraha-kalpa*); now, therefore, the rule for the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta-vidhi*); now, concerning the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya; now, the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of those who are dull-witted, deaf, or mute; now, therefore, the consecration of the *aśvattha* tree; now, the well-known initiation (*upanayana*) following the oblation; likewise, that which pertains to the planets (*grahāṇām*); now, therefore, the ritual for the installation of Viṣṇu (*viṣṇupratiṣṭhā-kalpa*); now, therefore, the daily [rite] of the Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*).

"Now, therefore, I shall fully declare [the ritual] for Viṣṇu; now, therefore, the ritual manual for the installation of Rudra; now, therefore, the daily [ritual] for Mahādeva; now, therefore, the procedure for the bathing and worship of Rudra; now, therefore, again the ritual manual for installation; hereafter I shall declare [it]; now, therefore, I shall fully declare [the ritual] for the God; now, regarding the performance of the worship of the two Gods. 23. Thus ends the second book in the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra. Now begins the first chapter of the third book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual manual (kalpa) for the syllable *oṃ*, dedicated to the Purifiers (*pavitra*), the Most Purifying (*atipavitra*), the Unconquered (*aparājita*), the Secret (*guhya*), and the Heart of Brahman (*brahmahṛdaya*).

(1) In a place where one does not hear the sound of domestic animals, near water, one should have a small hut constructed with a single pillar made of a sacred tree (*brahmavṛkṣa*), facing the east. (2)

Wearing a crown of *kuśa* grass, dressed in *kuśa*, clothed in garments of *kuśa* bark, with a *kuśa* girdle as his sacred thread, seated upon *kuśa*, holding *kuśa* in his hand, wearing a *kuśa* belt, bathing at the three periods of the day, sleeping on *kuśa*, subsisting on alms of either vegetables or barley-gruel, and standing facing the sun, he should mutter the syllable *Oṃ* five thousand times; then all his mantras will be perfected, all the Vedas will be mastered, he will have fulfilled his vows in all the Vedas, he will be as one who has bathed in all sacred fords, and he will become a knower of all the Vedas.

He becomes known by all the gods; he has performed all sacrifices and rituals; he purifies the lineage up to the seventh generation; he becomes free from fault and purified of the defects of his mother and father as well as the defects of men; and he purifies even the Caṇḍālas and Śvapākas. 3.

Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* (a mess of boiled rice) in the milk of a white cow that has a calf of the same color, and having consecrated it while facing the sun with a thousand recitations of the syllable *Oṃ*, one should consume it oneself; this drives away the misfortune (*alakṣmī*) of seven generations of men, one attains the memory of past births (*jātismaratva*), one partakes in the goddess Śrī, and one's celibacy (*brahmacarya*) becomes uninterrupted and continuous.

The Vedas, beginning with the *Praṇava* (the sacred syllable), are established within the *Praṇava*; the *Praṇava* is the entirety of the world of speech. Therefore, one should practice the *Praṇava*.
"That mantra which is devoid of the *praṇava* is breathless; among all mantras, the *praṇava* is said to be the breath of the mantras.
Thus spoke the venerable Bodhāyana.
This concludes the first chapter in the third book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the second chapter of the third book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the *vyāhṛtis*. One should bathe at the three periods of the day, sleep on the ground, and remain seated; having fasted for three nights or for a day and night, one should mutter twelve thousand *vyāhṛtis*.
(1) Having thus completed the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*), one then commences the ritual acts. (2)

One who desires Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a thousand oblations of *palāśa* fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one desiring luster (*tejas*) with clarified butter (*ājya*); one desiring cattle with milk; one desiring sensory power with curd; one desiring food with cooked rice; one desiring grain with *vrīhi* or barley; and one desiring a daughter with parched grain (*lāja*). [With] sesame seeds, there is the destruction of demons and the removal of evil; fever perishes instantly. One desiring sons [should sacrifice] with *nyagrodha* wood from trees; one desiring a house with *plakṣa*; one desiring prosperity with *aśvattha*; and one desiring peace (*śānti*) with wood of the *śamī* tree.

"One desiring subjugation [should sacrifice] with *pāmārga* stalks; one desiring sovereignty with *khadira* wood; one desiring wealth with *arka* fuel-sticks; and one desiring all desires with *palāśa* fuel-sticks.
As long as he offers oblations, for so long does he obtain [his goal]," so said the venerable Bodhāyana.
Thus ends the second chapter in the third book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the third chapter of the third inquiry.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for Durgā. Having prepared the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), red lotus flowers, and the necessary materials, month by month during the morning of the *Kṛttikā* constellation, one who is pure and firm in his vows should prepare a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung, sprinkle it with water, and while standing, invoke the Blessed Lady with the verse "To Jātavedas" (*jātavedase*). Having invoked her with "Om, I invoke the noble Raudrī," and having offered a seat (*kūrca*) with the verse "Her color like fire" (*tām agnivarṇām*), he offers the sacred thread with "O Agni, do thou carry us across" (*agne tvam pāraya*). Then he bathes her.

Having performed the ritual purification (*mārjana*) with the three verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ," with the four verses beginning "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," and with this entire section (*anuvāka*) beginning "pavamānaḥ," he should worship her with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps using these eleven names—Āryā, Raudrī, Mahākālī, Mahāyoginī, Suvarṇapuṣpī, Devasaṅkīrtī, Mahāyajñī, Mahāvaiṣṇavī, Mahāpṛthivī, Manogamī, and Śaṅkhadhāriṇī—saying "Obeisance to [Name]," and likewise with the *Sāvitrī* mantra.

Having offered the oblation with the words, "I offer this oblation to the Blessed Goddess Durgā," and having sacrificed the remainder with the eleven names [of Viṣṇu], one should mutter the *pañcadurgā* hymns and recite the ten *svasti* verses: *jāto yad agne*, *vaṣaṭ te viṣṇo*, *vāstoṣpate*, *evāvandasva*, *ā no niyudbhiḥ*, *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, *abhayaṃ kṛṇotu*, *aśvāvatīḥ*, *tvaṃ varuṇaḥ*, *bṛhaspate yuvam indraś ca*, and *svasti na indro vṛddhaśravāḥ*. Having thus recited them, one should recite: *śaṃ ca me mayaś ca me*.

One should mutter these eleven sections and the Sāvitrī; having offered the oblation to the Blessed Goddess Durgā with the words, "I set aside the sacrificial food for the Blessed Goddess Durgā," and having given the remainder to the Brāhmaṇas, one should perform the observance for a year. All desires are fulfilled; so says the Blessed Bodhāyana.
Thus ends the third chapter of the third book in the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the fourth chapter of the third book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the *upaśruti* (underground voice). It should be performed on a Sunday or a Tuesday, or on the fourth, eighth, or fourteenth lunar day, or under the asterisms of Bharaṇī or Kṛttikā. 1.

On the preceding day, having refrained from food, being pure and observing celibacy, he then, at nightfall, having kindled the fire and strewn grass around it, invokes Upaśruti to its south: "Om Bhūḥ! I invoke the goddess Rātri; Om Bhuvaḥ! I invoke the goddess Upaśruti; Om Suvaḥ! I invoke the goddess Mahārātri; Om Bhūrbhuvassuvaḥ! I invoke the goddess Mahākālarātri. Having thus invoked her, he then bathes her with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ" and with the verse beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ".

Having performed the purification with the Anuvāka beginning with "catasṛbhiḥ pavamānaḥ," and having adorned [the deity] with perfumes, black flowers, incense, and lamps, he prepares the clarified butter (ājya) and offers oblations, saying: "Svāhā to the goddess Night; Svāhā to the goddess Upaśruti; Svāhā to the goddess Mahārātri; Svāhā to the goddess Mahākālarātri; Svāhā to Niśā; Svāhā to Kṣapā; Svāhā to Kṛṣṇā; Svāhā to Andhakāriṇī. He also offers oblations with the two verses beginning with "yata indra bhayāmahe" and "svastidā viśaspatiḥ. Then, having performed a circumambulatory sprinkling all around, he worships with the Rātrisūkta.

Having dismissed the goddess Night with the *vyāhṛtis*, saying, "I dismiss the goddess Night," he should then depart. He should go to a cremation ground, a temple, the house of a *śrotriya*, or a potter's workshop.
(4) At a distance of nine bows, he ties his two ears.

(5) Having muttered this verse, "May Indra of great renown grant us well-being," he should release them. "Let that which is manifest be accepted; let it be joined appropriately; and let there be the commencement of all rites"—thus says the venerable Bodhāyana. (6)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the third book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra;
now begins the fifth chapter in the third book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the Śrī-kalpa. On the fifth day of the bright fortnight, or on the full moon day, having fashioned an image of Śrī out of Kadamba wood or Bilva heartwood, or having prepared it upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one who has fasted for a day and a night, being pure and having performed the purificatory rites, should smear a square sacrificial mound the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung on a level spot. Having scattered fragrant flowers there, and having filled a golden vessel with water, he should pour the fragrant flowers into it while reciting the two verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇām hariṇīm" and "oṃ bhūḥ."

"I invoke Śrī: Oṃ Bhuvaḥ, I invoke Śrī; Oṃ Suvaḥ, I invoke Śrī; Oṃ Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ, I invoke Śrī. Having thus invoked her, he sprinkles [the image] with water in the well-known manner using the two verses beginning with "By the mud... (RV 7.99.1-2). He bathes her with the verse "Horses preceded... (RV 1.162.18). He offers perfume with the verse "The door of fragrance... (RV 10.125.3). He offers a flower with the verse "Who am I? She is she... (RV 10.125.4). He offers incense with the verse "May she come to me... (RV 10.125.5). He offers a lamp with the verse "The golden one, like the moon... (RV 10.125.6). He offers the food offering (naivedya) with the verse "The moon-like, radiant one... (RV 10.125.7). ||1||

Then, having established the fire to the south of the Goddess and strewn it around, having cooked a *caru* of milk-rice with large grains of rice, and having divided the oblation into two parts, he—intending "the desire of the mind"—offers the oblation with the *Śrīsūkta* consisting of fifteen verses, [using] either food or clarified butter mixed with the oblation.
(2) With that same hymn, he presents the sacrificial offering (*bali*) saying: "Homage to Śrī, homage to Puṣṭi, homage to Dhātrī, homage to Sarasvatī.
(3) Having taken lotus flowers as they are available, he rubs them over each limb, thereby driving away misfortune (*alakṣmī*) with the verse beginning "Hunger and thirst. (4)

"In this very way, whether day by day or month by month, he who nourishes a great prosperity—bringing fortune, renown, health, long life, offspring, and cattle—attains a great blessing; so said the Blessed Bodhāyana.
(5) Thus ends the fifth chapter in the third book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the sixth chapter in the third book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for Sarasvatī. On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, or under the two Uttaraphalgunī constellations, or under an auspicious lunar mansion, one should perform the rites beginning with the drawing of lines for the sacrificial ground up to the pouring of water for the *praṇītā* vessel. Then, in front of the fire, one invokes Sarasvatī: "May the boon-granting goddess come, she who is the imperishable syllable equal to Brahman; O Mother Gāyatrī, among the meters, graciously accept this our sacred prayer. (1)

"I invoke Sarasvatī"—having thus invoked her, he prepares the seats here, saying: "I prepare a seat for Vāgdevī; I prepare a seat for Gīrdevī; I prepare a seat for Sarasvatī; I prepare a seat for Brāhmī. (2)

Then he bathes them with the anuvāka beginning, "The waters, indeed, are most refreshing; golden-hued, purifying, dwelling in heaven. Having cleansed them with this, and having satiated them with water, he honors them with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps using their respective names, saying, "Salutation to so-and-so! Salutation to so-and-so! Then, having performed the rites from the laying on of the garments up to the "mouth of the fire" (the invocation of Agni), he offers the cooked oblation—either milk-rice or barley-milk—with the two verses: "The inspirer of true words... and "The daughter of the thunderbolt... (RV 10.125.1–2).

Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with the hymn beginning: *pra ṇo devī*, *ā no divaḥ*, *ye te sarasva ūrmayaḥ*, *uta naḥ priyā priyāsu*, *imā juhvānā*, *yaste stanaḥ śaśayaḥ*, *devīṃ vācamajanayanta*, and *yadvāgvadantī*. (4) The rite is completed from the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards up to the granting of the boon of the cow.

(5) Then, having offered the remains of the oblation upon *palāśa* leaves in front of the fire and having presented the external *bali* offerings, he comes forward, seats the boy facing east in front of the fire, and performs the commencement of learning (*vidyārambha*). (6)

Immediately thereafter, one should bid farewell to the Goddess on the highest peak, O Goddess, upon the earth, at the summit of the mountain: "O Goddess, having received the permission of the Brāhmaṇas, go as you please.
(7) Thus, for the sake of her return and for the sake of further offerings.
(8) "In this very manner, month after month, one who desires knowledge should worship Sarasvatī," so said the Blessed Bodhāyana. (9)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the third book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the seventh chapter in the third book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for Viṣṇu. On the twelfth day of the bright fortnights of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, or Phālguna, when faith arises, one who has fasted for a day and night, on the following day, having purified himself in a forest or at home—wherever his mind finds pleasure—should kindle a fire upon a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila). Having strewn it around and performed the rites up to the *apraṇītā* water, once the milk-rice (*pāyasa*) is prepared, he should recite: "That which is thy purifier, thy purifier is spread out," and saying "Oṃ," [he should offer] the Blessed One made of *vidyut*, *gandha*, and *uśīra*.

Having wrapped [the vessel] with a fringe of white, yellow, and red threads and having set it down, he should invoke [the deity] with: "Oṃ bhūḥ, I invoke Puruṣa; oṃ bhuvaḥ, I invoke Puruṣa; oṃ suvaḥ, I invoke Puruṣa; oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ, I invoke Puruṣa. Having thus invoked him, he should offer the well-known seat, bath-water, water for sipping, and water for rinsing the mouth. Having worshipped with all kinds of fragrant scents, flowers, incense, lamps, and garlands, he places upon the sacrificial grass (barhis) or on a bed of Aśvattha leaves as available, in the incense burner, [the substance] which is cherished by cows, with the mantra: "By the cows... (RV 10.19.4). 1.

Then he offers sixteen oblations of clarified butter with the *Puruṣasūkta* and with the three verses beginning with "paro mātrayā. Having poured the *pavamāna* [milk] into the rice-oblation mixed with clarified butter, he offers four oblations: "To Vāsudeva, svāhā! To Baladeva, svāhā! To Viṣṇu, svāhā! To Śrī, svāhā! (2)

Having taken the portion for Sviṣṭakṛt and placed it within the enclosing sticks, he worships the deity with these very names: "Homage to so-and-so! Homage to so-and-so! with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps; "Svāhā to so-and-so! Svāhā to so-and-so! with food; and "I satisfy so-and-so! I satisfy so-and-so! with fruit and water. From the Sviṣṭakṛt offering onwards, the procedure is established up to the giving of the cow as a boon.

With the verse, "With these [verses], may he overcome all assailants," he should kneel on his right knee and circumambulate four times to the right, saying: "Salutation to Viśvabhuja; salutation to Sarvabhuja; salutation to the Self; salutation to the Supreme Self. Having recited the *Dhruvasūkta*, he should dismiss the Puruṣa, saying: "Oṃ bhūḥ, I dismiss the Puruṣa; oṃ bhuvaḥ, I dismiss the Puruṣa; oṃ suvaḥ, I dismiss the Puruṣa; oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ, I dismiss the Puruṣa. Having thus dismissed him, he should go to where there is water and perform the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) rite. 4.
With the two verses, "What has been entrusted to you today? and "O Viṣṇu, what is to be proclaimed to you?", he unties the protective amulet (*pratisara*).
(5) With the verse, "Viṣṇu strode across this [universe]," he consumes the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
(6) He says, "Thus let him proclaim: 'I belong to Viṣṇu'. To him who replies, "I belong to Viṣṇu," he should give the remainder; he consumes it with these very same mantras. (7)

Having consumed [the food] and sipped water, and having muttered the twelve-syllable mantra "Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya," one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice by worshipping the Eternal One even once. 8. Thus ends the seventh chapter in the third book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the eighth chapter in the third book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the Sun (Ravikalpa). Having prepared a square or circular sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung, one should, on a Sunday, forty-eight times invoke the Sun—whether as *ghṛṇi*, *sūrya*, or *āditya*—into a copper vessel containing red sandalwood paste or red flowers. Then, one should offer the *arghya* water with the mantra "ā satyena," the *pādya* water with "sa śuciṣat," and the *ācamanīya* water with "agnirmūrdhā. [One should also offer water] with this entire section [of the Veda]: "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ," "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," and "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ."

Having cleansed [the area] with water, he satiates them: "I satiate Dhātṛ; I satiate Vidhātṛ; I satiate Aryaman; I satiate Mitra; I satiate Varuṇa; I satiate Bhagavant; I satiate Hasa; I satiate Pūṣan; I satiate Parjanya; I satiate Vivasvant; I satiate Indra; I satiate Ravi. With these very names, using perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, he says, "Salutation to such-and-such! Salutation to such-and-such! and with the *vyāhṛtis*.
Saying, "I release the person," one should release him; then one should offer forty-eight cakes.
(1) By worshipping once, one afflicted with leprosy or consumption [is freed].
(2) One who is bound is released from bondage; the sick man is released from disease. (3)
Thus spoke the Blessed Bodhāyana. 4.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the third book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the ninth chapter in the third book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for Jyeṣṭhā. One should prepare the following materials: sesame oil, clarified butter, milk, curds, parched grain flour, parched rice, honey-mixtures, and black garments.
(1) Under the constellation Proṣṭhapadā or Anurādhā, one should eat food that is not sacrificial (non-vegetarian). (2)

Then, when the next day has dawned, having risen while recollecting Jyeṣṭhā, he prepares a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in a temple or in a secluded place wherever his mind finds pleasure. Then, having performed the rites beginning with the sweeping of the *devayajana* up to the preparation of the *praṇītā* waters, he invokes the goddess Jyeṣṭhā in front of the fire with this verse: "She whose lions are yoked to her chariot and whose tigers are her followers—her, this lotus-eyed Jyeṣṭhā, I invoke. (3)

Having thus invoked [the deities], he offers libations with: "Homage to Lokākīrti; homage to Paralokākīrti; homage to Śrī; homage to Jyeṣṭhā; homage to Satyā; homage to Kapilapatnī; homage to Kapilahṛdayā; homage to Kumbhī; homage to Kumbhinī; homage to Prakumbhī; homage to Jyāyā; homage to Varadā; homage to Hastimukhā; homage to Vighnapārṣada; homage to Vighnapārṣadī. Thus he performs the libation. 4.

Having performed the purification with this Anuvāka beginning, "The waters indeed are yours, the sources of bliss, golden-hued, the purifying ones, belonging to the world of light," and having honored them with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps by their respective names, saying, "Homage to such-and-such! Homage to such-and-such!"—starting from the laying of the enclosing sticks up to the invocation of the fire—he offers the cooked oblation. Having recited the Puronuvākyā, "Indra follows the constellation Jyeṣṭhā," he offers it with the Yājyā, "To the breaker of forts, the bull, the bold one. (5)

Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter: "To Indra, svāhā! To the Eldest, svāhā! To the Best, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! [He recites] the six verses beginning with "Obeisance to thee, O Nirṛti," according to their respective meters. (6) Then he offers with the Kutsa-verses.
(7) "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ, I present the oblation to the Eldest"—with these words he presents it. (8)

Then, having offered the *bali* to the quarters, having presented two garlands of perfume and two garments as an offering, and having given food to the Brahmins, he should worship with the six verses beginning with "namassute nirṛte. From the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation onwards until the gift of the cow and the granting of the boon, the rite is established.
"Upon whose chariot lions are yoked and tigers are her followers—her, this Puṇḍarīkākṣī Jyeṣṭhā, I now cause to shine forth.
Having thus dismissed Jyeṣṭhā, he should repeat the Jyeṣṭhā-mantra one thousand times, or a hundred times, or an unlimited number of times, at least ten times.

"Eating vegetables, barley-gruel, alms-food, roots, or fruits; sleeping on the ground; and performing worship in the same manner on the following day—if one practices this for six months or more, one obtains all desired objects that are worthy of being sought," so said the venerable Bodhāyana.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the third book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the tenth chapter in the third book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for Vināyaka. On the fourth or fifth day of the bright fortnight in every month, or on occasions such as a festival, one who desires success, prosperity, or cattle should offer an oblation to the Blessed Vināyaka. 1.

Having eaten only one meal on the previous day, being pure, and having sipped water for ritual purification (*ācamana*), he then performs the rites from the drawing of the lines for the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*). Then, having seated the Brāhmaṇa to his right facing south—[the deity] Hastimukha facing south—he rises and invokes the deity: "O Vighna, O Lord of Obstacles (*Vighneśvara*), come! O you who are saluted as Vighna, may you, O Lord, truly and always be for our freedom from obstacles. (2)

Then he offers the *arghya* mixed with *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and *sumanaḥ* flowers, saying: "May these waters—which are auspicious, most auspicious, peaceful, most peaceful, pure, most pure, meritorious, most meritorious, sacred, most sacred, pleasing, most pleasing, immortal, having the taste of nectar, worthy of being offered for the feet, worthy of *arghya*, worthy of honor, worthy of ceremonial sprinkling, worthy of sipping, and worthy of purification—be accepted! May the Blessed Vināyaka accept them! Salutation to Vināyaka! (3)

Then, either silently or having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, he stands in attendance, saying: "Homage to the Lord of the Earth! Homage to the Lord of the World! Homage to the Lord of Beings! (4) Having stood in attendance, he offers three oblations to Vināyaka: "Homage to Vināyaka, the Lord of the Earth; Svāhā to Vināyaka! Homage to Vināyaka, the Lord of the World; Svāhā to Vināyaka! Homage to Vināyaka, the Lord of Beings; Svāhā to Vināyaka! (5) [The ritual] from the *jaya* offering onwards is established as being performed until the bestowing of the boon by the *dhenu*.

He then offers to him as a sacrificial oblation: "To Vighna, svāhā! To Vināyaka, svāhā! To Vīra, svāhā! To Śūra, svāhā! To Ugra, svāhā! To Bhīma, svāhā! To Hastimukha, svāhā! To Varada, svāhā! To the male attendants of Vighna, svāhā! To the female attendants of Vighna, svāhā! (6) Then he offers a bali-oblation to the spirits with the verse: "Those spirits who roam about... (7)

Then, with the *vyāhṛti* mantras, he ties a bracelet of five threads upon the hand [of the image], saying: "O Vināyaka of mighty arms, O Lord of Obstacles, by your command all my desires have been accomplished; thus I tie this bracelet. (8) Then, having circumambulated Vināyaka together with the sacred fire, and having prostrated and offered salutations, he dismisses Vināyaka, saying: "O Lord of the Gaṇas, whatever has been performed by me, whether through attainment or through faith, arise, O virtuous one, along with your attendants; go in peace, and be gracious unto me. (9)

When that [twelfth day] has passed, having kindled the sacrificial fuel twelvefold, he places a fuel-stick above, one in the middle, and likewise one on the right side; then, having mixed curds, honey, milk, and clarified butter with *soma*, he performs the sprinkling around and the dismissal.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the third book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhya-śeṣa-sūtra.
Now begins the eleventh chapter in the third book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the *mṛtyuñjaya* (conquest of death). On one's birth-star, or on an auspicious star, or on the third birthday, having served food to the Brāhmaṇas and having caused them to pronounce "Auspicious day!", "Well-being!", and "Success!", he then performs the rites from the marking of the sacrificial ground up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*). Having offered the cooked oblation with the Sāvitrī verse, he brings three pieces of *dūrvā* grass each measuring a span, as well as one fuel-stick; then, having mixed together curds, honey, clarified butter, and milk, and having anointed [the sticks], he offers them into the fire eight thousand times, or eight hundred times, or twenty-eight times.

One should repeat eighty-six times the following mantras: *apaitu mṛtyuḥ*, *paraṃ mṛtyo*, *mā no mahāntam*, *mā na stoke*, *tryambakam*, and *ye te sahasram*; thus, it amounts to eight thousand [repetitions]. (1) Then one offers oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the following: "May death perish, may life increase; *bhūḥ* svāhā! May death perish, may life increase; *bhuvaḥ* svāhā! May death perish, may life increase; *suvaḥ* svāhā! May death perish, may life increase; *bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ* svāhā! (2) The ritual from the *jaya* offering onwards is established as complete up to the granting of the boon by the cow. (3)
Then, in front of the fire, he places the remnants of the oblation upon clumps of *dūrvā* grass with the verse: "That auspiciousness and well-being we choose" (RV 10.9.4).
Then he gives a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), such as a milch cow, a bull, a draft ox, a bronze vessel, gold, or a garment; "thereby one conquers death no more," so said the venerable Bodhāyana.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter of the third book in the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now, in the third book, the twelfth chapter:

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual for prosperity (*abhivṛddhikalpa*). Desiring prosperity for a village, a temple, a house, or in the most fertile fields, one should—during the bright fortnight, under a fixed zodiac sign (*sthirarāśi*), and at a fixed auspicious moment (*sthiramuhūrta*)—dig a pit knee-deep in a place of Brahmā, in the direction of Indra or Īśāna. Having smeared a square sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung, sprinkled it with water, scattered sand over it, and drawn a lotus leaf in the center with the tips of *kuśa* grass, one should [pour] the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) with the verse beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā."

Having sprinkled [the site] with the *vyāhṛtis* and this *anuvāka* beginning with "mayobhuvaḥ," "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," and "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ," having scattered flowers and caused [the officiant] to recite benedictions, he should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with sand in the center of the lotus, kindle the fire, spread grass around it, and perform the rites from the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhāna*) up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*). Then, having mentally visualized a lotus seat in the middle of the fire, he invokes Śrī with the verse "gandhadvārām" and worships her with perfumes and other offerings, using *bilva* fuel-sticks while reciting the *Śrīsūkta*.
Having offered [the oblations], he offers cooked food with two verses: "O Vāstoṣpati" and "O Vāstoṣpati.

Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with six verses beginning with "Brahma jajñānam," according to their respective meters. From the Sviṣṭakṛt offering onwards, the rite is established as completed up to the gift of the cow and the granting of the boon.
Then, in front of the fire, he places the remnants of the oblation upon lotus leaves with the verse, "That which he beheld around... (VS 13.54).

Having washed a lotus leaf and filled it with stirred *pañcagavya*, and having worshipped it with perfumes and other offerings, he sprinkles his own fields with the *Śrīsūkta*; thus says the venerable Bodhāyana.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the third book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.

Now, the thirteenth chapter in the third book. Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual for the *śithilī*. According to the rule for the square directions at the boundary of the house, the final rite is performed within. (1) If a *śithilī* appears in the middle of the house, it brings good fortune for seven days; beyond that, it causes affliction by disease among the inhabitants. One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of *palāśa* wood fuel and clarified butter with the verse "yata indra bhayāmahe"; this removes the defect. (2)

If a crack appears in the direction of Indra (the east), great danger shall befall the family; one should offer oblations with fuel-sticks of *khadira* wood while reciting the mantra: "sadasaspatim" (RV 10.85.7).

If a crack appears in the direction of Agni (the southeast), the arrival of a friend will occur within seven days; thereafter, however, it causes agitation among the king's subjects; one should offer oblations with fuel-sticks of *audumbara* wood while reciting: "ayamu te samatasi kapota iva garbhadhim vacastacchinna ojase svāhā" (RV 10.165.1–3).

If a *śithilī* arises in the direction of Yama, one obtains the gain of wealth within eight days; thereafter, it causes the death of one's wife. One should offer oblations with *plakṣa* wood fuel using the *tryambaka* mantra. 5. If a *śithilī* arises in the direction of Nirṛti, it brings rain within three days; thereafter, it causes the destruction of one's wife. One should offer oblations with *apāmārga* wood fuel using the mantra "O Prajāpati, not by you... (*prajāpate na tvat*). 6. If a *śithilī* arises in the direction of Varuṇa, it brings the attainment of pregnancy; thereafter, it may cause fear of thieves. One should offer oblations with *dūrvā* grass fuel using the mantra "Of the hosts, thee... (*gaṇānāṃ tvā*). 7.

If a crack occurs in the direction of the wind (the northwest), it brings about defects in daughters; one should offer oblations with *dūrvā* fuel-sticks while reciting "sapta te agne" (TS 1.5.3.1). 8.

If a crack occurs in the direction of Soma (the northeast), it causes the devouring of enemies and, beyond that, the destruction of grain; one should offer oblations with *vaṭa* fuel-sticks while reciting the Aghora mantra. 9.

If a crack occurs in the direction of Īśāna (the northeast), it causes affliction by disease for the master of the house; one should offer oblations with *śamī* fuel-sticks while reciting "yeṣām īśe" (TS 4.1.11.1). 10.
If a crack appears at the doorway, it brings about the destruction of the housewife; one should offer oblations with *bilva* wood-sacrificial sticks while reciting the *Tryambaka* mantra.
(11) If a crack appears at the place of the bed, it brings about the death of the master of the house; one should offer oblations with barley while reciting the *Vyāhṛtis*.
(12) If a crack appears in the place where cows and buffaloes stand, it brings about the loss of sight for the offspring; one should offer oblations with barley while reciting the *Vyāhṛtis*. (13)
If a crack appears in the place where water vessels are kept, it causes the destruction of the group of servants; one should offer oblations of barley with the seven *vyāhṛtis*.
(14) If a crack appears in a temple, it causes fear of fire in the village; one should offer oblations of *bilva* fuel-sticks with the *triyaṃbaka* mantra.

(15) If a crack appears in the assembly hall, it will certainly cause instability for the village together with its households; one should offer oblations of *dūrvā* grass with the *ā tvā hārṣam* hymn. (16)
One should perform a remedial rite for a red anthill that has arisen in a temple, an assembly hall, a pond, or even in one's own house.
(17) One should separately perform one hundred and eight oblations with sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, oblation-material, sesame, and mustard seeds, using the Vyāhṛti mantras.
(18) When an anthill arises on a site of Dharma, one should predict death; at the site of Indra, one should declare prosperity; and likewise at the site of Agni, misfortune. (19)

In the south (Yāmya), there will be the destruction of kinsmen; in the southwest (Rākṣasa), it will take away the wife; in the southeast (Āruṇa), there will be the gain of kinsmen; in the northwest (Vāyavya), there will be a return from afar.
In the north (Saumya) there is happiness, and likewise in the northeast (Raudra) there will be harsh speech and death—so said the venerable Bodhāyana.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the third book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now, the fourteenth chapter in the third book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual for twins (*yamalakalpa*). If a woman or cows give birth to twins, their consecration (*saṃskāra*) must be performed before the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*). (1) Having requested the Brahmins [for permission], they should bring the decoctions (*kaṣāya*) of four milky trees—*plakṣa*, *nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, and *udumbara*. Having filled four water-jars with these, four widows or celibate students (*brahmacārin*), having placed gold between [the child and the jars], should bathe [the child]; or, having prepared [the water] with a hundred streams, they sprinkle [him]. (2)
Then he performs the *bhūtabali* offering. Having adorned the teacher, he should present a pair of cattle.

For a male child, [he offers] barley-meal; for a female, cow’s urine. Having offered with the eight verses beginning "In the beginning, the Golden Germ (Hiraṇyagarbha) evolved," he should prepare a *māruta* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*). "No fear exists for him"—thus the naming ceremony is established. Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the third book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter of the third inquiry.

Now, therefore, on the eighth day of every half-month, Brāhmaṇas who are students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*), as well as women desiring sons, longevity, health, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and good fortune, observe a fast.

Then, at nightfall, having invoked Rudra Virūpākṣa together with his wife, his sons, his retinue, and his attendants, saying, "I invoke [you]," he welcomes him with a greeting: "Welcome! You have returned again."

"To the Blessed One, Mahādeva, Virūpākṣa, together with his wife, his sons, his attendants, and his retinue—this seat has been prepared; may the Blessed One, Mahādeva, Virūpākṣa, together with his wife, his sons, his attendants, and his retinue, be seated here.

3. Then he offers a grass mat (kūrca): "This is the grass mat for the Blessed One, made of Darbha grass, triple-stranded, green, and golden; please accept it. "May the Blessed One, Mahādeva, [accept it] for Virūpākṣa, together with his wife, his sons, his attendants, and his retinue. 4.
Then he designates the places here [with the formulas]: "Homage to Mahākāla; homage to Śaṅkara; homage to Babhrukarṇa; homage to Nandikeśvara; homage to Daṇḍimuṇḍa; homage to Caṇḍikeśvara.

(5) Then, having performed the rites from the drawing of the lines for the sacrifice to the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), he offers oblations of cooked food with the two verses beginning, "Rudra with his fresh weapon... and "The weapon of Rudra... (6).

Then he offers oblations of clarified butter with the twenty-four [mantras] beginning with "Svāhā to the god Bhava," and having offered to the Sviṣṭakṛt with "Havyavāha, well-sacrificed," he places the remains of the offering on Arka leaves in front of the fire with the mantra, "He who is Rudra in the fire.
Having honored him with the remaining perfumes and garlands, they praise him with Raudra hymns from the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, and with the praises of the seers.

He dismisses the deity with the words: "May the Blessed Lord Īśāna, who is worshipped by all the worlds, depart, being satisfied by this oblation, for the sake of returning again. He touches himself for the sake of the departure.

(9) "He who, knowing thus, performs the dismissal, becomes possessed of sons and cattle; he crosses over all evil, he crosses over the murder of a Brahmin, and he conquers repeated death," so said the Blessed Bodhāyana.
(10) Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the third book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter of the third book:
On the Release of a Bull. It should be performed on the full moon day of Kārttika, or alternatively on the full moon day of Āśvayuja or Vaiśākha, in a cow-pen in the midst of the cows.

(1) Then, having performed the rites from the drawing of the lines for the sacrificial ground up to the "mouth of the fire" (the *agnimukha*), he offers an oblation of cooked food, reciting the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*): "May Pūṣan follow our cows," and then offers with the offering verse (*yājyā*): "One [part] of thee is bright. (2)

Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with the formulas: "Here be stability, svāhā! Here be separation, svāhā! Here be delight, svāhā! Here be enjoyment, svāhā! Then, while placing the calf near the mother cow and supporting her, he recites: "May the supporter, suckling, maintain for us the nourishment of waters, food, and strength, svāhā! He continues with the hymn beginning, "The cows have come, and they have performed what is auspicious," and with the section ending with "Obeisance to thy wrath, O Rudra" (Rudrādhyāya). 3. From the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the rite is established until the gift of the cow as a boon.
4. Then, having murmured the *rudra-japa*, he gives a pair of cattle to the *adhvaryu*. 5.

With the *lāja* mantra, he should cause [the bull]—whether it be of one color or two colors—to circumambulate three times to the right; thus he covers the herd. Four of the herd’s leading heifers are to be bathed and clothed, and [the performer] takes up water with sesame seeds while reciting the verse, "The east is the direction of the Ṛcs.
(6) Having drunk the drops of water, they should shake them off, saying, "May the ancestors depart satisfied.
(7) Then he releases this [bull] among the cows in their midst, saying, "I entrust this youth to you. (8)
He recites the mantra "tvāṃ gāvaḥ" over the one who is entering. (9) He recites the mantra "mayobhūrvāto abhi vātūsnāḥ" over the one standing in the middle.

(10) Having cooked milk-rice (*pāyasa*) in the milk of all [the cows], having honored the Brāhmaṇas, and having caused them to pronounce blessings, he gives a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his ability. (11)

He purifies twenty-one generations—ten preceding, ten following, and himself—even if they have entered the womb of animals or exist in other births, or are oppressed by low-born families; he purifies the row [of ancestors] and does not return to rebirth, he does not return to rebirth.
12. Moreover, they cite this example: "One should desire many sons, so that even if only one should go to Gayā, or marry a Gaurī maiden, or release a dark-blue bull. 13.
That which is red in color, with a white tail as its mark, and white at the hooves and the hump—that indeed is known as the 'dark-blue bull' (nīlavṛṣa). 14.
Thus spoke the Blessed Bodhāyana. 15.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the third book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter in the third book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for the Thousand-fold Feeding (Sahasrabhojana). It may be performed during the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, on a day of one's own birth among the three [births], or during the southern course of the sun.

(1) In one’s own house or in a temple, wherever there is a pure place, having purified oneself, having had an even number of Brāhmaṇas wash their hands and feet and sipped water, having prepared seats for them, having honored them with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, and having caused them to recite, "May there be the fulfillment of my resolve," one should honor the Brāhmaṇas with threefold food, cause them to pronounce blessings, and perform circumambulation and prostration. (2)

Having worshipped the thousand-fold Īśvara with a thousandfold meal, twelve or six Brāhmaṇas are made to hear the ten *anuvākas* at the end of the meal, beginning with "Svāhā to one, Svāhā to two. (3) Having served food to the Brāhmaṇas and caused them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity!", he then performs the rites from the marking of the altar for the sacrifice to the gods up to the *agnimukha* (introductory oblation to Agni), and offers the cooked oblation. Having recited the *puronuvākyā*, "viṣṇornukaṃ," he offers it with the *yājyā*, "viṣṇo rarāṭamasi. (4)

Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with the twelve names, beginning with "To Keśava, svāhā," and so forth; the rite from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering until the granting of the boon by the cow is completed as established.

(5) Then, having fed the Brahmins with rice-milk mixed with sugar and ghee, he presents an offering of food to the deities with their twelve names, saying, "To such-and-such, svāhā! To such-and-such, svāhā!
(6) Then, having informed the Brahmins, he should give them pairs of garments, pairs of earrings, a finger-ring, sandals, an umbrella, and a water-pot. (7)

Both the husband and wife should eat the remnants of the food, the remnants of the clarified butter, and the remnants of the cooked offerings; they obtain all desires and are liberated from all defilements and great sins. Having passed through the world of Brahmā for sixty thousand years, one is honored in the world of Viṣṇu—so said the venerable Bodhāyana.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the third book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter in the third book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the *sahasrabhojana-sutyā* (the sacrifice of feeding a thousand). On the occasion of the equinox (*viṣuva*), the solstice (*ayana*), one’s birth-star (*janmanakṣatra*), an eclipse of the moon or sun, or when one is seized by a planet or afflicted by disease, a person desiring offspring or desiring prosperity should, having obtained the permission of the Brahmins and having performed the formal invitation (*varaṇa*) for those who are desired, feed a thousand Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas. When the number of a thousand has been completed, on an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), he should invite twelve or six Brahmins, honor them with baths, seats, and so forth, as well as perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, and then—

Having performed the rites from the drawing of lines for the deity's altar up to the placing of the *praṇītā* waters, he rises, invokes Viṣṇu with the *vyāhṛtis* in front of the fire, and having performed the rites from the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), he worships the deity. Having sprinkled [the offering] with the three verses beginning with "The waters are indeed our source of bliss," with the four verses beginning with "Golden-colored," and with this entire section beginning with "Pavamāna, the winner of heaven," and having honored him with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, he then offers the cooked oblation. Having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*) "Viṣṇoḥ nukam," he offers the oblation with the offering verse (*yājyā*) "Viṣṇo rarāṭam asi. 1.

Then he offers oblations of clarified butter with the twelve names, beginning with "To Keśava, svāhā! The rite from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering until the bestowing of the cow and the granting of the boon is performed as established.
Then, having fed the Brahmins, he presents an offering of food consisting of jaggery, milk-rice mixed with ghee, saying "To such-and-such [name], svāhā! with the twelve names.
Then he should give to the Brahmins pairs of garments, pairs of earrings, a finger-ring, sandals, an umbrella, and a water-pot.

Both the husband and wife should eat the remnants of the food, the remnants of the clarified butter, and the remnants of the cooked offerings; he obtains all desires and is purified from great sins. Having passed sixty thousand years in the world of Brahmā, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu—thus said the venerable Bodhāyana.
(5) Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the third book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter in the third book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the *jīvaśrāddha*. He who desires his own welfare should fast on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight and, on that very day, prepare the necessary materials—those required for the funeral rites of the deceased: a set of six garments, a golden needle, a hook, a rope made of woven threads, a patched garment, a stalk of the *palāśa* tree, a stool made of *udumbara* wood, and water-jars, as well as other items. 1.

On the following day, having bathed and remained in the water at midday, he should rise and cause [others] to recite, "An auspicious day! Well-being! Prosperity! He should give a garment and a ring as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and facing south, he should eat milk-rice mixed with ghee. 2.

Then, having established the fire according to the rules for the *śrāddha*, having strewn grass around it, and having performed the *agnimukha* rite, he offers from the cooked food. Having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*), "Four are the horns," he offers with the offering verse (*yājyā*), "Established in three ways. Having recited the invitatory verse, "That most excellent glory of Savitṛ," he offers with the offering verse, "The uniter of pleasant truths. Having recited the invitatory verse, "Those four," he offers with the offering verse, "Two paths. Having recited the invitatory verse, "O Agni, lead us," he offers with the offering verse, "She who is transverse. ||3||

Then he offers oblations of clarified butter, having sacrificed with the eighteen-verse Puruṣasūkta; he should sacrifice eight thousand, one hundred and eight, or twenty-eight times with the Gāyatrī mantra. From the Sviṣṭakṛt offering onwards, the rite is established until the granting of the boon by the cow. (4) The fire must be maintained until the completion [of the rite]. (5) Having gone to a crossroads and given a needle, a hook, a patched garment, and a rope to a short-statured Brāhmaṇa of dark complexion, and having caused him to say, "May the servants of Yama be pleased," he should place the water-pots upon rice grains. (6)

Having wrapped [the jars] with thread and fashioned them into the form of a person—placing three [jars] on the head, three in the mouth, twenty-one on the neck, four on the body, two on each arm, one on the *liṅga*, and five on each foot—one should say: "May the Blessed Lord Yama be pleased.

(7) Then, having prepared a throne and washed it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and having fashioned the form of a person out of *palāśa* stalks upon a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), one should project the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) into the jar-person and project the physical body into the body made of stalks, and then go to sleep. (8)

When the sun has risen, one should personally perform an ablution upon the body with water from ritual jars, using the *Puruṣasūkta* and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), as well as pure water. In the evening, one should eat food mixed with sesame seeds and clarified butter. (9) One should also feed Brāhmaṇas for the satisfaction of the servants of Yama. (10) On the fourth day, the burning of the mechanical device (*yantra*) takes place. (11)

Having performed the concluding salutation with the words, "Water and the funeral ball for my [deceased] of such-and-such lineage; this is the funeral ball for the sake of the next world; Svadhā," one should conclude the rite.
(12) In that case, the period of impurity shall be ten days for oneself, but it does not apply to the [deceased's] kin.
(13) On the eleventh day, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is commenced. (14)

Moreover, they cite this: "When a woman who has committed a sin or a Śūdra has burnt their own bodies with mechanical devices, one should perform all the rites on that very day; such indeed is the Vedic revelation.
(15) For women, however, it may be performed either silently or with mantras.
(16) This should be done month after month for a year, and after a year, until twelve years have passed; beyond that, there is cessation. (17)
When one is unable to do it oneself, then sons and others should perform it.

18. Furthermore, they cite this: "Even while living, one should perform the *śrāddha* for oneself, even when others are present; it should be performed immediately according to the rules, with the exception of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
19. One should not delay its prescribed time, because life is uncertain; thus said the venerable Bodhāyana. 20.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the third book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the twentieth chapter in the third book:
Hereafter we shall explain the Nārāyaṇabali. It should be performed on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight during either the southern or northern solstice. 1.

On the preceding day, he invites twelve or six Brahmins who are endowed with noble birth, lineage, sacred learning, and good conduct. 2. Then, on the following day, having established the fire in a temple or on a riverbank and having strewn grass around it, having performed the rites up to the *āpraṇītā* waters, he rises and invokes the deity in front of the fire. Having recited two verses from the *Puruṣasūkta*, he invokes Puruṣa with the *vyāhṛtis*.
3. Then he bathes him with the *Puruṣasūkta*. 4.
Then, having honored him with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps using the eight-syllable mantra, he satiates him with water using the twelve names, beginning with "I satiate Keśava.

(5) Having performed the rites from the laying on of the undergarment up to the *agnimukha* (the invocation of the fire), he offers oblations of cooked food, reciting the *puronuvākyā* "viṣṇornukam" and offering with the *yājyā* "paro mātrayā.
(6) Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with these very names, beginning with "To Keśava, svāhā! (7)

Then he offers food mixed with jaggery, milk-rice, and ghee, saying: "By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I offer this oblation to Viṣṇu, the Great Puruṣa. He mutters [the mantra] with the seven vyāhṛtis and the word svāhā. With the vyāhṛtis, he offers water for sipping. 8.

Then, having invited the Brahmins and seated them on seats prepared with Darbha grass, and having honored them with garments, perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and garlands, he—being thus authorized—prepares the sacrificial oblation mixed with sesame seeds and clarified butter and offers it into the hand [of the Brahmin], reciting twenty-four mantras beginning with: "To the ancestors, *svadhā*! Homage! To Nārāyaṇa, *svāhā*! (9). Then:
"To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, *svadhā*! Homage! To Nārāyaṇa, *svāhā*! (10).
Then, having satisfied the Brahmins with food and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), he gives them a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his ability. (11)
