Having circumambulated [the fire] and requested permission for the remainder, he spreads *darbha* grass with the tips pointing eastward to the south of the fire and offers the oblation (*bali*) upon it, saying: "Obeisance to the Viśvedevas; obeisance to the Sādhyas; obeisance to all the gods; obeisance to all deities; obeisance to Viṣṇu; obeisance to Nārāyaṇa; obeisance to the Thousand-headed One; obeisance to the Soul of Sacrifice; obeisance to the Person of Sacrifice; obeisance to the Soul of the Universe; obeisance to the Soul of All; obeisance to the Lord of All. (12) From the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the rite is completed up to the granting of the boon by the cow. (13)
"He attains all the ancestors and is honored in the world of Brahman," so said the venerable Bodhāyana. 14.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the third book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter in the third book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the Nārāyaṇabali. Death caused by a Caṇḍāla, water, a snake, a Brāhmaṇa, lightning, or even from fanged animals, as well as death through poison, hanging by a rope, falling from a rock, or dying in a foreign land—whether for those who have committed evil deeds, those accused of crimes, drunkards, those who have abandoned their own selves, those killed by twice-born men, or others—the rite should be performed at the very place where such a person died, for twelve years, three years, or one year. 1.
Having gathered unjoined tips of Palāśa leaves along with their stalks, one should fashion a human figure on a black antelope skin and consecrate it according to the *Hotṛkalpa* or the *Pitṛmedha*.

(2) Now, having extracted the ritual formulas (*prayogamantra*), there shall be a separate application for each verse of the *Puruṣasūkta* in place of those respective formulas. (3) Or rather, everything may be performed silently. (4)
The fasting is performed with the Yāmya-sūkta;
the worship is performed with the Puruṣa-sūkta;
from this point onward, it is the same as before.

Having bathed at a sacred ford (tīrtha) and performed the water-rite for the deceased, he mentally utters the name and lineage [of the deceased] and should verbally declare: "O Nārāyaṇa, this water is for you. 8.
He performs this very rite every evening and morning for ten nights, or for three nights. 9–10.
In the offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa), the distinction is that one says, "O [Name], this rice-ball is for you.
(11) On the eleventh day, the rite is performed for a single individual (ekoddiṣṭa).
(12) Likewise, in the fire-offering (agnau karaṇa), one should say, "Svāhā to the deceased [Name] and to Yama. (13)
In receiving, giving, and dismissing, he acts with the mantra "To Nārāyaṇa.
(14) He should form all intentions with the mind and express them through speech. (15) This is the same for the three-year vow and the six-month vow. (16)

The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is performed in the [first] year; in place of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the *nārāyaṇabali* ritual is performed. (17) Neither the evening nor the morning [offerings] exist; this is according to the view of Bodhāyana. (18) [This is done] during the two solstices (*ayana*), at the two transits (*saṅkrānti*), or on auspicious days. (19)
Alternatively, the rite for the opposing side (the deceased) may take place.
(20) The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for these and others is the same.

(21) One should pour the vessel of the deceased into the vessels of the ancestors, or one should pour it into the three [vessels]. One should place the *piṇḍa* of the deceased upon the *piṇḍas* of the ancestors with the words: "O you, unite with the fathers, the grandfathers, and the great-grandfathers! Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ om! Thus said the venerable Bodhāyana. (22)
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the third book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter in the third book:

He who desires his own spiritual welfare regarding the funeral rites—if they are to be performed for himself—then even while living he should perform everything from the cremation until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, exactly as it has been prescribed for the deceased. 1.

Thus Kaṇva said: "He who, while still living, desires to perform a śrāddha for himself, having performed the consecration by means of a mechanical device (yantra), as well as the water-libation and the bali-offering;

||2|| having then performed the sixteen śrāddhas, he should give whatever is dear to himself, and having given that himself, he should then complete the śrāddha. ||3|| In that case, there shall be impurity (aśauca) for ten days for himself, but none for his relatives. ||5||

"In this very matter, Viṣṇu has said: 'Whatever pertains to the next world for one's own sake, all that one shall obtain; for indeed, an action performed by men never goes to waste. (5) Therefore, he who has no performers—neither kinsmen, nor sons, nor disciples—should, while still living, perform everything pertaining to the hereafter in its entirety. While pronouncing the name, he should say: 'It will be done for the sake of the lineage and the personal name [of the deceased]. (6) Or else, he may give according to the procedure for the *pravidāna* offering; this also is one way. (7)
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the third book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter in the third book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the offering (*bali*) for the crows that portend auspicious and inauspicious signs. On the thirteenth, eighth, or ninth day of the bright fortnight, having gone out from the village toward the east or north, one should prepare a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung at the temple of a deity, in a cow-pen, or on a riverbank; having smeared it, sprinkled it with water, and drawn the ritual marks (*lakṣaṇa*), one sprinkles it again with water and prepares seats by circling clockwise with *darbha* grass, saying: "I prepare a seat for the Aṅkatas; I prepare a seat for the Kaṅkatas."
"I offer to the sons of Kadrū; I offer to the crows; I offer to the sons of Brahmā"—thus [he says] in the middle.
1. Then he invokes them: "Neither the tawny ones, nor the red ones, nor the *ariṣṭas*, nor the *mahāriṣṭas*, but those who are merely crows.
2. "May the swift birds, the crows that feed on offerings, come hither. 3.
"I invoke the Aṅkatās; I invoke the Kaṅkatās; I invoke the sons of Kadrū; I invoke the crows; I invoke the sons of Brahmā"—thus in the center. 4.

Then he bathes them with the three verses beginning "The waters, indeed, are most healing," with the four verses beginning "Gold-colored, pure," and having sprinkled them with the entire section beginning "Pavamāna, born of heaven," he then satiates them with water, saying: "I satiate the Aṅkatas; I satiate the Kaṅkatas; I satiate the sons of Kadrū; I satiate the Vāsases; I satiate the sons of Brahmā"—thus in the middle. 5.

Then he offers these [birds] with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, presenting the sacrificial food—either milk-rice (*pāyasa*) or boiled rice—with the words: "Homage to such-and-such! Homage to such-and-such! In the center, he says: "To the *aṅkatās*, svāhā! To the *kaṅkatās*, svāhā! To the sons of *kadru*, svāhā! To the crows, svāhā! To the sons of Brahmā, svāhā! (6) Then he instructs them: "You are the truthful ones; speak the truth, delight in the truth, O crows! Let that which is true here be spoken by him who would eat this offering falsely. (7)
Now, he who would eat a false sacrificial offering (mithyābali) would take upon himself the evil deed of killing a mother or a father.
(8) He who would eat a false sacrificial offering would take upon himself the evil deed of killing a hundred Kapila cows, and especially Brahmins.

(9) One should first accept [the offering] for existence; afterwards, for non-existence, one should accept the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). One should accept the subsequent [offering] saying "it does not exist," and also the following [offering] saying "it will come to be. (10)
"Knowing that this is the most excellent among omens for the attainment of all goals, one should undertake all undertakings"—thus said the venerable Bodhāyana. 11.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the third book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.

Now, therefore, [the section] on auspicious and inauspicious omens; now, for one who desires his own welfare, the procedure for the Nārāyaṇabali consecration; now, the Nārāyaṇabali; now, the Jīvaśrāddha; now, the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice involving a thousand feedings; now, the procedure for the thousand feedings; now, the release of a bull; now, [the rite] performed every half-month; now, the ritual for twins; now, the ritual for the Śithilī; now, the ritual for prosperity; now, the ritual for overcoming death; now, therefore...

The ritual manual for Vināyaka; then, the ritual manual for Jyeṣṭhā; then, the ritual manual for Ravi; then, the ritual manual for Viṣṇu; then, the ritual manual for Sarasvatī; then, the ritual manual for Śrī; then, the ritual manual for Upaśruti; then, the ritual manual for Durgā; then, the ritual manual for the Vyāhṛtis; then, the ritual manual for the purificatory rites (pavitra). 23.

Now, therefore, [the ritual] of the purifiers; now, therefore, the ritual procedure for the *vyāhṛtis*; now, therefore, the ritual procedure for Durgā; now, therefore, the ritual procedure for Upaśruti; now, therefore, the ritual procedure for Śrī; now, therefore, the ritual procedure for Sarasvatī; now, therefore, the ritual procedure for Viṣṇu; now, therefore, the ritual procedure for Ravi; now, therefore, the ritual procedure for Jyeṣṭhā; now, therefore, the ritual procedure for Vināyaka; now, therefore, the ritual procedure for Mṛtyuñjaya; now, therefore, the ritual procedure for Abhivṛddhi; now, therefore, the ritual procedure for Śithilī; now, therefore, the ritual procedure for Yamala; now, therefore, every half-month... Now.

The release of a bull; now, therefore, the procedure for feeding a thousand; now, therefore, the Soma-pressing for a thousand; now, therefore, the Jāvaśrāddha; now, therefore, the Nārāyaṇabali; now, therefore, the consecration of the Nārāyaṇabali—for he who desires his own welfare; now, therefore, the signs of auspicious and inauspicious omens. 23. Thus ends the third book in the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣa-sūtra; now begins the fourth book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the *mithyāsatyabali*. Having bathed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras should go out from the village toward the eastern or northern direction. Then, at a temple or on a riverbank, having performed the rites beginning with the drawing of lines for the sacrificial ground up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), he offers cooked food with the two verses: "From which we fear, O Indra... and "The giver of well-being, the lord of the people... (RV 7.87.5; 6.47.11). 1.

Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with the following verses: *apaitu mṛtyuḥ*, *paraṃ mṛtyo*, *mā no mahāntam*, *mā nastoke*, *tryambakam*, *ye te sahasram*, *viṣṇornukam*, *jātavedase*, *agne tvaṃ pāraya*, and with the *vyāhṛtis*: "May death perish, may life increase—*bhūḥ svāhā*. May death perish, may life increase—*bhuvaḥ svāhā*. May death perish, may life increase—*suvaḥ svāhā*. May death perish, may life increase—*bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ svāhā*. From the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the rite is established as usual until the giving of the cow and the granting of the boon.
Then, in front of the fire, he places the remnants of the oblation upon clumps of *dūrvā* grass with the mantra, "He who is Rudra in the fire. [This is] the marking out of the ashes.
(3) One should give a calf to the teachers.
(4) Having prepared food, honored the Brahmins, and caused them to pronounce blessings, one should give eleven bulls as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Thus says the venerable Bodhāyana. (5)
Thus ends the first chapter of the fourth book in the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the second chapter of the fourth book:

The Dhūrta-bali, which is an imitation of the Āhuti-anukṛti and the Bali-haraṇa-anukṛti, should be performed every four months on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna; or else on the thirteenth day. Likewise in Āṣāḍha, and likewise in Kārttika. 1.

He prepares the ritual implements beforehand: sacrificial grass, fifteen fuel-sticks of *bilva* wood, a *mekṣaṇa* ladle of *bilva* wood, enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), white and red perfumes and garlands, white and red amulets (*pratisara*), incense, cooked foods, various kinds of snacks, and he cooks a *sthālīpāka* oblation. 2.

Then, taking them along with his pupils, he goes out from the village toward the east or the north; having gone to where there is water, he bathes, sips water, and purifies himself by sprinkling with water that is fragrant, with verses containing the word *aliṅga*, with those addressed to Varuṇa, with those of golden color (*hiraṇyavarṇābhiḥ*), and with the *pāvamānī* verses. Having entered into the water, he performs three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while reciting the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn. Emerging from the water, wringing out his garment, and putting on another clean garment, he sips water and leads them to the place of sacrifice.
3. Then, in a pure and level spot, they prepare an altar (*vedi*) measuring one man’s height or of unlimited size. 4.

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in its eastern half, and having fixed an udumbara branch that has many leaves, many branches, and undried tips, they fashion an image of the venerable Dhūrta with darbha grass. To the west of the udumbara branch, they gird themselves with a protective cord (pratisara) together with the branch. 5. They put on the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), [reciting]: "The sacred thread, the supreme purifier, which was born together with Prajāpati in the beginning—put on this bright, life-prolonging, foremost sacred thread; may there be strength and splendor for you. 6.
"By that, I accept you for long life, for sacred knowledge, and for spiritual luster.

(7) Having prepared a mound on the western half of the altar, and having performed the rites beginning with the drawing of lines up to the sprinkling of water, he strews grass upon the altar so as not to be seen through it. (8)

To the north of the fire, having spread *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward, he places the vessels upon it in pairs, turned face down. Having silently turned the vessels face up with water consecrated by silent formulas, he unties the fuel-bundle and sprinkles it three times with all the water. Having seated a Brāhmaṇa to the south on the *darbha* grass and placed a vessel of water to the north, he sprinkles with water the cooked rice or milk-rice (*pāyasa*) which has been obtained unasked; he then places the clarified butter over the fire, heats it, carries fire around both of them, and performs the rite of encircling them with the enclosing-sticks.

When the pupils have been initiated, he sprinkles water around the fire from left to right, then anoints the fuel and places it on the fire with this verse: "This hymn of praise for Jātavedas, who is worthy of it, let us fashion with our intellect as one fashions a chariot. For his providence is auspicious in the assembly; O Agni, in your friendship may we never suffer harm. Svāhā! (9) In the same manner, having anointed it, he places the second piece of fuel on the fire with this verse: "That which you sacrifice for me, accomplish that perfectly. He dwells free from enemies and possesses great heroism. He prospers; no misfortune reaches him. O Agni, in your friendship may we never suffer harm. Svāhā! (10)

In this very manner, having anointed it, he places the third kindling stick upon the fire with the verse: "May we be able to perfect thee as a fuel-stick through our prayers; in thee the gods eat the oblation offered. Bring hither the Ādityas, for we long for them. O Agni, in thy friendship may we never suffer harm; Svāhā! || 11 || In this very manner, having anointed it, he places the fourth kindling stick upon the fire with the verse: "That is auspicious for thee, that, kindled in thine own abode and invoked with Soma, thou art most gracious. Thou bestowest jewels and wealth upon the donor. O Agni, in thy friendship may we never suffer harm; Svāhā! || 12 ||

In this very manner, having anointed [the fuel], he places the fifth piece of wood on the fire with the verse: "O Aṅgiras, we make thee grow with fuel and with ghee; shine brightly, O youngest one, svāhā! (13).
In this very manner, having anointed [the fuel], the remaining pieces are offered with the six-syllable formula "Bhava namas svāhā," decreasing by one [syllable] each time. (14).

Having performed the rites from the pouring of the *āghāra* libations up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), they circumambulate three times to the right while dancing, invoking the deities. (15).
I invoke this Skanda, the son of the Maiden, to whom lions are yoked to his chariot and tigers follow as his attendants.

(16) May Kartikeya, the supreme deity, the son of Brahmāṇī, come together with his mothers, Dhātrī, Viśākha, and Viśvarūpa; accompanied by his followers, may you accept this offered oblation which is pleasing to you.
(17) I take refuge in him who was born on the seventh day, whose power is the Śakti, the subduer of enemies with seven joints, surrounded by tigers, the great deceiver, and one of firm vows. (18)

I take refuge in the supreme god, the giver of boons, the rogue, the leader of the army, the son of Ugrasenā and Aparṇā, who has six faces like the Kṛttikās. With the fires and the prescribed Cāturmāsya sacrifices, we worship you, the seventh [deity], in the forest with perfumes and with devotion, O Śakti; grant us wealth, O King, and the knowledge of wealth, and let the rogue grant our desires. Homage to Śaṅkara, homage to Sthāman, homage to Nīlagrīva, homage to the son of the Kṛttikās. May the ritual application be propitious; may Viśākha be pleased.

"May the son of the Kṛttikās be pleased; may he be pleased, salutations! May he be pleased, salutations again and again! (19) As he approaches, [the host] addresses him: "Welcome, welcome back, O Blessed Dhūrta! This seat has been prepared; may the Blessed Great Dhūrta sit here. (20) There, he offers a seat of grass (*kūrca*) and an offering of honor (*arhaṇa*): "This is the Blessed One's seat of grass, made of *darbha* grass, triple-stranded, green, and golden; please accept it. (21)

Then, having covered [the vessel] with a larger, radiant lid containing flowers, fruits, and unbroken grains in either a bronze cup (*kaṃsa*) or a wooden goblet (*camasa*), they present the waters of honor (*arghaṇīyā āpaḥ*) with these words: "May these waters—auspicious, most auspicious, pure, most pure, sacred, most sacred, immortal, of immortal flavor, intended for washing the feet, for the *arghya* offering, for sprinkling, and for purification—be enjoyed; may they be accepted! May the Blessed One, the Great Deceiver (*Mahādhūrta*), accept them! [He then recites] the three verses beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed... (*āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*) and the four verses beginning with "The golden-colored ones... (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*).

Having purified himself with this *anuvāka* beginning with "evamānassuvarjanaḥ," having turned clockwise and then turned back toward the west, he sits behind the fire; while [the disciples] hold on to him, he offers oblations of clarified butter: "To Skanda, svāhā! To Kumāra, svāhā! To Bāla, svāhā! To Hiraṇyacūḍa, svāhā! To Aṅgiras, svāhā! To Guha, svāhā! To Bhadrāsana, svāhā! To Nīlagrīva, svāhā! To Bhavaputra, svāhā! To Dhūrta, svāhā! To Paśubhū, svāhā! To Ṣaṣṭhī, svāhā! To Viśākha, svāhā!"
"Sanatkumāra, svāhā! To the attendants of Skanda, svāhā! To the attendants of Ṣaṣṭhī, svāhā!"—with these very names, he offers oblations from the *mekṣaṇa* spoon into the eastern half [of the fire].

(22) Having taken a portion for the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering from the northern half [of the oblation], and having placed it within the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he rises and worships the deities with these very names, using perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, saying: "Homage to such-and-such! Homage to such-and-such! With food, he says: "To such-and-such, svāhā! To such-and-such, svāhā! With fruit-water, he says: "I satiate such-and-such; I satiate such-and-such. (23)

Here he pays homage: "Whatever desire I may desire, may that desire of mine be fulfilled; when that desire is fulfilled, I shall offer a *droṇa* [of grain]. May he increase my desire. When the desire is fulfilled, he will offer food from a *droṇa*. 24. Then he worships him with the verse: "Homage to Bhava-udbhava! Guha is Bhava, the Lord of Secrets. 25.
"Homage to Vasu, the Lord of Wealth! May Dhūrta-svāmī be gracious! 26.

"May the one of great fame, great splendor, great army, and great form; may he of great austerity accept this offering from me, his devotee. (27–28) Then, having sat down and offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, they rise and, while escorting the deity, dance and circumambulate three times counter-clockwise, saying: "May that chariot yoked with lions and tigers, the best among chariots, proceed—the Blessed One, the rogue, the sweet-spoken, the doer of what is dear. Om, obeisance! (29) Then, having sat down again, [the ritual] proceeds from the *jaya* offering onwards until the successful completion ending with the granting of the boon of the excellent cow. (30)

Then, taking this image and placing it upon his head, he immerses it in water with the *avabhṛtha* mantra; having adorned himself with the remaining perfumes and garlands, he binds on an amulet (*pratisara*) with the following:

"The well-made thread by Aditi, made threefold by Indra, knotted by the Aśvins, and fashioned as an amulet by Brahmā—by this, all sorcery and whatever evil I have done are neutralized; for me there is no fear from any quarter as long as I wear this thread.
Then they cause one another to sip water, saying: "May the venerable Great Deceiver be pleased."
Then, taking from the cooked portion, he eats it.
(34) A woman and a young boy should not eat it. (35) The mantra for eating that is: "Thou art life. (36)
Having consumed [the food] and sipped water, he touches his belly with two verses: "From whatever we fear, O Indra... and "The giver of well-being, the lord of the people... (RV 10.151.1–2).
Having sprinkled [water] repeatedly, [he performs this] at the end; it is life-prolonging, bestowing luster, slaying demons, a means of well-being, and successful.
The imitation of the oblations has been explained; the imitation of the offering of bali-oblations [is now described].
Having invoked the deity, worshipped with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food, fruits, and water, and having paid obeisance, they dismiss [the deity].
40. By performing the *dhūrtabali* in this manner every four months, the sacrificer obtains the fruit of the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices; so said the venerable Bodhāyana.
41. Thus ends the second chapter in the fourth book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the third chapter of the fourth book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the *mṛtabali* (offering for the deceased). Having smeared a square area extending toward the southeast with cow dung, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), facing south, and having knelt with the left knee, he draws a line once, sprinkles it with water, spreads *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south, and purifies [the vessel] with water. He then takes a portion of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*)—once, mixed with sesame seeds, and either the size of a handful or the size of a hen’s egg—with his hand, saying: "O [Name], of such-and-such lineage, this rice for you; *svadhā*, homage! (1)

Then, having touched [the child] with the thumb, and having performed the rites with collyrium and ointment, honey, a garment, or a woolen fringe, and having offered perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps from hand to hand in reverse order for ten nights both morning and evening, and having fed the village with auspicious blessings on the tenth day, and having given the evening *bali* offering with unconventional food on the tenth day, they then perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite on the eleventh day.
(2) One should never ward off birds such as hawks or crows, for the Vedic tradition declares: "Beings of that very form come as his ancestors.
(3) Thus ends the third chapter of the fourth book in the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.

Now begins the fourth chapter of the fourth book. Now follows the imitation of the *prahuta* offerings; we shall explain the rules for the enjoyment of merit. The construction of embankments, rivers, moats, ponds, lotus-pools, tanks, wells, temples, palaces, and dwellings, as well as [the planting of] medicinal herbs and trees, constitutes *pūrta* (meritorious works). One who desires prosperity offers oblations at night. 1.

During the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, the *adhvaryu* prepares the sacrificial materials. Having fashioned a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) three *aratnis* in length from either *khadira* or *palāśa* wood, he prepares golden figures of a serpent, a porpoise, a tortoise, a crocodile, a crab, a lotus, a water-lily, a white water-lily, and a blue lotus; silver figures of a swan, a fish, and a frog; and representations of medicinal herbs and trees corresponding to the forms of temples, palaces, and dwellings, as well as figures of their fruits made of gold and gems. He also prepares clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain flour, and milk.

"Cakes, parched grain, flour-meal, perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, garments, fuel, and sacrificial grass—[these are for] the twice-born at the time of dusk; [their] oblation is performed with these. For Śūdras, it is performed with salutations or with ritual circumambulations."

Having smeared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) on the north-eastern bank of the pond and having dug a pit for the sacrificial post (yūpa), the Adhvaryu establishes the post with the formulas: "O Brahman, [this is] the Brāhmaṇa" for a Brāhmaṇa; "In this kingdom... for a Rājanya; and "A milch-cow" for a Vaiśya. 5.

Having scattered jewels, pearls, coral, gold, elephants, and sesame seeds, and having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) behind the sacrificial post (yūpa), he then performs the rites beginning with the sweeping of the altar for the sacrifice to the gods up to the point of the *praṇītā* water-vessel. Then, rising, he invokes the gods in front of the fire: "To Brahmā, to Viṣṇu, to Śrī, to Sūrya, to Candra, to Agni, to Yama, to Nirṛti, to Varuṇa, to Vāyu, to Soma, and to Īśāna. Having thus invoked them and scattered gold, silver, and sesame seeds, and having worshipped the deity of the sacrificial post with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, he stands in worship before the post with the verse:
"That supreme abode of Viṣṇu... (Tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam). 6.

Having wrapped it in cloths and fastened forms upon it, and having performed the rites from the *paridhāna* (laying of the enclosing sticks) up to the *agnimukha* (offering to Agni), he offers oblations of cooked food with the two verses: "Forgive our sin" (*avataṃ naḥ*) and "Raise up the highest [sin]" (*ud uttamam*). 7. Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with these two sections: "To the waters of the well, svāhā! To the waters, svāhā! and with the following mantras: "This prayer of mine, O Varuṇa... (*imaṃ me varuṇa*), "I approach you... (*tattvā yāmi*), "Whatever indeed... (*yacciddhi*), "Whatever this [debt] of the gamblers... (*yat kiṃcedam kitavāsaḥ*), "The golden-colored, pure, purifying ones... (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*), "Be thou unto us, O Agni... (*tvaṃ no agne*), and "So be thou unto us, O Agni... (*sa tvaṃ no agne*). 8.

Then, after the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers the oblations for the sacrificial post (*yūpāhuti*): "To Brahman, svāhā! To Viṣṇu, svāhā! To Śrī, svāhā! To Sūrya, svāhā! To Candramas, svāhā! To Indra, svāhā! To Agni, svāhā! To Yama, svāhā! To Nirṛti, svāhā! To Varuṇa, svāhā! To Vāyu, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! To Īśāna, svāhā!
(9) Then he offers cooked portions of herbs and trees with two verses beginning, "O Mother, those which have been born, a hundred are your abodes... (10)
Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter, verse by verse, with three sections beginning: "The flowering, the fruit-bearing... svāhā to the plants; svāhā to the trees.
(11) Then, after the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers cooked food to the dwellings with two verses beginning: "O Lord of the Dwelling, O Lord of the Dwelling...
(12) Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with six verses beginning: "O Lord of the Dwelling, a firm pillar... (13)
Then, after the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he recites the verses of the remaining portion of the *anuvāka*, beginning with "Obeisance to you, O Rudra, to your wrath," verse by verse (14).
Then, having offered the *kūśmāṇḍa* oblations, before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he says: "We announce this to Vaiśvānara" (15).

Then, on *darbha* grass, he presents an offering (*bali*) consisting of cakes mixed with rice, sesame flour, milk, and ghee, along with parched grains, groats, and honey-mash, using the twelve names previously mentioned, beginning with "Obeisance to Brahman" (16).

The sacrificer, having circumambulated three times from left to right, having scattered the offerings (bali), and having caused [the officiant] to recite the Yama-sūkta and the Puruṣa-sūkta; having made the ocean wavy and bathed therein, and having sipped water (ācamana); he should give garments to the Brāhmaṇas, give a pair of cows to the teacher (ācārya), and give eleven cows including a bull. Having caused [them] to pronounce blessings, he should dismiss the forms (rūpas). 17.
One who performs it in this manner purifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, himself as the twenty-first, and the row (paṅkti). 18.

Moreover, they cite this example: "At dawn, they awaken [the king] with the sounds of dance, song, and instrumental music. For those [sacrifices] that have been lost, performing them again yields a superior fruit; he is honored in the world of Brahmā for sixty thousand years," so said the venerable Bodhāyana. (19) Thus ends the fourth chapter of the fourth book in the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the fifth chapter of the fourth book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual for optional rites (*kāmyavidhi*). For one desiring food, he offers oblations with the following: "O Lord of Food, grant us food"; "What has been born, O Agni"; "The *vaṣaṭ* of thee"; "O Lord of the Dwelling"; "Thus do thou worship"; "With thy teams of horses"; "Golden-colored ones"; "Rich in horses"; "Thou, O Varuṇa"; "O Bṛhaspati"; "Ye two, Indra and [Varuṇa]"; "May Indra grant us well-being. These are the food-oblations and the offerings (*balayaḥ*).
(1) Then follows the fuel-wood offering (*samiddhoma*) with the verses: "O Agni, whatever [fires there are]... (2).
One who desires peace should offer fuel-sticks made of *udumbara* or *śamī* wood with the verse: "May the goddesses be propitious for our aid" (*śanno devīrabhiṣṭaye*). (3)

One desiring long life [should offer] *dūrvā* grass with the following mantras: "O Agni, may life be given to you; may life depart to the wind; may it be abundant there for the sake of breath. Do not harm me, the great one; [protect] my offspring. [And further: "O Lord of the Dwelling, O Jātavedas," "That most excellent splendor of Savitṛ," "By the Law, whom the Ādityas [protect]," and "O Prajāpati. 4.

"That there is an offering of *apāmārga* [plants] is for the destruction of the *rakṣases*," so says the Brāhmaṇa. The *apāmārga* offering is a remedy for everything. "Since the *apāmārga* is the destroyer of rivals, may it increase my prosperity; may the *apāmārga*, the remedy for everything, sweep away whatever evil is upon my head, placed in my hair, on my forehead, my back, or my belly—*svāhā*!
(5) An offering of sesame seeds with the *vyāhṛtis* destroys the *rakṣases* and annihilates evil. (6)
Moreover, they quote: "Herbs, groats, flowers, wood, roots, fruits, and grass—these may be offered with the hand; nothing else, because there is no injunction [to that effect].
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the fourth book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the sixth chapter in the fourth book.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the rules for purification. Having gone far from the village, having placed the sacred thread on his head or on his right ear, he takes up earth.
(1) Placing a piece of wood between [himself and the ground], he should sit down in the middle.
(2) During the day he should go toward the north; at night, toward the south; and during both twilights, facing the north. (3)

One should not discharge [excrement] near fire, nor in water, nor naked; nor at the root of a tree, nor at the foot of a mountain, nor at a crossroads, nor in a fire-sanctuary, nor in the midst of cows, nor in a cow-pen, nor in a place devoid of fire or sand, nor within water, nor in a temple, nor on an anthill, nor on a mouse-hill; nor facing fire, nor facing the sun, nor facing a house, nor facing a cow, nor facing a Brāhmaṇa. (4) One should apply one application of clay to the penis, three applications of clay to the left hand, and two applications of clay to both hands; this is prescribed as purification similar to that for urine. (5) Five applications of clay are for the anus, ten for one [hand], and seven for both; this is the purification for a householder, which is twofold for a student. (6)

For one living in the forest, the penance is threefold; for ascetics (*yati*), it is fourfold. [The sage] does not speak of approaching the wife of a teacher or a guru. (7) Bodhāyana says that if [the husband] has died, she does not die [with him], because of the rite of purification at birth. (8) Thus ends the sixth chapter in the fourth book of the *Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra* of Bodhāyana.
Now begins the seventh chapter of the fourth book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for sipping water (ācamana). Facing either the east or the north, with his topknot tied and wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, he should not use water that is hot, nor alkaline, nor discolored, nor foul-smelling or foul-tasting, nor frothy, nor taken with only one hand, nor defiled, nor with the knees outside [the vessel], nor with fingers spread apart, nor bubbling, nor while standing, nor laughing, nor talking, nor looking around, nor while stooping, nor while bowing down, nor while showing preference [for certain parts]. 1.

In the right hand of a Brāhmaṇa there are five *tīrthas*: the *devatīrtha* is in the middle of the fingers, the *ārṣatīrtha* at the tips of the fingers, the *agnitīrtha* in the middle [of the palm], the *paitṛkatīrtha* between the thumb and the index finger, and the *brahmatīrtha* is the line drawn behind the base of the thumb after moving it aside. (2) Having taken water just enough to submerge a *māṣa* bean, he should drink it three times; he should perform the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) three times with his hand in the shape of a cow's ear. (3)

That which he drinks first, with that he gratifies the Ṛgveda; that which he drinks second, with that he gratifies the Yajurveda; that which he drinks third, with that he gratifies the Sāmaveda. That which he wipes first, with that he gratifies the Atharvaveda; that which he wipes second, with that he gratifies the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. With his mouth he gratifies Agni; with the water he sprinkles on his left hand, the constellations; with the water he sprinkles on his foot, Viṣṇu; with his eyes, the Moon and Sun; with his nostrils, Prāṇa and Apāna; and with his ear—

By his arms he gratifies the quarters; by his heart, Indra; by his navel, Rudra; by his two thumbs, the Earth; and by the waters flowing from them, Kubera and all other deities—namely Agni, Vāyu, Prajāpati, Arka, Candra, and Maghavān, according to the Vedic tradition. 4.

One should touch the two eyes with the ring finger and the thumb; the two nostrils with the forefinger and the thumb; the two ears with the thumb and the little finger; the two arms with the thumb and the middle finger; the heart with all four fingers; the navel with the thumb; and the head with all the fingers. One who is joined by this ritual procedure is never defiled. (5) Thus ends the seventh chapter in the fourth book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the eighth chapter in the fourth book.

Now, it is indeed said: "In the beginning, this world was water, a mere ocean. In it, Prajāpati moved about having become Vāyu. He saw this earth; having become a boar, he seized it; having become Viśvakarman, he smoothed it out. It expanded; it became the Earth (Pṛthivī). That is the 'earth-nature' of the Earth. Upon it, he labored. Regarding this, some indeed maintain that the *aupāsana* fire alone is for the sake of the consecration of women. The *aupāsana* fire must be maintained perpetually; if it goes out, it should be produced by friction, or it may be fetched from the house of a learned *śrotriya* for twelve days.

If it has been interrupted, it must be re-established; now, if it has been interrupted for twelve days, there should be a re-establishment, and the fetching [of materials] should be from the original model—thus it has been stated, and this concludes. 1.

Now, if the householders have not offered the *aupāsana* for six months, they should—having fetched fuel as it becomes available, established the fire, and strewn grass around it—perform the expiation for twelve days (*dvādaśāha-prāyaścitta*). Then, having again strewn grass around the fire, performed the rites up to the *āpraṇītā* waters, and cooked a mess of rice in four *śarāva* measures, they should pour clarified butter over it, remove it from the fire towards the north, and once it is set down, pour more butter over it. Having performed the rites beginning with the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) up to the *agnimukha* (the oblation to Agni), they offer portions of the cooked rice using a stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), saying: "To Agni, Svāhā! To Soma, Svāhā! To Agni possessed of food, Svāhā!"

"To Agni, the eater of food, svāhā! To Agni, the lord of food, svāhā! To Agni, the purifying, svāhā! To Agni, the purifier, svāhā! To Agni, the bright, svāhā! To Agni, the luminous, svāhā! To Agni, the protector of vows, svāhā! To Agni, the maker of paths, svāhā! To Agni, the thread-possessor, svāhā! To Agni Vaiśvānara, svāhā! To Sūrya, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! To Brahman, svāhā! Bhūḥ svāhā! Bhuvaḥ svāhā! Suvaḥ svāhā! Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ svāhā! To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā!"—thus [he offers] in the eastern part of the northern half. 2.
Having silently placed the stirring-spoon (mekṣaṇa) into the fire, he performs the rites beginning with the *jaya* offerings up until the granting of the boon by the cow.

3. Then, after the sun has set, he offers these two oblations with his hand using rice or barley: "To Agni, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! in the evening; "To Sūrya, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! in the morning. He may also offer [the oblations] with any one of the materials used for the Agnihotra sacrifice. 4.
And at every change of the moon (*parvan*), he should sacrifice with a cooked offering (*sthālīpāka*) dedicated to Agni. 5.
The fast itself consists of eating at another time and not being satiated with food. 6.
In this very manner he proceeds with the evening oblation; thus the *aupāsana* ritual is concluded. 7.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the fourth book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now, the ninth chapter in the fourth book:
How indeed do the New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa) take place for one who has not established the sacred fires?

On the day of the full moon and on the day of the new moon, having bound the sacrificial fuel (idhma) and the sacrificial grass (barhis), he observes the fast, performing the ritual form of the Upavasatha.
Then, when the next day has dawned, having kindled the fire and strewn grass around it, he seats a Brāhmaṇa to the south.
Having placed a vessel of water to the north, he pours out rice grains upon a black antelope skin behind the fire.

Then, having poured water or milk through a strainer into a cooking pot, having set it over the fire, having carried fire around it, and having cleansed the *sruk*, *sruva*, and stirring-ladle, he cooks this sacrificial porridge (*caru*); having sprinkled it with clarified butter and removed it from the fire towards the north, he sprinkles it again once it is firmly established.

Having performed the rites beginning with the putting on of the garments up to the opening of the sacrifice before the fire, he offers from the cooked oblation with two verses: "Agni is the head" and "Of the earth. (6) For those who offer five-fold portions, there is first the under-layering of ghee (*upastaraṇa*), then the cutting of portions from the eastern half and the western half, followed by the sprinkling of ghee; then the cutting of portions from the middle, the eastern half, and the western half, followed by the sprinkling of ghee and the re-anointing (*pratyañjana*). (7) Then, prior to the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering. (8)

On the full moon day, having offered the two ājya oblations with the verses “ṛṣabhaṃ vājinaṃ vayam” and “amāvāsyā subhagā,” and on the new moon day, having offered the oblation to Sviṣṭakṛt with the verse “havyavāhaṃ sviṣṭam,” he places the stirring-stick (mekṣaṇa) back into the fire, pours the remnants of the offering over it, and then, using the ladle, pours water inside the enclosing sticks with the verse “vaiśvānare haviridaṃ juhomi.

Having washed the ladle, heated it, and filled it with water, he pours it outside the enclosing sticks with the verse “imaṃ samudraṃ śatadhāram. The rite from the Jaya-oblations onwards is established as complete up to the giving of the cow as a boon.
Then, taking from the cooked portion, he eats it with the formula: "Thou art life.
(11) Having eaten and sipped water, he touches his belly with two verses: "From whatever we fear, O Indra... and "The giver of well-being, the lord of the people... (12).

At the first *sthālīpāka* sacrifice, having prepared clarified butter, one should offer oblations with the *Kūśmāṇḍa* formulas; or one should offer with these [verses] beginning with "karma" [and so on]. "Purified, he attains the worlds of the gods"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. (13)
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the fourth book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter in the third book.
Now, if a householder should take two wives, how should he act in that case? 1.
At whatever time he should obtain [the means], he should tend the two fires.

Having kindled the secondary fire (aparāgni), having strewn [grass] all around it, having melted the clarified butter (ājya) and purified it, having heated and wiped the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and having taken four portions of butter into the *sruk*, the sacrificer, while the wife holds on to him, offers the oblation with: "Homage to you, O Seer; for non-distress, for the sake of the *svadhā*-call, I offer to you. May we, unharmed, not be struck down by you, O Indra. Thus, O Brahman, may this be known to you, *svāhā*!
Then he consigns [the fire] into himself with: "This is your seasonal womb."

Then, having kindled the eastern fire, having placed a fuel-stick with the verse "Being invoked, awaken, O Agni," having strewn grass around it, having melted the clarified butter and purified it, having heated and wiped the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and having taken portions of the butter, the sacrificer offers oblations while his two wives hold on to him from behind, using the entire hymn beginning with "He who is the Brahman of the Brahman" and taking four portions for each offering. (5) Having performed the standard rites up to the mouth of the fire, he offers from the cooked food, reciting the invitatory verse "Be united, be in harmony," and offers with the offering verse "O Agni, you who belong to the soil. (6)

Then he offers oblations of clarified butter with the formulas beginning "Thou art the soil-born, O Agni," up to the end of the section. From the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the procedure is established until the giving of the cow as a gift.

Then, in front of the fire, he places the remnants of the oblation upon bunches of *darbha* grass with the two verses, "The Brahman was born first" and "The Father of the Virājs. The *Pārvaṇa* offerings are performed in the domestic fire according to the well-known rule; thus the ritual procedure for the domestic fire is concluded.

Thus ends the tenth chapter in the fourth book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*. Now begins the eleventh chapter in the fourth book. Now, indeed, there is this [text]: "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is born burdened with three debts: toward the seers by means of studentship (*brahmacarya*), toward the gods by means of sacrifice (*yajña*), and toward the ancestors by means of offspring (*prajā*). From this Brāhmaṇa passage, "Do not cut off the thread of progeny," [it follows that] if no offspring should be produced for ten years after [the age of] ten for one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), what should he do in that case? (1)

Having again performed the consecration of the maiden on the tenth day, the eleventh day, or the twelfth day, he should consign the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*), move away from the dwelling, churn out the fires, carry them forward, and either shift them or transport them elsewhere.

At that very time, having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods, he should cook the *brahmaudana* (sacrificial porridge) at the domestic fire; then, beginning with the oblation of the fast-day (*upavasatha-havis*), they perform the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) according to the established procedure.
When that is completed, he should sacrifice with the *pavitra-iṣṭi*.
When that [offering] has been completed, he should offer the *tantumatī*.

When that has been completed, he should offer the *traidhātavīyā*. Alternatively, he should sacrifice with an animal dedicated to Indra and Agni, or he should perform the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādheya*).
"Now, if one man has many wives, he should act in exactly this same manner; therefore, one man takes many wives"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter of the fourth book in the Bodhāyana Gṛhya-śeṣa-sūtra.
Now begins the twelfth chapter of the fourth book.

Now, if he should observe the release of the fires, he should kindle the fire, strew grass around it, melt the clarified butter, purify it, heat the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, wipe them, take four portions of butter into the *sruk*, and while his two wives hold on to him, the sacrificer offers the oblation for the release of the fires with the verse: "Suck this milk-yielding breast, rich in vigor, swollen with waters, O Agni, in the midst of the flood. Enjoy the honeyed spring; enter your seat, the oceanic dwelling. Svāhā! Having offered the oblation for the release of the fires, he should divide that fire. 1.
"Reunion does not occur again, for that which has been divided should not be joined together," according to the traditional law (smṛti).
2. If one should marry into the previous fire, it indeed becomes common property; there is no division there because of the oneness of the fire—so says the venerable Bodhāyana.
3. Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the fourth book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now, the thirteenth chapter of the fourth book.

Now we shall explain the procedure for the worldly worship, the taking up [of the fire], the maintaining, and the descent. There are three kinds of consigning [the fire]: into oneself, into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*), and into the fuel-stick (*samidh*). (1) One consigns it into the fuel-stick. Having taken a fuel-stick made of *pālāśa*, *aśvattha*, *khadira*, *udumbara*, or *śamī* wood, one consigns it with the verse: "This is thy seasonal womb. (2)
Or, having placed [the fire] upon two kindling woods and having churned it out, he should offer the oblation.
Or rather, there is the placing [of the fire] within oneself with the mantra: "O Agni, that body of yours which is worthy of sacrifice.
Then he makes it descend with the mantra: "Descend, O Jātavedas."

Wherever he may go, he should not carry [the fire] with him; having reached that place, he fetches a common (laukika) fire, establishes it, kindles it, and offers that fuel-stick upon which [the sacred fire] has been consigned within himself, using the two verses: “Being invoked” (*ājuhvānaḥ*) and “Awake, O Agni” (*udbudhyasvāgne*).

6. Then he attends to the fire with rice or barley. 7. With barley for one who desires a village; with husked rice for one who desires vigor; with milk for one who desires cattle; with curds for one who desires sensory power; with clarified butter for one who desires splendor. 8.
Then, if [the time] has passed, he performs the expiatory oblation (pratijuhoti). 9. The service of the sacred fires is well known. 10.
The performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices is well known. 11.
The performance of the five great sacrifices (mahāyajña) is well known. 12. This very same procedure continues daily throughout one's life. 13.
The worldly [duty] has been explained. 14.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the fourth book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter in the fourth book.

Now, if the *aupāsana* fire of a householder should become extinguished after his vital breaths have departed, one should re-establish it at the word of two learned *śrotriyas*. Having fetched it from the house of a *śrotriya*, having established it with the *vyāhṛtis*, having added fuel, having sprinkled water around it, having strewn grass around it, having melted the clarified butter, having purified it, having heated and wiped the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and having taken four portions of butter into the *sruk* while the sacrificer holds on to him, he offers oblations with the two verses: "Seven are thy [tongues], O Agni," with the seven *vyāhṛtis*, and "The gods were in front... and "The out-breath and in-breath behind... and "May the two trees not [crush] thee... and so forth.

With the two verses, "Do not press us together" and "May the two trees not press upon you," and with the two verses, "O Agni who returns," and "O Agni Aṅgiras," he offers four ladlefuls for each [tree].
There is no *brahmā*, no *praṇītā* water, no cooked rice oblation (*caru*), and no *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
From this point onward, he proceeds with the rites pertaining to the funeral sacrifice (*paitṛmedhika*).
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the fourth book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter in the fourth book:
"Now, if one who has established the sacred fires should marry two wives and one should die before their formal union [with him], how then should he act? (1)

Having strewn grass around the *aupāsana* fire, having melted the clarified butter (*ājya*), purified it, heated the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and wiped them clean, he takes four portions of butter into the *sruk*. When the fire is provided with fuel and enclosed by a curtain, he offers the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the verse, "Be united, O you two, be in harmony. Having offered the two *mindā* oblations and the *vyāhṛti* oblations, he consigns that fire into a fuel-stick with the verse, "This is your womb," and places a fuel-stick upon the *gārhapatya* fire with the verse, "May you two be of one mind for us. Then, having melted the clarified butter on the *gārhapatya*, purified it, and heated the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles...
Having wiped the *sruc* and taken four portions of clarified butter, he offers it in the *gārhapatya* fire with the verse: "Fire moves within fire, having entered it.
(2) Having taken another four portions, he offers it in the *gārhapatya* itself with the verse: "Consciousness is the *sruc*.
(3) Then, in the *gārhapatya*, he offers oblations with the *sruva* spoon using the ten verses beginning: "The Brahmin is the sole Hotṛ-priest. (4)

Then, having arranged the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), he offers oblations in the Anvāhāryapacana fire with two verses beginning, "Those who are equal" and "Those who are kinsmen. 5.
Then, in the very same Anvāhāryapacana fire, he offers spoonfuls (sruvāhuti) with the formula: "To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, svadhā, homage, svāhā! 6.

Then, having arranged the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavīta) and having filled the offering-ladle (sruk) with twelve portions of ghee, he makes an offering in the Āhavanīya fire while mentally reciting the Puruṣasūkta. 7.

Then he offers oblations with the *sruva* spoon: "To Agni Viviciya, svāhā! To Agni Vratapati, svāhā! To Agni Pavamāna, svāhā! To Agni Pāvaka, svāhā! To Agni Śuci, svāhā! To Agni Pathikṛt, svāhā! To Agni Tantumant, svāhā! To Agni Vaiśvānara, svāhā! (8) Then, having taken four portions of clarified butter into the *sruc* ladle, he offers the *manasvatī* oblation: "May the mind, as light, enjoy the clarified butter; may it join together this interrupted sacrifice. Those dawns that have passed and those that are yet to set—I unite them by means of this oblation of ghee, svāhā! (9)
"From this point forward, the ritual pertaining to the funeral rites (paitṛmedhika) is undertaken.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the fourth book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter in the fourth book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual for the renunciation (saṃnyāsa) of Kapila. One who is without the sacred fires—whether shaven-headed or wearing a topknot—having fasted for a day and night, bathed, and sipped water, offers oblations of water with his own hands into the water itself, saying: "The waters are indeed all the deities; svāhā! (1).

"I have withdrawn from the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, and from all beings; svāhā! (2). Having uttered three times in a low voice, "Renounced by me! Renounced by me! Renounced by me!", he then says it three times aloud; for it is known that "the gods are based on the triple truth" (triṣatyā hi devāḥ). (3)

Having taken up the staff with the mantra, "Fearlessness to all beings from me, svāhā," and having taken up the water-strainer with the mantra, "The purifier is the purifier," he should cast it down in the presence of his son, friends, well-wishers, kinsmen, and relatives; then, having fetched [food] from the village, he should wash a single bowl with water and eat once, with a small amount.
(4) He should not converse with anyone. (5) He should not beg for anything. (6)

He should dwell in mountain caves, on river sandbanks, in empty houses, in temples, or in holes and clefts. (7) Having washed what has fallen of its own accord, he should accept that which is free from the concern for life. (8) He should bring back worn-out items and wear firm, unhemmed deerskins for the purpose they were intended for. (9)
One should perform one's duties after begging for food before sunrise. (10) One who is capable of bathing should not fail to observe the vow.
(11) Then, having washed himself and wiped away the water from his body with a wet cloth, he should wear an undergarment and perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana) on all sides. (12)
"One should always bathe at midday and in the morning," so said the venerable Bodhāyana. 13.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the fourth book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter in the fourth book.
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the supreme rite of purification for those high-souled ascetics who are concentrated and disciplined:
having diligently washed the body with the Sāvitrī mantra in a pure place.

Having adorned [the vessel] with perfumes and garlands individually according to the Gāyatrī, all those Brāhmaṇas who carry it must indeed be pure; for those carrying it properly, immediate purification is ordained. 2–3.

For those who perform tasks such as washing for their superiors, immediate purification is likewise ordained for them. Having placed him in a clean place, whether he be a son or a close relative, ||4||
Having descended those fires with the *upāvaroha* mantra,

having silently performed the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*), and having sprinkled [them] with the seven *vyāhṛtis*, he should place that wooden body [of the fire-altar] down while reciting the appropriate mantra. 5–6.
Saying "O Viṣṇu, protect the offering," he places a water-purifier in [the disciple's] mouth with the mantra "Thou art the purifier," and likewise again;
having placed a triple staff in the right hand with a verse dedicated to Viṣṇu.
And likewise, he places the bowl upon his belly with the Sāvitrī verse.
Having placed the sling on his left side beyond the reach of dust, and the water-pot at his secret part with the verse "The earth has gone to the earth," [he proceeds]. 8–9.

One should indeed cremate [the deceased] with the fires using the ritual procedure for the Pitṛmedha; likewise, there is no period of impurity (aśauca) for the performer of the rite, nor is there the offering of water libations (udakakriyā).
One should never perform the Ekoddiṣṭa rite for those who have renounced the world (saṃnyasta).
When the eleventh day has arrived, the pārvaṇa rite is prescribed;
or on the twelfth day, or on an auspicious day, the Nārāyaṇa-bali should be performed.
One should carry out everything dedicated to Nārāyaṇa according to the procedure for an ekoddiṣṭa rite.

And for those great-souled ones who have renounced the world, even though they have not maintained the sacred fires, [the rite] should be performed according to the rules for the *hotṛ* priest, using either the *gāyatrī* or the *praṇava*. This applies to those noble beings who are extraordinary and whose minds are fixed in Brahman.
The wise have declared that their sounding must be performed.
(14) Having dug a hole to the depth of a staff using the three *vyāhṛtis*, the learned one should install the triple-staff and other items in their proper places without reciting mantras. (15)
One should cover [the remains] so that they are not touched by jackals, beasts of prey, and the like;
for if dogs and such creatures devour them, a great fault will arise.
Therefore, having dug the earth deeply, one should properly cover [the remains] for the ascetics.
For one who has desisted from all attachments and is devoted to the practice of meditation, there shall be no cremation, no impurity rites, and no water libations.
The sacred rites beginning with the *niṣeka* (conception) and ending at the cemetery—which are based upon the status of a Brāhmaṇa—do not apply to him. || 17-18 ||
Therefore, householders should diligently perform purificatory rites for those twice-born ones who, by touching or seeing them, carry the Great Soul;
for the wise declare that such people obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice. 19–20.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the fourth book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*. Now begins the eighteenth chapter of the fourth book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*). Having served food to the Brāhmaṇas and caused them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Hail! Prosperity!", one should, on a pure and level spot, smear a square sacrificial mound (*staṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung. Having scattered unbroken rice grains over it and sprinkled it with water, one takes five small bowls—made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, according to what is available. (1)
One should visualize Caturmukha in the center, Vajrin in the east, Yama in the south, Varuṇa in the west, and Śaśin in the north; thus, one should place the vessels in their proper order. 2.
Having taken anthill earth and likewise cow dung, one should place these into those small clay pots in the proper sequence;
[and also] dūrvā grass, a leaf of the aśvattha tree, a śirīṣa flower, and a bilva leaf.

One should tie them at their roots and wrap them with white thread. (4) In the central [line], one invokes Brahmā with the *vyāhṛtis*: "Oṃ bhūḥ, I invoke Brahmā; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I invoke Prajāpati; Oṃ suvaḥ, I invoke the Four-faced One; Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ, I invoke Hiraṇyagarbha. With these very same [mantras], in the eastern direction, [one invokes] Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the lord of Śacī, the performer of a hundred sacrifices. With these very same [mantras], in the southern direction, [one invokes] Yama, the son of Vivasvat, the lord of the ancestors, the King of Dharma. With these very same [mantras], in the western direction, [one invokes] Pracetas...
"To the handsome lord of the waters"—with these [verses] he worships the eastern direction; "to the moon, the maker of night, Candra, Soma"—with these [verses] he worships the northern direction.

(5) Then he bathes them with the three verses beginning "The waters, indeed, are most healing," with the four verses beginning "Golden-colored, pure, purifying," and having sprinkled them with this entire Anuvāka beginning "Pavamāna, who dwells in heaven," he then honors them with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, saying, "Salutation to such-and-such, salutation to such-and-such. (6) Then he stands in worship before them.
I bow to the lords of the directions, who bestow the fruits of all desires; may they cause my actions to bear fruit and may they constantly perform what is auspicious. (7)

Having mixed rice, barley, beans, sesame, and mung beans, and having washed them with milk, he consecrates them with the *Oṣadhisūkta* (the hymn of herbs) and the section beginning with "Those which were born" (*yā jātāḥ*). He scatters them in order: with the two verses beginning "The Brahman was born" (*brahma jajñānam*) and "The father Virāj" (*pitā virāj*), in the center; with the two verses beginning "From what we fear, O Indra" (*yata indra bhayāmahe*) and "The giver of well-being, the lord of the people" (*svastidā viśaspatiḥ*), in the east; with the two verses beginning "He who is his, O Kauṣṭhya, sing of Yama" (*yo 'sya kauṣṭhya yamaṃ gāya*), in the south; with the two verses beginning "This my prayer, O Varuṇa" (*imaṃ me varuṇa*) and "To thee I go" (*tattvā yāmi*), in the west;
and with the two verses beginning "Soma, the milch-cow" (*somo dhenum*) and "Make swell" (*āpyāyasva*), in the north. 8.
One should cover it in sequence with pure *śuddhābhi* and *sikatā* [sand].
(9) One should sprinkle it in sequence with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
(10) Having sealed it with the *praṇava* alone, one should protect it well until the ritual is completed. (12)
When the rite is completed, one should feed five Brāhmaṇas.
With the *vyāhṛtis*, one should dismiss the deities in their proper order.
[The rite] up to the seventh [generation] brings about the desire for progeny; up to the sixth, it prevents the loss of sons.

In the fifth [day], there is the offering for those desiring devotion to Viṣṇu, the Self of All; likewise, in the fourth, one should know the "sprout" (aṅkura), for he becomes even more sinful. The offering of the sprouts for all desires may take place after three days or even immediately.
Thus spoke the Blessed Bodhāyana. 16.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the fourth book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter in the fourth book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the Nāndīmukha rite. At the very outset, having invited two Brahmins for the gods and at least four for the ancestors, and having honored them as far as possible with the shaving of beards, anointing, and bathing; having established the fire and strewn grass around it; having melted the clarified butter, purified it by straining, and mixed it with curds and ghee; having cleansed the *sruva* ladle; having seated the two Brahmins representing the gods and adorned them; having assigned their portions; and having placed the barley-water within two purifiers (*pavitra*) at the places of the seats where they will eat, mixed with flowers, fruits, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).

Having scattered barley and sand, and having seated those representing the ancestors, he pours water with barley into their hands—which hold *pavitra* grass—reciting the mantra, "May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased. Having offered this from another vessel and performed the *dvirālaṅkaraṇa* (double-decoration) in the same manner, he requests permission for the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire). Having performed the decoration and taken a portion of the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) with a *sruva* ladle, he makes the offering into the fire with the words, "Svāhā to the Nāndīmukha ancestors. Then, having spread a base layer of food and sprinkled clarified butter over it, he portions out the food into the vessels along with the speckled butter.

Having mixed [the food], placed it upon *darbha* grass, and covered it with *darbha* grass, he should touch it while modifying the mantra to "May you be most excellent for the *Nāndīmukha* ancestors in that world, in that place," and then, having spread a double layer [of clarified butter] for the Brahmins, having taken two portions of the touched food, and having sprinkled clarified butter over them twice, he should feed them according to the rule. 1.

Having caused the Brahmins to hear Vedic texts associated with the *svadhā* formula that denote the commonality of the ancestors; when they have eaten and rinsed their mouths, having smeared their hands, having scattered curd-rice upon their laps, having sprinkled water twice around them clockwise with the rinsing-water, having given the barley and water as before, having presented the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and having caused them to say, "May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased," he salutes them. Then, at the place of the *svadhā* formula, all together lowering the right knee and raising the left, he mutters the portion of the Anuvāka beginning with "Iḍā devahūḥ" until its end.

Having recited the mantra, he pours out water with the words, "May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased. Then, having caused the Brāhmaṇas to rise, having gratified them, having sent them away, and having circumambulated them, he asks permission regarding the remnants and dismisses the deity. To the south of the fire, upon Darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward, he should offer [the remainder] to the Nāndīmukha ancestors with the formula, "Svāhā to the Nāndīmukha ancestors! Having sprinkled water around the fire clockwise with the rinsing-water, some desire that an oblation be performed as before with *pṛṣadājya* (clotted butter) for the sake of future victory and so forth, using the verse "ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ. This is called the Nāndīmukha rite. 2.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the fourth book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra;
now begins the twentieth chapter in the fourth book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the pacification of portents occurring in a village. One should perform a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) in the event of a fire, when the village is attacked by tigers and other predators, when it is harassed by jackals, when outcasts (*caṇḍāla*) settle within the village, when the pillars of the village hall sink down, when honey settles upon it, when anthills or lotuses appear [on sacred sites], when there is sweating or trembling of the limbs of deities, when the village is overcome by fever, when many Brahmins die, when a cremation ground is established in the middle of the village, when it is harassed by bandits, when a tank or embankment breaks at night, when the water becomes discolored or sinks inward, when lightning strikes, when a village long abandoned is re-entered, and in other such portents. ||1||

On an auspicious day, under an auspicious lunar mansion and at an auspicious moment, having appointed two Brāhmaṇas each for the purpose of bathing Viṣṇu and for the consecration of Mahādeva, and having appointed four Brāhmaṇas for the sake of pacifying the nine planets with the same number [of assistants], one should then, for the village-pacification oblation (*grāmaśāntihoma*), prepare a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) smeared with cow dung the size of a cow-hide on a pure and level spot in the northeast of the village, either in a temple or at a crossroads.

Having strewn the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) with sesame seeds, mustard seeds, parched grain, perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, having prepared the site for the water-jar (*kumbha*), and having established the fire and spread the sacred grass around it, he performs the rites up to the *apraṇītā* waters; then, rising, he invokes the deities in front of the fire with the *vyāhṛtis*: "I invoke Yajñapuruṣa; I invoke Brahmā to the south of the deity; I invoke Tryambaka to the north; I invoke Vāstupuruṣa in the fire of the deity; and I invoke Indra and the other deities. Having thus invoked them, he proceeds.

Having worshipped Viṣṇu with the Puruṣasūkta, the four-faced Brahmā with the Brahmasūkta, and Tryambaka with the Rudrasūkta, and having worshipped the other deities in the order of invocation (āvāhana) and so forth by their respective names, he sits down to the west of the fire facing east; having performed the rites beginning with the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), he offers oblations from the cooked food, reciting the invitatory verse (puronuvākyā): "O Lord of the Dwelling, recognize us," and then offering with the sacrificial verse (yājyā): "O Lord of the Dwelling, with your auspicious assembly... || 2 ||

With that same mantra, one should offer one thousand and eight fuel-sticks (*samidh*) made of *śamī* wood. With the mantra "O Vāstoṣpati, be our protector," one should offer one thousand and eight oblations of cooked food (*anna*).
With the mantra "O Vāstoṣpati, do not harm us," one should offer one thousand and eight oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*).

Having offered clarified butter oblations verse by verse with the hymns *mṛgāreṣṭi*, *vratam*, and *homuce*—which are known by the wise—and having offered twelve oblations with the hymn *yā vām indrāvaruṇā*, and having offered clarified butter oblations verse by verse with this section beginning *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*, and having offered clarified butter oblations verse by verse with the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Brahmasūkta*, and the *Rudrasūkta*, [one should recite] the two verses *yata indra bhayāmahe* and *svastidā viśaspatiḥ*, the five verses beginning *agnir āyuṣmān*, and the six verses beginning *agne naya supathā*. As for that which is his...

Having offered thirteen oblations with the mantras "kauṣṭhya" and "eṣa te nirṛte bhāgaḥ," and with the two [mantras] "imaṃ me varuṇa" and "tattvā yāmi," and with "samudrāya tvā vātāya svāhā," and having offered clarified butter oblations for each with the two [mantras] "āpyāyasva" and "saṃ te payāṃsi," and with "īśānassarvavidyānām" and "tryambakaṃ yajāmahe," and having offered clarified butter oblations with the mantra of the nine planets beginning with "ā satyena" and ending with "ketuṃ kṛṇvannaketave," the rite from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering down to the granting of the boon by the cow is established. 5.

Then, in front of the fire, he places the remains of the oblation upon *śamī* leaves with the verse, "He who is Rudra in the fire. (6) Then he should present the sacrificial food to the deities. (7) Then he worships [the weapons] with the formula, "You are named spears. (8)

Having approached the directions in due order, caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made, taken hold of a water-pot, and recited the *pañcaśānti*, one should pour the remnants of the oblation and the remnants of the clarified butter into the full pot. Then, with a branch of the *udumbara* tree, a branch of the *śamī* tree, or a handful of *darbha* grass, and while reciting "Auspicious, auspicious," "May the goddesses [be] for our well-being," and the *Śākuna Sūkta*, one should sprinkle the village three times clockwise. Having given abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins, one should perform this for seven days or twelve days;
thus the entire pacification of portents is accomplished—so says the venerable Bodhāyana. 9.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the fourth book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter in the fourth book.

Then, having dug up the earth knee-deep at the spot where the lightning struck, having sprinkled it with water, and having placed *patrāvakā* grass there, he serves food to the Brāhmaṇas and causes them to recite "An auspicious day!", "Prosperity!", and "Success!". To the west of the digging site, he prepares a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*). Having performed the rites from the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhāna*) up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), he offers oblations of clarified butter with the three mantras beginning with "May Indra and Agni be propitious to us. Then, with the hymn beginning "He, being born by power as of old," he offers oblations of cooked rice (*caru*). 1.

Having begun with "May [the gods] grant us well-being" (*svasti no mimītām*), and having recited the *svastyātreya* hymn beginning with "May Bṛhaspati grant us well-being" (*svasti no bṛhaspatirdadhātu*), he honors the Brahmins, causes them to pronounce blessings, and gives a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the teacher (2).
He should feed a learned Brahmin with the *caru* oblation (3).
He should give to a Brahmin land equal in extent to a burnt area, saying, "This much is for my livelihood," or he gives gold; thus says the venerable Bodhāyana (4).
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the fourth book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣa-sūtra.

Now, regarding the fall of a thunderbolt; now, therefore, the pacification of portents affecting a village; now, therefore, the *nāndīmukha* rite; now, therefore, the procedure for the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*); now, therefore, I shall fully explain [this]; now, therefore, the procedure for the renunciation of Kapila (*kapilasaṃnyāsa*); now, if one is a maintainer of the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*); now, the domestic fire (*aupāsana*) of the householder; now, the procedure for the taking up, maintaining, and lowering of the worldly and domestic fires; now, if there is the release of the fires; indeed, it is said: "being born"; now, as for the householder; how indeed is it for one who does not maintain the sacred fires? Indeed, it is said: "the waters."

Now, therefore, the rule for sipping water (*ācamana*); now, therefore, the rule for purification (*śauca*); now, therefore, the rule for optional rites (*kāmya*); now, the rule for the enjoyment of dharma through imitation of the *prahuta* offering; now, therefore, the offering to the deceased (*mṛtabali*); the imitation of the *āhuti* offering, the imitation of the *baliharaṇa* offering, and the *dhūrtabali*; now, therefore, the offering for falsehood and truth (*mithyāsatyabali*). 21.

Now, therefore, [concerning] the *mithyāsatya-bali*. The *dhūrta-bali* is a mimicry of the *āhuti* offerings and a mimicry of the presentation of the *bali* offerings. Now, therefore, [concerning] the *mṛta-bali*. Now, the rule for the enjoyment of dharma as a mimicry of the *prahuta* offerings. Now, therefore, the rule for optional rites (*kāmya-vidhi*). Now, therefore, the rule for purification (*śauca-vidhi*). Now, therefore, the rule for sipping water (*ācamana-vidhi*). Now, it is said: "The waters... How indeed [is it] for one who has not maintained the sacred fires? Now, concerning the householder. Now, it is said: "Being born... Now, if there is the release of the fires. Now...

The rule for the worldly *aupāsana* fire: its taking up, maintaining, and descending. Now, the *aupāsana* of the householder. Now, if he is one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). Now, therefore, the rule for the renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) according to Kapila. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain. Now, therefore, the rule for the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*). Now, therefore, the *nāndīmukha* rite. Now, therefore, the pacification of portents affecting a village. Now, in the event of a lightning strike. 22. Thus ends the fourth book in the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*. Now begins the first chapter of the fifth book.

Now follows the procedure for the *agnimukha* (the mouth of the fire). 1. Having smeared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung on a clean, level spot, one should sit there facing east and perform the fivefold rite beginning with bathing. Having dug up [the ground] with a wooden sword (*sphya*) and sprinkled it with water, one should prepare the mound with five *prastha*s of sand. Having established it with the *vyāhṛti*s and made it a square of one *aratni* in measure, one should draw three lines toward the east upon that square measuring one *prādeśa* with *darbha* grass—using the thumb and ring finger, or the little finger—with the verse "Brahma jajñānam" in the middle, and with "In the southern sky... in the south.

[He places] a *suparṇa* [leaf] to the north with the mantra "āpyāyasva" (SvB 1.1.1), three times facing north. Having touched water in the middle with the mantra "yo rudraḥ" (VS 16.2), he discards a blade of *darbha* grass to the west with "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" (RV 1.22.17) and to the east with "indraṃ viśvā avīvṛdhan" (RV 8.96.14), touches water, prepares a seat for the fire, and having established the fire—brought by the wife in the form of embers—as prescribed, he pours unbroken rice-grains and water into that vessel. 2. Then, having silently added fuel with three large, sprinkled pieces of wood, he stands in worship of the fire with the mantra "agnim juṣṭo damūnāḥ" (VS 3.1). 3.

Then, having prepared a seat, having cast away a blade of grass, and having sipped water, he should sit here—either facing east, or south, west, or north—and then, having swept around the fire from left to right, sprinkled water around it, and strewn grass around it, placing the southern blades over the northern ones and the northern blades under the southern ones.

Having prepared everything—the seat for the vessel (pātra), the seat for Brahman to the south, the seat for the Praṇītā water to the north, and finally the seat for oneself—he should set down the vessels: the vessel for the clarified butter (ājyasthālī), the dipping-spoon (sruva), the offering-spoon (juhū), the Praṇītā vessel, the vessel for the sacrificial porridge (carusthālī), the sprinkling-water (prokṣaṇī), the fuel and sacrificial grass (idhmabarhis), the wood-cutters (idhapravraścana), and the stirring-ladle (mekṣaṇa). Having covered these with Darbha grass, he should also set down the winnowing-basket (śūrpa) and the black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina); in this regard, the oblation with a ladle (darvīhoma) is optional. 5.

Then he prepares two strainers from sacrificial grass (*barhis*), each a span (*prādeśa*) long, equal in size, with untrimmed tips, not cut by the fingernails, and fresh.
