Having silently wiped them with water, having placed them in the sprinkling vessel (*prokṣaṇī*), having poured water into it, and having purified it three times, he sprinkles the vessels with water. Having turned the vessels upside down and untied the fuel-bundle (*idhma*), he sprinkles it three times. Having seated the Brāhmaṇa to the south as in the *iṣṭi* sacrifice, he stands before the Brāhmaṇa, saying: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O Brāhmaṇa, you are the Brāhmaṇa; homage to you, O Brāhmaṇa, to the Brāhmaṇa! He remains there until the pointing out of the directions (*vyunnayana*). 6.

Alternatively, having seated the *kūrca* grass-bundle and worshipped it, and having worshipped Varuṇa in the *praṇītā* water-vessel which contains a purifier (*pavitra*), they lift it up together with the purifier to the level of the nose and place it to the north, saying: "Bhūḥ bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ; you are Varuṇa, whose vow is ghee; you belong to Varuṇa. Having worshipped it thus and covered it with *darbha* grass, he then pours out the rice grains, either with the formula, "I pour you out, acceptable to [Name]," or silently. In this manner three times, once silently. (7)

Having sprinkled them in that manner, he threshes them, husks them three times, washes them three times, and sets them aside; or he pours out the rice grains. Having sprinkled those [grains], he washes them three times and sets them aside in the same way. Having poured water or milk into the cooking pot and placed it on the fire, he pours the rice grains into it across the strainer.
Then he asks for the cooked rice or milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Having sprinkled that, he pours the *praṇītā* water over it with the *sruva* ladle.

Having placed [the vessel] over the fire, then having poured ghee into the ghee-pot, having drawn out embers toward the north, having made them cool, having placed [the vessel] over them, having illuminated it with a lighting-stick, having cut off two tips of *darbha* grass, having washed them and thrown them back [into the vessel], having illuminated it again, having carried fire around both [the vessel and the ghee] three times while tracing a path, having removed [the vessel] to the north, and having pushed back the embers, he then purifies it three times by moving it back and forth through the two strainers whose tips point north; then, having loosened the strainers and touched them with water, he throws them into the fire.

Then, having cleansed the *sruva*, the *juhū*, and the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*)—cleansing them three times on the inside and three times on the outside, likewise cleansing the base with the bases, sprinkling them with water, and heating them again—he places them down in their respective order.
(12) Then, having touched the *darbha* grass with water, he throws it into the fire.

(13) Having spread sacrificial grass (*barhis*) behind the fire, he places the clarified butter (*ājya*) there; having poured [the butter] over the cooked rice (*caru*), having moved it toward the north, and having set it upon the sacrificial grass, he pours the butter over it once it is firmly established. (14)
He places two fuel sticks upright: the thickest and longest on the south, and the thinnest and shortest on the north.

(15) Then he sprinkles water around the fire: with "O Aditi, give your consent," he sprinkles from the south toward the east; with "O Anumati, give your consent," from the west toward the north; with "O Sarasvatī, give your consent," from the north toward the east; and with "O God Savitṛ, impel," he sprinkles all around clockwise. Or rather, he sprinkles all around silently. (16)

Then, having worshipped the fires in the order beginning with that of Indra, he leaves one fuel-stick remaining. Having been authorized by the Brāhmaṇa, and having placed the after-offering fuel-stick (anūyāja-samidh) and the cord used for binding the sacrificial wood (idhma-saṃnahana) [into the fire] with the utterance of *svāhā*, and having set down the vessel for the *praṇītā* water, he pours the two *āghāra* libations. With the formula "To Prajāpati, svāhā," he makes contact at the northern junction of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), touching them obliquely and continuously, mentally. With "To Indra, svāhā," he does so in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), making contact at the southern junction of the enclosing sticks, touching them obliquely and continuously. (17) Then he offers the two *ājyabhāga* portions: with "To Agni, svāhā," in the eastern part of the northern half [of the fire]. (18)

He offers oblations continuously and face-to-face, saying "Svāhā to Soma," in the eastern part of the southern half; then he offers the Agnimukha oblation, beginning with the four [verses] for the yoked [horse] and offering up to the end of the *vyāhṛtis*. Then, having offered the expiation for the *caru*, having sprinkled the *caru* with clarified butter, and having performed the expiation for the violation of the vow, he makes an under-layer of butter in the *juhū* ladle with the *sruva* spoon, stirs the *caru* with the stirring-stick (*mekṣaṇa*), takes a portion from the eastern half, takes a portion from the western half, and sprinkles it with butter; he then anoints the place from which the portion was taken. Having first offered a *sruva*-oblation, he offers from the cooked [caru] as prescribed, and finally offers another *sruva*-oblation. 19.

Then, having spread a layer [of ghee] in the ladle, he cuts once from the northern half for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and pours ghee over it twice. He does not anoint the edge [of the cake]. Having placed it within the enclosing sticks together with the stirring-spoon, he offers the oblations of clarified butter as previously prescribed. (20) Then, having offered a spoonful before the *sviṣṭakṛt* and a spoonful after it, and having touched water, he throws the stirring-spoon into the fire and then sprinkles it with the remains of the oblation using the large and small spoons. (21) He pours the rinsing-water of the *juhū* ladle inside the enclosing sticks. (22)
Having washed the *sruva* spoon, heated it, and filled it with water, he pours it out outside the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
(23) In the case of the *sthālīpāka* offering, he does so inside the enclosing sticks; [in both cases] it is accompanied by the mantra.
(24) Then, having placed the fuel-stick for the *anūyāja* offerings upon the bundle of fuel (*idhma-saṃhana*), and having touched it with water, he throws it into the fire. (25)

Then, having offered the Jaya, Abhyātāna, Rāṣṭrabhṛt, and Amātya oblations, and having offered the Prājāpatya oblation with the sruva-spoon using four portions [of ghee], he places the wood-chips from the faggot onto the fire; then, having offered the expiatory oblations and the Sviṣṭakṛt oblation, he anoints the enclosing sticks (paridhis) with the sruva-spoon.

(26) Then, having wiped the strewn grass (paristaraṇa), and having anointed the sacrificial grass (barhis) in the butter-pot as one does the prastara-bunch, he covers it with a blade of grass and throws it into the fire.
(27) Having touched water, he throws the middle enclosing stick into the fire along with the blade of grass. (28)
Then he adds the other two [sticks] together with the two upright fuel-sticks.
Then he makes an offering over them with the residue of the oblation, saying, "To the Vasus.

At this point, there is the offering of the *bali* and the consumption [of the remains], except for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*); all other rites are performed as previously specified for each respective occasion.
Then he sprinkles water around the fire with the words, "You have assented; you have given your impulse" (32).

Having removed Varuṇa, having spread out the directions over the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the formula beginning "In the eastern direction," and having himself sprinkled [the area], he gives a boon to the Brahman priest and dismisses the Brahman priest after giving him the remainder of the *caru* together with clarified butter (33).
In rites such as the *sthālīpāka*, the *nakṣatra-homa*, and the *āyuṣya-homa*, the consumption [of the remnants] has been prescribed (34).
For those who offer five portions, he cuts five oblations: from the middle, from the eastern half, and from the western half.
(35) For the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he cuts twice from the northern half.
(36) The remainder is as before. (37)

Now, in the case of an offering to many deities, having taken the second portion from the rear half, he takes [the first] from the front half; he does so for all [deities] in this manner until the end.
(38) Then, having spread an underlayer of ghee for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he takes as many portions as there are deities, one by one; the remainder is the same.
(39) In that same way, he takes [portions] from the middle, from the rear half, and from the front half. (40)
He cuts portions for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering twice each; the remainder is the same [as before]. 41.
Having understood the entire method through the mouth of the teacher, one should perform it.
42. Thus ends the first chapter of the fifth book in the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the second chapter of the fifth book.
Now we shall explain the rules for the expiation and other rites concerning a girl who has reached puberty while the marriage is being prepared;
when the sacrifice for the marriage has been spread out and the time for the oblation has arrived.
Having seen a maiden who has reached puberty, how do the performers of sacrifice act?
[1] One should sprinkle her with sacred waters consecrated by the Sāvitrī mantra and with this following section beginning with "pavamānaḥ suvādinā. [2]
Then, having had her bathed by the learned, she should be adorned with new garments and ornaments;
then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* along with the *mindā* oblations and the *mahāvyāhṛtis*,
as well as the *tantumatī* oblation together with the *vyāhṛtis*.
The learned should perform the remaining rites once that which was unknown has been understood.
When the principal oblation is completed, she becomes one whose garments are soiled;
then, after three days have elapsed, she should perform the remaining rites.
Having placed the parched grain, the clarified butter, the dipping-spoon, the *praṇītā* water, and the stone entirely within, the Brahman priest alone should remain outside.
[6] Yama and Mṛtyu stand there, taking recourse to the southern direction.
For the sake of protecting the couple, only the Brahmin should go outside.
One should not offer oblations with the tips of the fingers, nor by breaking the *añjali* gesture;
it is traditionally taught that the offering of parched grain (*lājahoma*) is performed from the left side of the *añjali*.

A person should perform the first circumambulation together with the Brahmin; afterwards, some say that three circumambulations should be performed without him. [9] Then follows the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), the *nāndī* rite, the pronouncing of blessings, and the feeding of the twice-born.
The binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandhana), the offering of food and so forth, and the ritual of the sprouts (aṅkura) for the first tonsure (caula) and other rites—

these are performed prior to the festival [of the deity's birth], on the day of the conjunction (ayuga), or on the day of sowing the sprouts; this is desired either at dusk or in the late afternoon, as it possesses superior merit.

Excluding the rites of conception (*ādhāna*), the sacrament of the womb (*garbha-saṃskāra*), the birth-rite (*jāta-karma*), and the naming ceremony (*nāma*), the sowing of the auspicious sprouts (*maṅgala-aṅkura-vāpana*) should be performed on other occasions; likewise for the male-naming, the first feeding (*anna-prāśana*), the tonsure (*caula*), the ritual bath (*upasnāna*), and the taking of the hand in marriage (*pāṇi-graha*). 12. In the case of a male, [it is performed] during these [rites].
In the establishment of the sacred fires and in the Soma sacrifice, prosperity is ordained for ten [members of the family].

In the establishment of the fires and in the Soma sacrifice, the auspicious rite (kautuka) belongs to both husband and wife; however, during the *sīmantonnayana* and *puṃsavana* rites, it belongs to the woman alone.

Thus ends the second chapter in the fifth book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra. Now begins the third chapter in the fifth book. Now we shall explain the Ṛtuśānti (the pacification of the seasons). For the purpose of pacifying defects in the lunar day, weekday, asterism, yoga, karaṇa, or the ascendant, one should perform the propitiatory bath on either the fourth or the fifth day. 1.

In a temple or at home, having prepared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) measuring one *aratni* in size, rising higher and higher with eight *prasthas* of grain, half that amount of rice, and half that amount of sesame seeds; having drawn a lotus in its center and placed a water-pot wrapped with thread upon it, having sprinkled it with water consecrated silently, having placed the pot with the mantra "Brahma jajñānam," and having filled the pot with water using a *pavitra* and the section beginning with "Āpo vā idaṃ sarvam" along with mantras containing the word "water" (*ab-liṅga*).

Having filled [the vessel] and adorned it with perfumes and other offerings, and having placed a tuft of grass inside, one should collect earth from an elephant, a horse, a chariot, and an anthill; and from a cow-pen, a crossroads, a royal palace, the roots of *tulasī* and *bilva*, ||2|| from a temple, or from a mountain—one should take these five types of earth. From among those suitable for sacrifice, one should take the sprouts and the bark of the *pālāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *vaṭa*, and *plakṣa* trees, ||3|| as well as the *jambū*, *bilva*, *kapittha*, *āmra*, and *śirīṣa*—provided they are available. ||4||

In the manner thus described, having placed five types of earth, five sprouts, and five barks; having covered [the vessel] with nine gems and a little gold, wrapped it in a new cloth, scattered mango sprouts or bilva sprouts over it, sealed it with a coconut fruit, and concealed and adorned it with *darbha* grass, *dūrvā*, and so forth; having strewn [the ground] all around, meditated upon the Person who has lotus-like eyes (*puṇḍarīkākṣa*), and worshipped the water-pot (*kumbha*), one should worship the Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*)—six or eight in number—after first performing their formal selection (*varaṇa*), and likewise worship the Preceptor (*ācārya*). 5.

Those officiating priests (ṛtvij), holding onto the water-pitcher, shall mutter eight thousand or eight hundred repetitions of the Gāyatrī verse dedicated to Viṣṇu; they shall recite the beginnings of the Vedas, the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ," the two sections beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ" and "pavamānaḥ," the Varuṇa-sūkta, the Śrī-sūkta, the Puruṣa-sūkta, the five-fold pacification (pañcaśānti), and the section of verses beginning with "prācī. Regarding this, the Brāhmaṇa states: "With the words 'namo brahmaṇe,' he recites the concluding verse three times.
Having raised [the pitcher] with the syllable Om (praṇava), they shall mutter the verse beginning with "ābhir gīrbhiḥ."

Then, having sprinkled with the three mantras beginning with *devasya tvā* the woman who is adorned and seated on a large seat in the courtyard, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should bathe her with the three mantras beginning with *ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca*.
(8) Thereafter, they should have the woman consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

(9) Taking the cow-urine with the *gāyatrī*, the cow-dung with *gandhadvārā*, the milk with *āpyāyasva*, the curd with *dadhikrāvṇo*, the clarified butter with *śukramasi*, and the water from *kuśa* grass with *devasya tvā*—this constitutes the *pañcagavya*. (10)

Then, having smeared a square area the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung on a clean, level spot, and having brought a common fire from the house of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), one should perform the *agnimukha* rite according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra* and offer one hundred and eight fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood with the *Viṣṇusūkta*.
Likewise, one should offer food with the *Brahmasūkta* and clarified butter with the *Rudrasūkta*.
One should repeat each of these *sūktas* eighteen times; thus, the total number of offerings becomes one hundred and eight.
Then, one should offer twenty-eight oblations each of fuel-sticks, boiled rice, and clarified butter for the constellation of the season, using its respective mantra (14).
One should repeat the two mantras fourteen times (15).
Then, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds with the Tryambaka mantra (16).

Then he should offer eight oblations of clarified butter with the *Ghṛtasūkta*. (17) From the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the procedure is established up to the granting of the boon and the cow. (18) Then he gives sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests, especially to the teacher (*ācārya*). (19)
If one should thus perform the rite for peace (*śānti*), then the woman is freed from her fault; "May there be the pacification of all calamities," so said the Blessed Bodhāyana.
20. Thus ends the third chapter in the fifth book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the fourth chapter in the fifth book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for the clay bath (*mṛttikā-snāna*). A student (*brahmacārī*), a householder (*gṛhastha*), a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), or a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) should consecrate the earth with *dūrvā* grass while reciting: "O Goddess, trodden by horses, whose highest limit is a thousandfold. Then, taking a clod of earth from the riverbank with the verse, "Thou art lifted up," and taking *dūrvā* grass with the two verses beginning, "Growing forth from joint to joint," he should place the *dūrvā* on the clod of earth with the mantra, "O Clay, destroy my sin. Finally, [he should recite]: "From whatever we fear, O Indra... and "The Giver of Well-being, the Lord of the People... and "May Indra grant us well-being."

Having cast a clod of earth toward each direction in a clockwise manner with each of the six mantras beginning with *vṛddhaśravāḥ*, *trātāramindram*, *āpāntamanyuḥ*, and *paraṃ mṛtyo anu parehi*; having taken up a clod with the mantra *gandhadvārām*; having shown the clod to the sun with the mantra *udutyaṃ jātavedasam*; having circumambulated the head with the mantra *śrīrme bhajatvalakṣmīrme naśyatu*; having anointed the head with the mantra *sahasraśīrṣā*; [he anoints] the face with *viṣṇumukhāḥ*, the neck with *ojo grīvābhiḥ*, and [the chest with] *mahāṃ indro*.

"Vajrabāhuḥ" (the thunderbolt-armed one) for the two arms; "somānaṃ svaraṇam" (the sounding of Soma) for the armpits; "śarīraṃ yajñaśamalam" (the body, the essence of sacrifice) for the body; "nābhir me cittam" (my navel is consciousness) for the navel; "āpāntamanyuḥ" (he whose wrath is restrained) for the waist; "viṣṇo rarāṭam asi" (you are the forehead of Viṣṇu) for the back; "varuṇasya skambhanam asi" (you are the support of Varuṇa) for the penis; "ānandanandau" (joy and delight) for the testicles; "uruvorojaḥ" (the wide space is vigor) for the thighs; "ūrū aratnī" (the thighs are the forearms) for the knees; "jaṅghābhyām" (with the two shanks) for the two shanks; "caraṇaṃ pavitram" (the foot is the purifier) for the two feet; and with the two [verses], "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" and "trīṇi padā," for the two feet.

Having placed a clod of earth together with *dūrvā* grass upon his head while reciting "O Indra, being well-pleased... (*sajoṣā indra*), and having gone to a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) while reciting "Hiraṇyaśṛṅga... (*hiraṇyaśṛṅgam...*), he should sprinkle himself with water while reciting "May the waters and plants be friendly to us" (*sumitrā na āpa oṣadhayaḥ santu*). Taking a handful of water and pouring it down at the spot where the clod was placed, he should recite "May they be unfriendly to him" (*durmitrāstasmai bhūyāsuḥ*) for the first time; "He who hates us" (*yo 'smān dveṣṭi*) for the second; and "And whom we hate" (*yaṃ ca vayaṃ dviṣmaḥ*) for the third. He should then recite "Hiraṇyaśṛṅga... for the fourth time, and [finally] the three verses beginning with "The waters are indeed our source of bliss" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*) and "The golden-colored ones" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*).

Having performed the purification with the four verses beginning with *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ* and the entire section (*anuvāka*) beginning with the same, and having paid homage with the mantra *namo 'gnaye 'psumate*, he should repeat three times with water the verse *yad apāṃ krūram*. Having consecrated the water with the verse *imaṃ me gaṅge*, he should plunge into the water while reciting the *Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta* beginning with *ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca*. Having purified himself with the verse *eṣa bhūtasya*, and having drunk water with the verse *ārdraṃ jvalati*, he should plunge again with the verse *akāryakārī*. Then, having offered libations to the gods, the seers, and the ancestors, [he should remember] those who are born in his family who are childless.

"May those of my lineage who have died accept this water squeezed from the cloth offered by me. Having said this, he wrings out the cloth. Then, having sprinkled the cloth with the mantra "Pure for you are the offerings" (*śucī vo havyā*), and having taken the cloth with the mantra "Thee for the God" (*devasya tvā*), and having shaken it out with "It is shaken off" (*avadhūtam*), and having shown the sun to the cloth with "Upward that [sun]" (*ud u tyaṃ*) and "The bright one" (*citram*), and having put on his garment with "Bringing [the light], spreading [the web]" (*āvahantī vitanvānā*), he sips water twice. Then he says: "May all those beings, ghosts, spirits, and the like, who are a burden to the earth, depart. Without the opposition of any, let the rite of Brahman proceed."

"I shall begin. Having thus established and spread out a seat of *darbha* grass, and having performed breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) three times, one should mutter the *gāyatrī* mantra one hundred and eight times.

(2) A Brāhmaṇa becomes purified. (3) It is traditionally known that this destroys all sins, such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, the killing of a cow, violating the teacher’s bed, drinking liquor, and stealing gold. (4)
"Having abandoned that body, one should take refuge in Janārdana," so said the venerable Bodhāyana.
5. Thus ends the fourth chapter in the fifth book of the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
Now begins the fifth chapter of the fifth book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the marriage of the *arka* (the sun-flower). [This applies] to those who are mute, blind, deaf, and the like, to the mentally dull, and to those who have undergone a third marriage. 1.

On an auspicious day during the first half of the lunar fortnight, under a favorable constellation, in the forenoon, having gone out from the village toward the east or north into a place where there is a solitary *arka* plant, he should smear the ground to the north of it. Having bathed himself, caused the *arka* plant to be bathed, washed his feet, sipped water (*ācamana*), and adorned himself, he should perform the *nāndīmukha* rite in brief, have the *svasti-sūkta* recited, take some gold, mutter the verse "ā satyena," give [the gold] to the Brahmins, adorn the *arka* plant, touch it, and worship the Sun with the five verses beginning with "sūryo devīm. (2)
Then, having tied a garment and an auspicious thread to the *arka* tree, he should cause [the officiant] to recite, "An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity! The deity here is Āditya.

(3) Having established the fire-mouth according to the previously mentioned procedure, having strewn [grass] all around, having prepared the clarified butter (*ājya*), and having cleansed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, while meditating upon Āditya, he takes hold of the *arka* with the verse: "O hand, bestow immortality upon him.
(4) Then he circumambulates the fire clockwise with the verse: "O Agni, we [take refuge] in thee as in a fortress. (5)
Then, having touched the root of an *arka* plant, he gazes at the sun with the verse: "Enveloped by birds, multiform... (RV 1.50.10).

Then, having offered the *vyāhṛtis*, and having taken four portions of clarified butter in the *sruva*-ladle, he offers oblations with the verses: "Up from the darkness," "Up that [sun] which," and "The bright one" (RV 1.50.10; 1.50.1; 1.115.1).
Having taken another four portions, he offers the *manasvatī* oblation with the verse: "Mind is the light" (VS 23.2).
Furthermore, having taken four portions and having turned them twice with the *lāja* mantra, he offers them as oblations. 9.

Then, having offered the *vyāhṛti*s with the *sruva*-ladle and having concluded, he worships the Sun with two verses from the *vrata* hymns: "The undeceivable Savitṛ gazes upon all beings; thrice through his greatness, he has looked across the mid-air. 10.

Then, having touched cow's milk and the *arka* plant, and having recited the *āyuṣya* hymns, he eats it, sips water, and again worships the Sun with [the verse]: "Whatever we have done through thoughtlessness... 11.
Then, having removed the presiding deity of the Arka tree and having uprooted the Arka, he becomes pure by burning it in the fire with the Vyāhṛtis, bathing, and giving whatever he can.
(12) One should perform the *kadaḷī*-marriage immediately in this manner.
(13) Having cut down a *kadaḷī* tree, one remains impure for three nights. (14)

Moreover, they cite this example: "The marriage of a younger brother who is dull-witted or otherwise deficient is prescribed by the best of sages for the sake of the marriage [of the elder]. One should uproot that [younger brother] and burn him with the *vyāhṛti* mantras; then, having given gold according to one's ability and bathed, one becomes immediately pure. Furthermore, if a third wife should die quickly during a third marriage, a wise man should act in this manner. Likewise, a person should perform the marriage of a *rambhā* (plantain tree) by cutting it down right there; Bodhāyana declared that there shall be impurity (*sūtaka*) for three nights. Thus ends the fifth chapter of the fifth book in the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the sixth chapter of the fifth book.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the *pañcamī-śrāddha*. One should begin on the fifth lunar day following the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa, Māgha, or Proṣṭhapada, and perform it for a year.
On the preceding day, the performer of the vow should resolve: "I shall do this; I shall do that."

He invites Brahmins who are endowed with noble birth, lineage, sacred learning, and virtuous conduct. (3) He may also invite those who, though not related by kinship, are endowed with sacred learning and virtuous conduct.
(4) Regarding his monthly *śrāddha*, this much alone is the distinction [from the annual *śrāddha*]. (5)
Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers these oblations: "O Agni, life for thee," "O giver of life, Agni," "Born," "O Agni," and "O Lord of food, give us of food"—these four [verses].
(6) He also offers of the food with the *Viṣṇusūkta*. (7) Then he offers parched grains (*lāja*) verse by verse with the *Puruṣasūkta*. (8)
Then he offers oblations of sesame seeds with the verses "śaṃ no devīḥ," "prajāpate," "imaṃ yama," "prastaram," and with the vyāhṛtis. 9.

Then he offers oblations of clarified butter with the four verses beginning, "O Agni, you purify our lives," "O Agni, purify yourself," "He who [worships] you with a humble heart," and "May Dhātṛ, the Lord, grant us wealth. He continues from the end of that section up to the end of each verse: "Avert your wrath," "Lift up the highest [sin]," "Hear this my cry, O Varuṇa," "For that I entreat you," "Be thou to us, O Agni," "So be thou to us, O Agni," "Thou, O Agni, art the Unswerving One," "We have risen above the darkness," "Upwards that [Sun]," "The wonderful [light]," "Vaiśvānara for our aid," "Touched in heaven," and "Soma, the cow. With these six verses beginning with the *daśahotṛ* formulas, [he offers], O Brāhmaṇa.
With the ten verses beginning with "ekahotā," [the rite] from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established up to the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). 10.
Having strewn Darbha grass with its tips pointing south to the south of the fire, he offers three rice-balls upon them using the remnants of the food. 11.

On the tenth day, as in the wedding *śrāddha*, having performed the rite on the ground up to the end of the three mantras for the smearing of the leavings, he then sprinkles those [rice-balls] three times from right to left with water from the rinsing vessel, [reciting] "ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ. 12.
Then he gives the middle portion of the ball of rice to his wife with the words, "O Fathers, give me a hero.

(13) The wife eats it with the words, "O Fathers, bestow upon us a fetus, a boy adorned with a lotus wreath, so that there may be a man here who laughs"—thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "May male children indeed be born to me. (14) From the *jaya* offering onwards, the ritual is established up to the gift of the cow as a boon. (15)

If his father is still living, he should not offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*). Instead, having suppressed the *svadhā* mantras addressed to the ancestors, he goes out toward the east or the north and offers an oblation (*bali*) upon clumps of *darbha* grass at a crossroads, saying:
"Salutation to the female, salutation to the male, salutation to the youth, salutation to the white one with black teeth, salutation to the lord of sinners!

To those who destroy my offspring while dwelling in the village or in the forest—to them let there be salutation; I offer this oblation to them. May it be well with me; may they bestow offspring upon me. (16–18)

In ancient times, gods and humans existed together in this world. Then, by means of their ritual acts (*karma*), the gods went to heaven, while humans were left behind. Those among them who undertake such acts become united with the gods and with Brahman in that yonder world. Now, Manu proclaimed this rite known by the word *śrāddha* for the sake of the ultimate welfare of progeny. By performing the *śrāddha* on the fifth lunar day, one becomes possessed of abundant food; nor does one die childless. "By the *śrāddha*, the Vārṣyas went to heaven," so it is said. And it is also known: "Thou art born after [thy] progeny; that, O mortal, is thy immortality. (19–20)
One must exert effort toward that Prajāpati. Regarding this, they cite the following:
He who steals from others, he who cuts down young trees, he who eats while constantly showing malice toward staff-bearers, children, or elders;

he who hates the sons of others, he who plays with bound animals and the like, he who is merciless toward all living beings, and he who causes the neglect of ancestral rites—[these are those who do not attain the world of Prajāpati]. (21–23)

He shall be liable to execution or his son shall die; however, there is an expiation for them: silent, observing vows, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), with senses restrained, he should offer oblations with ghee from a ladle using the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras, or eight groups [of mantras] with ghee-rice, or while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*, he should give gold, cows, land, and sesame seeds. One who performs the *japa* while undergoing the *Kṛcchra* and *Atikṛcchra* penances is instantly liberated from that sin; thus said the venerable Bodhāyana. (24–26)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the fifth book of the Bodhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra;
now begins the seventh chapter in the fifth book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the oblation to the Lord of the Forest (*vanaspatihoma*). Having arrived together with Brāhmaṇas and kinsmen at a ripe *kramuka*, *panasa*, *nāḷikera*, or *kadaḷī* tree—or any other such tree—the sacrificer, having performed the rites from the marking of the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), scatters rice grains to the south of the fire. He then invokes the goddess Śrī-Sarasvatī with the mantra "May Indra bestow wisdom upon me," invokes the eight guardians of the directions beginning with the East, and worships four trees—such as the *kramuka* and others—in each of the four directions. Four...

Having placed medicinal herbs at their sides, having placed cow-dung at the base of the betel-nut tree with the verse "O Lord of the Forest, rise up," having scattered parched grain, flowers, and unbroken rice, and having placed a full vessel, he worships the field with the verse "O Lord of the Field. Then, having offered oblations of sacrificial food, clarified butter, and cooked rice with this entire section beginning with "The plants that have been born," "Those which are your abodes," "The plants whose king is Soma," "A hundred of you, O Mothers," "I have heard," "O you two most liberal givers," and "To the Lords of the Forest, Svāhā," he proceeds to the Jaya and other offerings.

"Having performed the rites up to the final sprinkling, having fed the Brāhmaṇas, having honored them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās), and having had the Adhvaryu recite the blessings with the *Svastisūkta*, he gives a fee to the Ācārya—thus says the venerable Bodhāyana.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the fifth book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.
Now begins the eighth chapter in the fifth book.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual for the pacification of Ugraratha. Beginning from the day of birth of Brāhmaṇas, Rājanyas, and Vaiśyas, in the sixtieth year, during the month of birth and under the birth asterism, one should prepare a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide smeared with cow-dung. In the south-eastern quarter of that mound, having fashioned an image of Mṛtyu (Death) out of two *niṣkas* of gold, and having performed the ritual installation of the water-pot (*kalaśa*) upon a heap of grain according to the rules, one should worship the image atop the pot with the mantra: "May Death depart; O Death, [do not strike] our offspring... (*apaitu mṛtyuḥ paraṃ mṛtyo mā naḥ toke*).

Having recited the *triyambaka* mantra one hundred and eight times, and having performed the rites from the marking of the sacrificial ground for the deity up to the conclusion of the *agnimukha*, he offers oblations of cooked food. Having recited the *puronuvākyā*, "mā no mahāntam," he offers with the *yājyā*, "mā nastoke. Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter, verse by verse, with the *ghṛtasūkta*. The procedure from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established as usual, up to the granting of the boon and the presentation of the cow.
Then, in front of the fire, he places the remnants of the oblation upon clumps of *dūrvā* grass.

(4) Sitting to the west of the fire facing east, having sprinkled himself with water from the jar while reciting the *Mṛtyusūkta*, the *Purāṇa-mantras*, and the *Yantras*, and having honored the teacher (*ācārya*), he should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) according to his ability and feed the Brahmins—so says the venerable Bodhāyana.
(5) Thus ends the eighth chapter in the fifth book of the *Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra*.

Now, therefore, the ritual for the *ugraratha-śānti*; now, therefore, the *vanaspati-homa*; now, therefore, the *pañcamī-śrāddha*; now, therefore, the marriage of the *arka* plant; now, therefore, the ritual for the clay-bath (*mṛttikā-snāna*); now, the seasonal pacification (*ṛtu-śānti*); now, the girl to be married; now, the procedure for the mouth-offering to the fire (*agnimukha-prayoga*). 8. Now, the procedure for the mouth-offering to the fire; now, the girl to be married; now, the seasonal pacification; now, therefore, the clay-bath; now, therefore, the marriage of the *arka* plant; now, therefore, the *pañcamī-śrāddha*; now, therefore, the *vanaspati-homa*; now, therefore, the ritual for the *ugraratha-śānti*. 9. Thus ends the fifth book (*praśna*) of the *Baudhāyanīya-gṛhyaśeṣa-sūtra*.
Thus ends the Bodhāyanīya Gṛhyaśeṣasūtra.
